reportDetails_organization: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees; United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
project_text:
Internally Displaced Population in South Sudan supported through provision of protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience, protection advocacy and achievement of solutions. The project aims to strengthen community and rights-based protection response for IDPs, IDP returnees and vulnerable persons within their host communities. The project will focus on providing physical and legal protection through advocacy, timely protection monitoring, life-saving protection response based on identified needs and solutions. The project will address Housing, Land and Property (HLP) rights issues through the provision of legal assistance, facilitate issuance of property and identity documents, and work with mediation mechanisms to support HLP related dispute resolution. Community-based networks will be utilized as part of the protection response to foster community buy in and ownership of protection. The project will use evidence-based planning to expand outreach and develop the capacity of displaced communities to cope, recover, contribute to and ultimately achieve solutions. Out of 1.6 million IDPs, 475,000 IDPs and IDP returnees will be supported with protection interventions and assistance in seven (7) states and an administrative areas. Recognising the protection concerns linked to food insecurity, the Agency activities also include a scaling-up of activities in South Sudan’s highly food insecure and prioritised locations, i.e. Pibor County, Akobo, Aweil South, Tonj East, Tonj North, Tonj South. There will be continuous advocacy and support in the area of law and policy with relevant government bodies such as the   Ministries of Justice Home Affairs, Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, and the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC) to ensure the centrality of protection, enact the “Protection and Assistance to Internally Displaced Persons Act 2018” (IDP) Bill, National Framework on Returns, and various HLP initiatives. The relevant line ministries will also receive capacity building and technical assistance. Building on UNHCR’s existing operational presence in Bentiu Bor, Juba, Malakal, Wau, Yambio, Yei, the Agency will continue to advance on the 2020 geographic expansion of IDP activities by leveraging both static and mobile presence through 15 partners to Central Equatoria, Unity, Upper Nile, Joinglei, Western Bahr El Ghazal, Northern Bahr El Ghazal, Lakes, Western Equatoira, Eastern Equatoris and Warrap. Response and monitoring will cover 19 identified priority counties and Pibor Administrative Area, including remote or hard to-reach areas, in full support to the Protection Cluster Strategy for mobile assessments and response. Partners comprise of both national and international organizations, with selection undertaken on the basis of their pre-existing presence, access to populations of concern and capacity to carry out static and remote protection monitoring and response. While not all proposed activity locations fall under the severity 3, 4 or 5 in terms of food insecurity, recognizing the fluidly and unpredictable nature of sub-national violence in South Sudan, UNHCR’s protection by presence approach requires presence in areas affected by conflict as well as areas of potential return in light of increased momentum in terms of solutions 
Resources and advocacy will focus primarily on protection response and solutions, either durable or transitional (where the former is not yet possible), including assessments on needs, risks, and intentions and feasibility of durable solutions, while also strengthening community-based structures, supporting HLP initiatives, promotion of livelihoods and peaceful coexistence. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will be a key component. A mobile tool was introduced in late 2019 that has enhanced data collection and triangulation of information through timely collection and analysis capabilities, which will further improve information products, leading to a more fitting risk-mitigation approach, reduced response time; while underpinning protection mainstreaming across other operational interventions, including of other Clusters.

reportDetails_organization: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees; United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
project_text:
Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2021, there are more than 314,000 refugees from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, including from Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic.

At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for long-term stability, some 357,500 South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since November 2017, 122,000 of those in 2020 alone. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan at this stage, the increase in numbers warrants a scaling-up of support following an area-based approach, including strengthening linkages with development actors, to help returnees and the communities they settle in live in safety and dignity, with greater security and services.

Refugees largely reside in conﬂict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction of basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.

Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will beneﬁt from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Speciﬁc protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identiﬁed at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with speciﬁc protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as veriﬁcation exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the eﬃciency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to beneﬁt from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

project_text:
CCCM Assistance to Displaced Persons in South Sudan The displacement context in South Sudan remains fluid. The country continues to
experience conflict and natural disaster-driven displacements in communities in both
urban and hard-to-reach areas. Former PoCs, including those which have been re-designated
as IDP sites, and collective sites continue to host IDPs in a protracted
displacement situation across the country. Concurrent with this are spontaneous returns
and relocations of IDPs and refugees, the latter of which can end up finding themselves in
a new displacement situation once back in South Sudan.

Of the 1.2 million persons in need in 2021 IOM CCCM will target 435,000 of the 900,000 to be targeted by the CCCM Cluster. IOM will focus on providing camp coordination and camp management under the following areas:

I. Static Operations in former PoCs (Including re-designated IDP sites) and Collective
Centers: As CM agency in Bentiu and Wau, and care and maintenance focal point in
Malakal, IOM will continue to improve the living conditions and meet the basic needs of
affected populations in these sites.

Output 1: IDPs living in former PoCs, IDP camps and CCs have improved and dignified
living conditions in support of a conducive environment for durable solutions and with
meaningful community engagement.

II. Deploy mobile teams to new and unreached displacement sites as prioritized by the
Cluster.

Output 2: Deployment of sustainable mobile responses to unmanaged sites to ensure
coordination and community ownership in camp-like settings or spontaneous settlements.

III. Co-Lead the Camp Coordination and Camp Management Cluster
Output 3: Fully functional, staffed, and well-managed CCCM Cluster supports partner
agencies in accountable CCCM responses and systems.

project_text:

project_text:
CCCM Assistance to Displaced Persons in South Sudan The displacement context in South Sudan remains fluid. The country continues to
experience conflict and natural disaster-driven displacements in communities in both
urban and hard-to-reach areas. Former PoCs, including those which have been re-designated
as IDP sites, and collective sites continue to host IDPs in a protracted
displacement situation across the country. Concurrent with this are spontaneous returns
and relocations of IDPs and refugees, the latter of which can end up finding themselves in
a new displacement situation once back in South Sudan.

Of the 1.2 million persons in need in 2021 IOM CCCM will target 435,000 of the 900,000 to be targeted by the CCCM Cluster. IOM will focus on providing camp coordination and camp management under the following areas:

I. Static Operations in former PoCs (Including re-designated IDP sites) and Collective
Centers: As CM agency in Bentiu and Wau, and care and maintenance focal point in
Malakal, IOM will continue to improve the living conditions and meet the basic needs of
affected populations in these sites.

Output 1: IDPs living in former PoCs, IDP camps and CCs have improved and dignified
living conditions in support of a conducive environment for durable solutions and with
meaningful community engagement.

II. Deploy mobile teams to new and unreached displacement sites as prioritized by the
Cluster.

Output 2: Deployment of sustainable mobile responses to unmanaged sites to ensure
coordination and community ownership in camp-like settings or spontaneous settlements.

III. Co-Lead the Camp Coordination and Camp Management Cluster
Output 3: Fully functional, staffed, and well-managed CCCM Cluster supports partner
agencies in accountable CCCM responses and systems.

project_text: Apoyo integral para la mejora del acceso a la educación de calidad y de la permanencia escolar de alumnos y docentes Este proyecto pretende mejorar las condiciones ofrecidas en las escuelas referentes a alimentación escolar (para 406,338 niños, niñas y adolescentes- NNAs), disponibilidad de material educativo para incentivar el acceso y la asistencia regular de los estudiantes (1,250,000 NNA). También pretende mejorar las condiciones de trabajo y la capacidad técnica de los docentes mediante actividades de formación y distribución de incentivos (23,734 docentes) que reduzcan el absentismo y la deserción de los docentes. El proyecto ofrece soluciones a 150,000 NNAs que han abandonado el sistema escolar para que se reincorporen a la escuela o a oportunidades de aprendizaje alternativas. Igualmente se ofrecen actividades de apoyo socioemocinal para 300,000 NNA. También se pretende fortalecer las capacidades del sector para alcanzar a 400,000 con actividades de educación a distancia y llegar a 70,000 adolescentes con actividades de nivelación escolar y la promoción de habilidades para la vida. Todas estas actividades se desarrollarán primando un enfoque intersectorial que tenga en cuenta aspectos de protección infantil, WASH, nutrición y componentes de sensibilización dirigidos a promover cambios de conducta, todo ello con un enfoque inclusivo y de protección de derechos.

reportDetails_organization: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
project_text:
Restoring livelihoods of crisis affected population in Syria through light rehabilitation of irrigation infrastructure at community level The United Nations (UN) estimates that the number of crisis-affected people in need of humanitarian assistance in Syria is 14.2 million, of which 6 million are in acute need. The above figure of people in need includes 6.7 million protracted internally displaced persons (IDPs); estimated 320,000 spontaneous IDPs return; 75,000 refugees return; 438,000 Palestine refugees and the rest overburdened host communities.  

More than 75% of the number of people in need of humanitarian assistance are accessible from within Syria. Overall, 12.4 million of people are estimated to be food insecure (including 1.27 million severely food insecure) and 1.9 million people at risk of food insecurity. 

In this context, FAO has designed a project to assist 120,000 vulnerable crisis-affected food insecure farming households (equivalent to 750,000 people) in Syria. About 15% of the targeted householders will be selected from those who receive food support to help them shift from depending on food assistance to producing their own food and enhancing their self-sufficiency. The objective of the proposed action is to protect and enhance the livelihoods of vulnerable farmers and IDPs through the restoration of critical irrigation infrastructures to increase household food production and security. The project outputs include:

•	Output 1: Local small-scale irrigation infrastructures in the targeted governorates are assessed and light rehabilitation undertaken. 
•	Output 2: Capacity of technical staff and relevant stakeholders strengthened.

A training programme on enhancing irrigation management, water use efficiency in small-scale irrigation, agricultural land management will be based on FAO standards and approaches. It is expected that stakeholders and farmers (water user association) will join this training. 

This project is expected to contribute to increasing access to irrigation water for crisis-affected farmers and their families in the targeted areas through the light rehabilitation of local small scale irrigation infrastructure. Cultivation and other agricultural practices, including livestock and animal feed production, will consequently benefit from the water supply plans as an emergency response to crisis. The proposed intervention will strengthen household food production capacities and knowledge and address immediate food security and nutrition needs through increasing local availability and supply of food.  This may in turn promote flourishing of agricultural based livelihoods in the rural community, which would contribute to social cohesion, peace and stability. The project seeks to utilize intensive labour in order to maximize community participation and inject cash into the local community.  
FAO as part of the CWG will discuss at project level with the group to identify the rate, modality, etc. of the cash intervention to be in line with the CWG and to achieve the purpose of the intervention

project_text:
Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2021, there are more than 314,000 refugees from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, including from Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic.

At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for long-term stability, some 357,500 South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since November 2017, 122,000 of those in 2020 alone. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan at this stage, the increase in numbers warrants a scaling-up of support following an area-based approach, including strengthening linkages with development actors, to help returnees and the communities they settle in live in safety and dignity, with greater security and services.

Refugees largely reside in conﬂict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction of basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.

Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will beneﬁt from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Speciﬁc protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identiﬁed at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with speciﬁc protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as veriﬁcation exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the eﬃciency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to beneﬁt from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

Contribution to various operations based on Agreement QZA-18/0302 Addendum 1/2021. Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2021, there are more than 314,000 refugees from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, including from Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic.

At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for long-term stability, some 357,500 South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since November 2017, 122,000 of those in 2020 alone. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan at this stage, the increase in numbers warrants a scaling-up of support following an area-based approach, including strengthening linkages with development actors, to help returnees and the communities they settle in live in safety and dignity, with greater security and services.

Refugees largely reside in conﬂict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction of basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.

Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will beneﬁt from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Speciﬁc protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identiﬁed at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with speciﬁc protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as veriﬁcation exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the eﬃciency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to beneﬁt from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

project_text: Apoyo integral para la mejora del acceso a la educación de calidad y de la permanencia escolar de alumnos y docentes Este proyecto pretende mejorar las condiciones ofrecidas en las escuelas referentes a alimentación escolar (para 406,338 niños, niñas y adolescentes- NNAs), disponibilidad de material educativo para incentivar el acceso y la asistencia regular de los estudiantes (1,250,000 NNA). También pretende mejorar las condiciones de trabajo y la capacidad técnica de los docentes mediante actividades de formación y distribución de incentivos (23,734 docentes) que reduzcan el absentismo y la deserción de los docentes. El proyecto ofrece soluciones a 150,000 NNAs que han abandonado el sistema escolar para que se reincorporen a la escuela o a oportunidades de aprendizaje alternativas. Igualmente se ofrecen actividades de apoyo socioemocinal para 300,000 NNA. También se pretende fortalecer las capacidades del sector para alcanzar a 400,000 con actividades de educación a distancia y llegar a 70,000 adolescentes con actividades de nivelación escolar y la promoción de habilidades para la vida. Todas estas actividades se desarrollarán primando un enfoque intersectorial que tenga en cuenta aspectos de protección infantil, WASH, nutrición y componentes de sensibilización dirigidos a promover cambios de conducta, todo ello con un enfoque inclusivo y de protección de derechos.

project_text: Assistance humanitaire en Abris et en Biens non-alimentaires (BNA) pour les sinistrés d'inondation au Niger. Dans le cadre de HRP 2021 au travers de ce projet, l'OIM vise à apporter un appui au gouvernement du Niger dans le cadre de la réponse d'urgence aux personnes sinistrées des inondations. Ce projet propose de répondre aux besoins des ménages sinistrés à travers les requêtes qui seront exprimées par le Gouvernement au travers du Ministère de l’Action Humanitaire et de la Gestion des Catastrophes (MAH/GC). Cette réponse s’adressera uniquement aux ménages vulnérables victimes d’inondations dont les abris ou cases auront été endommagés et/ou ceux dont les Biens non-alimentaires (BNA) auront été emportés par les eaux. Le présent projet poursuit comme objectif d’atteindre 8 000 ménages soit 56 000 personnes à travers tout le Niger prioritairement dans les régions de Niamey, Dosso et Diffa. En coordination avec le MAH/GC et la Direction Générale de la Protection Civile (DGPC), l’OIM mettra à disposition 8 000 kits abris et 8 000 kits de Biens non-alimentaires qui seront distribués aux ménages sinistrés. En plus des kits, l’OIM couvrira les coûts liés à la logistique et à la distribution des kits. Ce projet ne couvrira pas une zone ou région donnée mais permettra d’intervenir là où les besoins se présentent et aussi de pouvoir compléter les activités des autres acteurs en cas de besoin en tant que prestataire de dernier recours pour la réponse humanitaire en abri d'urgence et BNA. L’OIM en tant que Co-Lead du Groupe de Travail Abri et Bien non-alimentaire (GTABNA) avec le MAH/GC s'assurera que les activités sont menées en étroite coordination avec les autres partenaires humanitaires membres du GTABNA pour la réponse en abri et Biens non-alimentaires pour les ménages sinistrés des inondations au Niger. Conformément à la logique de la stratégie du Secteur abris/BNA et en fonction de la faisabilité, les interventions pourront se faire en transferts monétaires conditionnels. Cela réduirait considérablement les coûts logistiques qui sont très élevés en période hivernale à cause du mauvais état des routes mais aussi et permettrait aussi de résoudre en partie le problème d’accès lié à l'insécurité qui souvent retarde les interventions. Enfin, la mise en œuvre du présent projet fera l’objet d’un suivi régulier de la qualité des interventions réalisées mais aussi de l’implication des bénéficiaires et autorités locales. Pour cela, les feedbacks de la communauté cible seront collectés à travers des évaluations post-distribution et des séances de discussion de groupe séparées par genre et âge avant et après l'assistance. Aussi, en tant qu’acteur humanitaire, l'OIM et ses partenaires de mise en œuvre s’assureront que ses actions n’induisent aucune tension ou problème dans la zone et n’exposent pas les bénéficiaires. A cet effet la phase d'évaluation de besoins sera réalisée de commun accord avec les populations dans les communes ciblées, les sessions d'information sur le projet seront organisées à l'attention de communauté bénéficiaires, le mecanisme de ciblage de bénéficiaires sera réalisé en etroite collabation avec les autorités au niveau local (do no harm). Une collaboration étroite faite avec les acteurs de protection pour un suivi de pret de toutes questions de protection. Le cout total du projet sera de 4.650.000 USD.

project_text:
Contribuer à l’amélioration des conditions de vie des populations vulnérables au Niger - RRM Le mécanisme RRM est financé par ECHO (le RRM est une priorité dans le HIP 2020 et dans la version préliminaire du HIP 2021) et USAID, avec le soutien de l’UNICEF pour la fourniture de kits Abri et BNA supplémentaire. Les secteurs d'intervention RRM sont les ABNA, l'EHA, la protection et la sécurité alimentaire. Le projet proposé pour 2021 vise à répondre aux besoins urgents des populations les plus vulnérables déplacées à la suite d'un choc depuis moins de 3mois (et/ou accessibles depuis moins de 3 mois). La réponse du Consortium RRM commence par une veille humanitaire et une série d'évaluations multisectorielles (MSA) afin d'identifier les secteurs dans lesquels des intervention d'urgence sont nécessaires pour chaque site accueillant des déplacés. Un réseau de points focaux est mis en place par chaque partenaire. Une MSA (évaluation multisectorielle) ou une évaluation flash sont ensuite déclenchées dans les 24h suivant la confirmation de l'alerte, et les rapports d'évaluation sont transmis à la communauté humanitaire à travers OCHA dans les 72h pour assurer une coordination avec les partenaires et permettre leur positionnement afin couvrir des besoins complémentaires ou quand l'intervention n'est pas du ressort du RRM, le cas échéant. Si les seuils de déclenchement sont atteints, une intervention RRM est lancée, et des consultations avec les communautés et leaders communautaires prennent place pour prioriser les besoins. Le ciblage des bénéficiaires se fait sur des critères de vulnérabilité établis, en prenant en compte les ménages hôtes affectés par l'arrivée des nouveaux ménages et de manière participative pour faire en sorte de réduire les risques de tensions communautaires. Dans les 30 jours qui suivent l'intervention, une évaluation post intervention prend place pour mesure l'impact et la satisfaction des populations supportées. La stratégie protection du Consortium RRM repose sur une approche transversale qui vise à renforcer les extrants de l'intervention en termes de réduction des risques et des vulnérabilités. Cela se base sur des évaluations rapides de protection (ERP) qui ont lieu en même temps ou juste après la réalisation d’une MSA. L’objectif des ERP est d'identifier les problématiques prioritaires de protection et donc de guider la réponse.
En fonction des cas, le Consortium assurera le référencement ou/et la prise en charge des cas de protection. L’assistance de protection consiste en une assistance individuelle (API) composée d’un appui matériel ou en transfert monétaire (BNA selon les besoins de la personne, ou prise en charge de frais nécessaires pour la personne mais ne pouvant être couverts par le ménage, comme les frais médicaux, les frais de transport vers un CSI etc.) et d’un référencement vers des services de prise en charge médicale, juridique, et de santé mentale.
Les acteurs humanitaires et étatiques qui ne travaillent pas dans les secteurs de la protection verront leurs capacités renforcées, afin qu’ils puissent bien/mieux prendre en compte les aspects de protection dans leur travail avec les populations déplacées suite à un conflit ou une catastrophe naturelle.
Les interventions du Consortium se font avec une prise en compte du COVID-19 pour préserver les agents et les bénéficiaires des risques de transmission du virus. Des SOP ont été mises en place pour le Consortium afin d’harmoniser les pratiques, en ligne avec les recommandations des autorités nigériennes et de l’OMS. Des séances de sensibilisation ont lieu. En cas de besoin, les activités de groupe sont reportées et/ou adaptées pour réduire les risques. Les partenaire font aussi en sorte d’adapter leur réponse à l’évolution de la situation grâce à un suivi de la progression du COVID au Niger.

reportDetails_organization: European Commission's Humanitarian Aid and Civil Protection Department
project_text:
Life-saving integrated food security and livelihoods support for Somaliland and Puntland communities The project is responding to humanitarian needs of drought, covid 19 and locust affected community in target locations of Puntland and Somaliland through cash injection to address the immediate food needs of the people. Cash transfer programming will be used to reach households that are in IPC 3 and above. While focusing on life-saving interventions, the project will also support recovery and resilience building of the people where possible. 
Findings from FSNAU  2020 post-Gu seasonal food security and nutrition assessment conducted across Somalia during July and August 2020 indicate that Due to the combined effects of widespread and severe flooding, Desert Locust infestation, socioeconomic impacts of COVID-19 and the cumulative impacts of previous shocks, up to 2.1 million people across Somalia are expected to face food consumption gaps or depletion of assets indicative of Crisis (IPC Phase 3)1 or worse outcomes through December 2020 in the absence of humanitarian assistance. In addition, 849 900 children under the age of five are likely to be acutely malnourished through August 2021. 
Desert Locust continues to pose a serious risk of damage to both pasture and crops at least until the end of 2020. The 2020 Deyr (October-December) rainfall season is likely to be below average to average across the country, which could lead to drought and trigger a worsening of the humanitarian situation if the 2021 Gu (April-June) season rainfall is also delayed or performs poorly.

The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the Somalis’s economy is significant impacting on poor urban and IDP households, as well as pastoralists in northern Somalia, namely Puntland and Somaliland.  External remittance flows from the Somali diaspora constitutes 1.4-2 billion USD every year and contribute 23-32 percent of Gross Domestic Product, according to the World Bank. However, after the onset of COVID-19, money vendors report that the volume of cash transactions declined approximately 30-40 percent from March to June 2020
Improving food availability through support to agricultural production in Awdal and Nugal  and introducing it in Sool and Sanag regions of Somalia is seen as an entry point to diversify pastoral livelihoods of those two regions. This plan involves also supporting communities’ recovery and livelihoods diversification interventions through livestock support with vaccination and treatment and Improving Agricultural Production/Food Security. 

Livestock production was severely affected by the drought leading to substantially reduced herds; which is the country’s prime investment especially in rural communities. The mains reasons leading to the death were water shortages and lack of pasture.  In view of this situation the project will explore fodder production combined with campaigns on livestock treatment. These include promotion of carrying capacity for sustained production. These actions will be coupled with Cash for Work activities which will be used for communal asset development linked to crop and animal husbandry. 

In times of shock and more critical food insecurity, Oxfam will utilize cash and voucher assistance to reach to the most affected households impacted by triple threats of drought, covid or locust  to meet the immediate emergency needs of at risk communities. cash is the preferred option for Oxfam to reach to people in remote areas, it is faster, sacure and easy to cover at scale. cash and voucher assistance also helps people to have flexibility on their needs and decision, choice and have multiplier effect on the economy

External remittance flows from the Somali diaspora constitutes 1.4-2 billion USD every year and contribute 23-32 percent of Gross Domestic Product, according to the World Bank. However, after the onset of COVID-19, money vendors report that the volume of cash transactions declined approximately 30-40 percent from March to June 2020
Improving food availability through support to agricultural production in Awdal and Nugal  and introducing it in Sool and Sanag regions of Somalia is seen as an entry point to diversify pastoral livelihoods of those two regions. This plan involves also supporting communities’ recovery and livelihoods diversification interventions through livestock support with vaccination and treatment and Improving Agricultural Production/Food Security. 

Livestock production was severely affected by the drought leading to substantially reduced herds; which is the country’s prime investment especially in rural communities. The mains reasons leading to the death were water shortages and lack of pasture.  In view of this situation the project will explore fodder production combined with campaigns on livestock treatment. These include promotion of carrying capacity for sustained production. These actions will be coupled with Cash for Work activities which will be used for communal asset development linked to crop and animal husbandry. 

In times of shock and more critical food insecurity, Oxfam will utilize cash and voucher assistance to reach to the most affected households impacted by triple threats of drought, covid or locust  to meet the immediate emergency needs of at risk communities. cash is the preferred option for Oxfam to reach to people in remote areas, it is faster, sacure and easy to cover at scale. cash and voucher assistance also helps people to have flexibility on their needs and decision, choice and have multiplier effect on the economy

project_text:
Provision of timely, equitable and integrated food security and livelihoods services to the conflict, epidemic and natural disaster affected populations in South Sudan South Sudan protracted crises have left 7.5 million people in dire need of humanitarian assistance in 2020 despite the signature of the Revitalized peace agreement, and continues to face conflict, natural disasters and climate instability, food insecurity, and lack of basic services. According to the latest IPC analysis for South Sudan published in December 2020, an estimated 7.7 million people are expected to experience acute food insecurity and worse (IPC 3, 4 and 5) in 2021. 
SI has started to implement its humanitarian response in South Sudan in 2006. Its long lasting presence has contributed to building a wealth of experience in Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) and Food, Security and Livelihoods (FSL). This allowed SI to pilot large-scale unconditional cash transfers, seeds distribution amongst IDPs and host communities in Western Bahr El Ghazal, Upper Nile, Jonglei and Central Equatoria states. SI aims at supporting the most vulnerable households, who are struggling to restore their livelihoods, in order to help them to improve their food security situation. In FSL specifically, this will mean emergency livelihood response to quickly replenish the destroyed assets. In second step SI will complement the response, wherever possible, with capacity building to allow for income generation and longer-term food preservation. SI will therefore aim at providing timely, equitable and integrated food security and livelihoods services to the conflict, epidemic and natural disaster affected populations of South Sudan.

project_text:
Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

destinationObjects_Project.name: Provision of Life-Saving Shelter and Life Sustaining NFI to Vulnerable Populations in Somalia
project_text:
Provision of Life-Saving Shelter and Life Sustaining NFI to Vulnerable Populations in Somalia Due to the ongoing humanitarian crisis, Shelter and Non-Food Items (SNFI) needs remain consistently high, with an estimated 3.1 million Somalis with SNFI needs according to the Humanitarian Needs Overview 2021, especially in Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) sites where many households (HHs) live in makeshift shelters. Oftentimes, these makeshift shelters do not provide adequate privacy and protection against weather elements, whilst a lack of tenure security, random evictions and vulnerability to fires further exacerbate the shelter needs of IDPs. It is therefore estimated that around one-third of the Somali population lack essential NFIs. 

Therefore, SNFI needs are the subject of much collaborative efforts; Collective Outcome 2 of the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) aims ‘to reduce the risks and vulnerabilities, and build resilience of displaced and host communities to reach durable solutions’, whilst Specific Objective 2.2 aims to scale-up and provide CCCM, WASH, education, health, nutrition, shelter and NFI services for 1.6 million people in established IDP sites across 68 districts by the end of 2021.

For the 2021 HRP, 75,000 individuals (12,500 households with an average of 6 individuals per household) will receive NFI support through a mixed-methods strategy of in-kind contingency stocks provision to be undertaken with contingency stock partners and direct implementation of Cash-Based Intervention (CBI) for NFI needs. A further 75,000 individuals will receive shelter support through emergency shelter, in-kind shelter kits, and CBI for shelter needs. Finally, 15,000 individuals will receive infrastructure support, both in-kind and through CBI. The transfer mechanism for CBI   will be evidence-based and linked to market assessment and needs analysis. The breakdown of the planned intervention is as follows: (1) the provision of contingency stock with in-kind NFI and shelter kits for 10,000 households (NFI: 7,500, Shelter: 2,500), available for distribution nationwide by shelter cluster partners where need arises; (2) emergency/transitional shelter (Emergency: 7,500; Transitional: 2,500) and NFI (5,000) support to newly displaced IDPs in the Gedo and Bay region targeting 15,000 households; (3) infrastructure support to 2,500 households in Gedo and Bay region.

project_text:
Provision of lifesaving assistance and sustainable solutions through safe Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services, for people in crises and their host communities in multiple regions in Somalia. IOM WASH is proposing to contribute to the continuation and restoration of access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to overall 380,000 beneficiaries from vulnerable IDP and host-communities in multiple regions in Somalia. 

Specifically, the project will target 228,000 Nondisplaced people (children 107,160; men 41,040; women 36,480; elderly 9,120 and disabled 34,200) and 152,000 displaced populations (children 71,440; men 27,360; women 24,320; elderly 6,080 and disabled 22,800). 

IOM will rehabilitate 50 strategic water sources for multi-use that will provide continued, equitable, safe, sufficient and sustainable water to regions, targeted by the cluster, prone to natural disasters. 

IOM further proposes to construct 3,000 new emergency sanitation facilities (following cluster specifications) targeting populations without access to basic sanitation and hygiene.

The project will also strengthen the capacity of the Federal Government of Somalia and Federal Members States, community leaders and water committees/technicians for better coordination with government authorities and communities and sustainability of the constructed/ rehabilitated WASH infrastructures. In addition, the project will nurture community participation in good hygiene practices through training and community sensitization campaigns.  All trainings, awareness raising and capacity building activities will follow national guidelines on COVID-19 preventive measures, e.g. on physical distancing, to avoid mass gatherings and minimize risks of exposure.

The project is aligned with protection mainstreaming to ensure safety and dignity of affected populations without causing harm. Affected populations and all relevant stakeholders including men, women, boys, girls, elderly and people with disability will be involved in decision making throughout the project activities/cycle. 

Furthermore, the project will be a part of an IOM integrated emergency response program and resilience building, where possible, efforts will be made to integrate IOM health, nutrition, shelter, CCCM and protection activities.

reportDetails_organization: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees; United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
project_text:
Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2021, there are more than 314,000 refugees from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, including from Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic.

At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for long-term stability, some 357,500 South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since November 2017, 122,000 of those in 2020 alone. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan at this stage, the increase in numbers warrants a scaling-up of support following an area-based approach, including strengthening linkages with development actors, to help returnees and the communities they settle in live in safety and dignity, with greater security and services.

Refugees largely reside in conﬂict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction of basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.

Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will beneﬁt from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Speciﬁc protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identiﬁed at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with speciﬁc protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as veriﬁcation exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the eﬃciency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to beneﬁt from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

reportDetails_organization: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees; United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
project_text:
Internally Displaced Population in South Sudan supported through provision of protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience, protection advocacy and achievement of solutions. The project aims to strengthen community and rights-based protection response for IDPs, IDP returnees and vulnerable persons within their host communities. The project will focus on providing physical and legal protection through advocacy, timely protection monitoring, life-saving protection response based on identified needs and solutions. The project will address Housing, Land and Property (HLP) rights issues through the provision of legal assistance, facilitate issuance of property and identity documents, and work with mediation mechanisms to support HLP related dispute resolution. Community-based networks will be utilized as part of the protection response to foster community buy in and ownership of protection. The project will use evidence-based planning to expand outreach and develop the capacity of displaced communities to cope, recover, contribute to and ultimately achieve solutions. Out of 1.6 million IDPs, 475,000 IDPs and IDP returnees will be supported with protection interventions and assistance in seven (7) states and an administrative areas. Recognising the protection concerns linked to food insecurity, the Agency activities also include a scaling-up of activities in South Sudan’s highly food insecure and prioritised locations, i.e. Pibor County, Akobo, Aweil South, Tonj East, Tonj North, Tonj South. There will be continuous advocacy and support in the area of law and policy with relevant government bodies such as the   Ministries of Justice Home Affairs, Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, and the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC) to ensure the centrality of protection, enact the “Protection and Assistance to Internally Displaced Persons Act 2018” (IDP) Bill, National Framework on Returns, and various HLP initiatives. The relevant line ministries will also receive capacity building and technical assistance. Building on UNHCR’s existing operational presence in Bentiu Bor, Juba, Malakal, Wau, Yambio, Yei, the Agency will continue to advance on the 2020 geographic expansion of IDP activities by leveraging both static and mobile presence through 15 partners to Central Equatoria, Unity, Upper Nile, Joinglei, Western Bahr El Ghazal, Northern Bahr El Ghazal, Lakes, Western Equatoira, Eastern Equatoris and Warrap. Response and monitoring will cover 19 identified priority counties and Pibor Administrative Area, including remote or hard to-reach areas, in full support to the Protection Cluster Strategy for mobile assessments and response. Partners comprise of both national and international organizations, with selection undertaken on the basis of their pre-existing presence, access to populations of concern and capacity to carry out static and remote protection monitoring and response. While not all proposed activity locations fall under the severity 3, 4 or 5 in terms of food insecurity, recognizing the fluidly and unpredictable nature of sub-national violence in South Sudan, UNHCR’s protection by presence approach requires presence in areas affected by conflict as well as areas of potential return in light of increased momentum in terms of solutions 
Resources and advocacy will focus primarily on protection response and solutions, either durable or transitional (where the former is not yet possible), including assessments on needs, risks, and intentions and feasibility of durable solutions, while also strengthening community-based structures, supporting HLP initiatives, promotion of livelihoods and peaceful coexistence. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will be a key component. A mobile tool was introduced in late 2019 that has enhanced data collection and triangulation of information through timely collection and analysis capabilities, which will further improve information products, leading to a more fitting risk-mitigation approach, reduced response time; while underpinning protection mainstreaming across other operational interventions, including of other Clusters.

reportDetails_organization: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
project_text:
Internally Displaced Population in South Sudan supported through provision of protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience, protection advocacy and achievement of solutions. The project aims to strengthen community and rights-based protection response for IDPs, IDP returnees and vulnerable persons within their host communities. The project will focus on providing physical and legal protection through advocacy, timely protection monitoring, life-saving protection response based on identified needs and solutions. The project will address Housing, Land and Property (HLP) rights issues through the provision of legal assistance, facilitate issuance of property and identity documents, and work with mediation mechanisms to support HLP related dispute resolution. Community-based networks will be utilized as part of the protection response to foster community buy in and ownership of protection. The project will use evidence-based planning to expand outreach and develop the capacity of displaced communities to cope, recover, contribute to and ultimately achieve solutions. Out of 1.6 million IDPs, 475,000 IDPs and IDP returnees will be supported with protection interventions and assistance in seven (7) states and an administrative areas. Recognising the protection concerns linked to food insecurity, the Agency activities also include a scaling-up of activities in South Sudan’s highly food insecure and prioritised locations, i.e. Pibor County, Akobo, Aweil South, Tonj East, Tonj North, Tonj South. There will be continuous advocacy and support in the area of law and policy with relevant government bodies such as the   Ministries of Justice Home Affairs, Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, and the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC) to ensure the centrality of protection, enact the “Protection and Assistance to Internally Displaced Persons Act 2018” (IDP) Bill, National Framework on Returns, and various HLP initiatives. The relevant line ministries will also receive capacity building and technical assistance. Building on UNHCR’s existing operational presence in Bentiu Bor, Juba, Malakal, Wau, Yambio, Yei, the Agency will continue to advance on the 2020 geographic expansion of IDP activities by leveraging both static and mobile presence through 15 partners to Central Equatoria, Unity, Upper Nile, Joinglei, Western Bahr El Ghazal, Northern Bahr El Ghazal, Lakes, Western Equatoira, Eastern Equatoris and Warrap. Response and monitoring will cover 19 identified priority counties and Pibor Administrative Area, including remote or hard to-reach areas, in full support to the Protection Cluster Strategy for mobile assessments and response. Partners comprise of both national and international organizations, with selection undertaken on the basis of their pre-existing presence, access to populations of concern and capacity to carry out static and remote protection monitoring and response. While not all proposed activity locations fall under the severity 3, 4 or 5 in terms of food insecurity, recognizing the fluidly and unpredictable nature of sub-national violence in South Sudan, UNHCR’s protection by presence approach requires presence in areas affected by conflict as well as areas of potential return in light of increased momentum in terms of solutions 
Resources and advocacy will focus primarily on protection response and solutions, either durable or transitional (where the former is not yet possible), including assessments on needs, risks, and intentions and feasibility of durable solutions, while also strengthening community-based structures, supporting HLP initiatives, promotion of livelihoods and peaceful coexistence. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will be a key component. A mobile tool was introduced in late 2019 that has enhanced data collection and triangulation of information through timely collection and analysis capabilities, which will further improve information products, leading to a more fitting risk-mitigation approach, reduced response time; while underpinning protection mainstreaming across other operational interventions, including of other Clusters.

project_text: Targeted support to displaced persons with specific needs with lifesaving non-food items and emergency shelter in hard to reach areas and areas of IDP returns The UNHCR ES/NFI project for 2021 is focused on responding to the humanitarian needs of internally displaced persons (IDPs) and ensure humanitarian standards are maintained. IDPs continue to be exposed dire living conditions with limited livelihood options, the lack of access to markets and often more than one displacement.  The need for provision of basic and domestic items remains a priority. Families are often displaced without substantial household items, fleeing with little more than they can carry. Inadequate shelter may also lead to increased protection risks and susceptibility to diseases. In addition, populations in situations of protracted displacement require replenishment of assistance to ensure basic humanitarian needs are met. With COVID-19 preventive measures mainstreamed, considerations for decongestion of sites and number of persons per shelter shall be taken into account in consultation with the CCCM cluster and other stakeholders. Emergency stocks need to be replenished and prepositioned on a regular basis in order to allow rapid response to the identified protection and assistance needs. UNHCR’s material assistance will continue to be targeted and protection focused, to ensure that the most vulnerable displaced households are not left without basic material support, including the specific needs of women and girls are catered for. In 2021, UNHCR will continue to identify the most vulnerable IDPs (up to 30% of the priority target) through protection monitoring, community-based mechanisms, and outreach efforts, to implement targeted interventions aimed at reducing the burden on communities. UNHCR both directly and through partners, will leverage their expanded operational coverage to ensure protection monitoring and participation of populations of concern in RPAs, IRNA and RRM. These assessments, ES/NFI analysis tools, and inter-cluster discussions will reinforce the centrality of affected persons to decision-making, and help determine the most appropriate methodology of distribution, taking each unique context into consideration. The project will focus on delivery of timely life-saving activities, streamlining prevention-oriented initiatives including COVID-19 preventive measures, evidence-based planning, and strengthening community-based protection for capacity development of displaced communities to cope, recover, contribute to and achieve solutions. In efforts to minimize risks including SGBV, prevention/response activities will continue with a focus on community engagement, strengthening referrals and prevention with awareness raising. At the same time, there is an increasing trend and willingness of IDPs to return to their homes. It is anticipated that more development-oriented programming will be implemented in South Sudan considering the R-ARCSS, 2019-2020 UN Cooperation Framework, and the 2018-2022 National Development Strategy for South Sudan. In order to increase the absorption capacity of receiving communities, UNHCR will focus support at the community level, maintaining targeted assistance at the individual level to persons with specific needs (PSNs) and the most vulnerable. UNHCR will use its age, gender and diversity policy and ES/NFI analysis tools, to ensure the entire population is reached, the voices of marginalised members of the community are taken into consideration and the response does not place any person at heightened risk. In 2021, UNHCR aims to reach 50% of the projected IDP population equal to 800,000 persons with targeted assistance to 200,000 persons. IDP and refugee returnees often face additional challenges of finding their houses damaged, destroyed and/or occupied. The need for decent shelter in areas of return is critical to realizing transitional and durable solutions. UNHCR will work with the Protection Cluster and HLP working group to address HLP rights issues through the provision of legal assistance, issuance of property and identity documents, and mediation mechanisms.

destinationObjects_Project.name: Humanitarian WASH Response in Somaliland and Puntland Regions, Somalia
project_text:
Humanitarian WASH Response in Somaliland and Puntland Regions, Somalia  Unreliable access to a temporary and/or inadequate WASH facility remains an important feature of the humanitarian landscape in Somalia. In 2020, over 4.6 million people (1.16 million IDPs and 3.36 million host communities) don’t have sufficient quantity of water and adequate sanitation (HNO 2020). This dire situation is even worsened by the COVID19 pandemic which require more water for frequent handwashing for prevention and containment. Schools in Somalia are reopening and due to COVID19, a number of schools are requesting urgent water supply for both students consumption and to support frequent handwashing. 

The water supply coverage in Somalia is strongly dependent on rainfall performance. In the last two rainy seasons namely 2019 Dayr and 2020 Gu, the performance of rains has improved slightly (SWALIM/FAO). From 2017 onwards, the water coverage has shown slight improvement due to improved rain performance. The National WASH Cluster estimates 59% as having sufficient drinking water with 66% of those with access walk less than 15 minutes for a water point and 20% having challenges to access the minimum quantity of safe water. (JMCNA ). 48% access their own improved latrines, while 52% use either unimproved latrines or practicing open defecation (22%) posing a huge public health risk. Furthermore, 2% used soap with water at latrines, 52% use soap at household level while 40% use other substitute for handwashing. 45% of women/girls access MHM materials. 
On the other hand, Oxfam needs assessment conducted late 2019 in Sool, Sanaag and Togdheer regions indicates that over 40% of both IDP and host communities rely on purchasing water from commercial trucks. There is no well-organized and reliable government data that shows the coverage of water, sanitation, and hygiene in Somalia. In December 2019 and January 2020, Oxfam and FAO/SWALIM conducted a WASH inventory in all regions of Somaliland. The inventory focused on sustainable and strategic water sources in the country including boreholes, springs, and protected shallow wells. The functionality of these sources is critical. However, the current functionality rate is estimated to be much below 70% and decreases as the stress level goes up during the drought period. The analysis of the final report is not yet finalized but expected to inform the sector on ways to increase functionality and reduce interruption of services. The COVID19 outbreak has increased the need for water to support frequent handwashing practices and this will further stress the few existing water sources. 
People living in the riverine areas in Somalia and other areas adjusted to seasonal rivers are affected by floods. The worst most recent flash-floods were reported from the Shabelle river basin particularly in Beletwayn town, Hiraan Region, and Qardho town of Puntland State. Until the end of May 2020, over 412,000 people are displaced by the floods (UNOCHA, Flood Bulletin). The capacity of regional states and the federal government is limited only to response instead of constructing large scale flood protection structures. 

Somalia is one of the worst hit Horn of African countries by COVID19. So far, over to 3,864 cases and 99 deaths are recorded. However, the figures are believed to be much higher since testing capacity is limited to only few major towns. The situation in Somalia is different compared to other countries with a strong governance system in the horn of Africa. Only 31% of people in Somalia reported having a functional handwashing facility with soap (WASH Cluster, March 2020). This estimate is based on an assessment conducted before the Covid19 lockdown. The federal government and humanitarian agencies confirmed the increased market price of soap and other detergents and 11% contraction of national GDP in the country. Covid19 prevention requires frequent handwashing and social distancing which both are difficult in Somalia context.

Women and girls continued to report protection-related risk

project_text:
Appui aux ménages pastoraux et agropastoraux (communautés hotes et des PDIs ) faisant face à l'insécurtié alimentaire, nutritionnelle et pastorale structurelle  Le projet a pour objectif général d'apporter une assistance sociale aux populations structurellement en insécurité alimentaire, nutritionnelle et pastorale indépendamment du statut résidentiel des chefs de ménages. Cette assistance sera intégrée de manière cohérente avec l'évolution du contexte particulièrement le fonctionnement des marchés, les principaux moyens d'existence des populations, la situation sécuritaire et les bonnes pratiques locales. Cette approche permettra de faire le pont entre l'humanitaire, le développement et la paix. L'assistance touchera principalement les couches vulnérables dont les capacités endogènes ne suffisent pas pour satisfaire leurs besoins alimentaires, nutritionnels et pastoraux sans recourir à des stratégies de survie néfastes. Ces ménages vivent généralement dans un cercle vicieux de pauvreté et d'insécurité alimentaire/nutritionnel et pastorale dont ils ne sauraient se relever dans un appui extérieur.  
Spécifiquement le projet vise à:
- Sauver des vies en apportant une assistance alimentaire, nutritionnelle  et pastorale d'urgence en nature ou à travers un programme de transfert monétaire selon le degré de fonctionnement des marchés, le niveau sécuritaire et les préférences des populations à près de 5000 ménages vulnérables avec une discrimination positive pour ceux dirigés par des femmes;

project_text:
ASISTENCIA Y PROTECCIÓN HUMANITARIA A FAMILIAS AFECTADAS POR LOS IMPACTOS DE LA CRISIS PROLONGADA DE VENEZUELA El programa está dirigido a las poblaciones las más vulnerables en Venezuela, es decir, que se seleccionaron las parroquias de intervención de acuerdo con los siguientes criterios de vulnerabilidad, operatividad y estrategia de inclusión política y social:
•	Altos niveles de pobreza
•	Altos niveles de desnutrición crónica y alta prevalencia de enfermedades infecciosas.
•	Estados fronterizos que han manejado regularmente la presión adicional del intercambio con poblaciones muy pobres y desplazados del territorio colombiano.
•	Exposición a amenazas naturales
•	Alto nivel de conflictividad y violencia social en los últimos meses, debido a la escasez.
•	Capacidad organizativa comunitaria y capacidad operativa de Cáritas consolidadas.
Los beneficiarios serán involucrados en la identificación de las necesidades para ciertas actividades, como es el caso de la selección de medicamentos a dispensar, el contenido de las bolsas complementarias de alimentos para las familias con niños/as desnutridos y la compra de filtros artesanales de agua. En otras actividades, como la detección de la desnutrición, los niños/niñas son sujetos pasivos, beneficiarios de una acción para diagnosticar y tratar la desnutrición detectada durante la primera fase del proyecto, motivada por la escasez de alimentos en el país a causa de la crisis económica. Durante la ejecución del proyecto, los beneficiarios serán implicados a través de los promotores comunitarios, quienes serán el enlace con el resto de los actores del proyecto. 
El presente proyecto se centrará en cuatro (4) resultados entre sí, que al tiempo que contribuyen a mejorar las condiciones de vida, refuerzan la resiliencia de las poblaciones más afectadas por la crisis. Ellos son: 1) Monitoreo de la situación nutricional y las condiciones de vida en las comunidades en riesgo de desnutrición en niños y mujeres embarazadas. 2) Suplementación nutricional de las comunidades vulnerables asociada a la desnutrición, con entrega de insumos terapéuticos, de insumos alimenticios y de transferencias en efectivo; 3) Atención a la salud y saneamiento, fundamentalmente a la familia de los niños menores de 5 años en situación de riesgo nutricional y de las mujeres embarazadas atendidas. Este enfoque ejecuta dos actividades que brindan respuesta a dos necesidades apremiantes, la salud y la higiene; 4) Fortalecimiento de capacidades de la Red de Cáritas de Venezuela que le permita poder adherirse a los protocolos de Cáritas Internacionalis (CI) y alcanzar un Plan de mejoras que permita incrementar la eficacia en la operatividad de los proyectos

project_text:
Emergency WASH Response in South Sudan UNICEF will provide women, men, girls, and boys affected by multiple shocks and hazards
in South Sudan with critical water, sanitation, and hygiene services, items, and facilities.
The objective of this project is to provide lifesaving emergency water supply, sanitation
and hygiene promotion services for con􀂧ict affected people, vulnerable host communities
and people in disease prone (high GAM famine and outbreak related) areas including
protection related actions to mitigate GBV, strengthening of communities’ resilience to
cope with the impact of emergencies and recurrent shocks. This emergency WASH project
will comprise of situation assessments, preparedness, transitional programs, frontline
emergency WASH response, strengthening of partners’ capacity, and cluster coordination
including sector information management. UNICEF will deliver emergency lifesaving
support by providing access to WASH services as per Sphere and WASH Cluster
standards.
The project will focus on addressing the following:
- Effective Cluster coordination mechanism in the country
- Provide timely equitable access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene for IDPs/host
communities and returnees, including transitional programming
- WASH in Nutrition for famine prevention with a minimum package of interventions.
- WASH in Health for outbreak control at wider community level (i.e. Ebola, Cholera, etc.)
- While implementing projects a special attention will be given to mitigate WASH-related
GBV.
The project will also support expansion of partnerships with local and international NGOs
and CBOs in highly affected areas to ensure basic services are provided and long-term
capacity built. The activities will be implemented in complementarity with other sectors
such as Health, Nutrition, Protection and where possible Education projects including
disaster risk reduction (DRR) focusing on strengthening community coping mechanisms.

project_text: Sustainable Agriculture and Livelihoods Empowerment project and Unconditional Cash/Food voucher to the Host and IDPs in Yirol and Awerial Counties. South Sudan underwent series of humans suffering before and after the attainment of Independence all brought by civil wars, communal conflicts and natural calamities such as flooding and COVID-19 pandemic and these hampers people's sources of livelihood and deteriorate the economy. In 2022, the Humanitarian Nee community in South Sudan estimated that two third (2/3) of South Sudan population which is approximately 8.2 million are in need of humanitarian assistance. This includes the 2 million in which 55% of them are women and girls with an additional 2.3 million residing in the countries as refugees. All these negative factors will only aggravate humanitarian conditions in South Sudan. The lands for farming will be limited by flooding and drought and this increases the risk of vulnerability rates and increase in the number of IDPs in the Country. Yirol East recently hosted a huge number of IDPs with 9473 HHs registered and verified by WFP through according to Yirol East Relief and Rehabilitation Commission office in Yirol East County with another 160 HHs that later arrived after the verification, and this will only exacerbate the humanitarian situation Yirol East County as the resources of the host communities are shared and soon will be depleted. In Yirol East County of Lakes State, Help-Hilfe zur Selbsthilfe has been implementing Food security and Livelihood project alongside WASH and nutrition. Major support under this this sector falls under distribution of farm inputs (seeds, tools and implements) and training (Climate Smart Agriculture), conservation agriculture and distribution of fishing gears. Help is scaling up to promote the enterprise farming that will boost other sectors of livelihood such as agribusiness. So far, Help previously supported and trained several groups in Yirol East and West Counties and many of those groups had progressed expectedly. Under the project “Multisector emergency aid for displaced persons and host communities in Eastern Lakes State”, Help is currently implementing a three (3) years project that is targeting 10,000 Households in Lakes and part of Jonglei states to benefit from seeds and tools distribution and agronomic trainings such as kitchen gardening, perm gardening, aerial gardening especially in the flood affected population places. Another 9500 HHs to benefit for unconditional Cash/food voucher where 4000 HHs already distributed food items and other essential things like washing soaps and another 5000 HHs to benefit from fishing gears. The proposed intervention is designed to contribute to Help Interim Country Strategic Plans of 2022-2024. The combination of these interventions will contribute to its work in realizing Sustainable Development Goal 2 to “end hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition, and promote sustainable agriculture” in South Sudan. As food insecurity problems in Lakes State are complex and interrelated, it requires multifaceted and integrated responses both at household and individual levels in addressing immediate and underlying causes of food insecurity and malnutrition to enhance their capacities and reduce vulnerabilities to disaster risks. The supplementary coping mechanism is acquired through consumption of wild fruits and greens. The IDPs and host community households prepare smaller portion of less nourishing food for survival and the number of meals per a day reduces to one. The project will also incorporate GBV, HIV/AIDS, accountability to affected populations, and gender equality during the implementation. In our intervention, Help implements hand in hand with the community stakeholders Chiefs, Women representatives, church leaders, youth representatives, and government representatives (boma and Payams administrators) during the identification of the most vulnerable households and the distribution of humanitarian assistance and agricultural inputs.  The targeting criteria include women headed HHs, Child headed HHs, destroyed HHs.
