description: Support for critical Desert Locust control operations in Ethiopia 56% Somalia 44% - (SOMALIA) (part of ECHO/-HF/BUD/2021/91003)
sourceObjects_Organization.name: European Commission's Humanitarian Aid and Civil Protection Department
destinationObjects_GlobalCluster.name: Food Security
destinationObjects_Organization.name: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
destinationObjects_Location.name: Somalia
destinationObjects_Cluster.name: Food Security
destinationObjects_Plan.name: Somalia Humanitarian Response Plan 2021
destinationObjects_Project.name: Saving Lives and Livelihoods in Rural Somalia
reportDetails_organization: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
project_text:
Saving Lives and Livelihoods in Rural Somalia Somalia faced a growing number of threats to its food security in 2020, starting with the ongoing Desert Locust crisis, followed by COVID-19 first reported in March, severe flooding between April and September and poor rains forecast for the Deyr 2020 season. Based on latest projections, 2.1 million Somalis are in IPC Phases 3 and above through December 2020. Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of the La Nina developing, which tends to trigger dry conditions in Somalia. If the forecast below-average Deyr rains (Oct-Dec 2020) is followed by below-average or delayed 2021 Gu rains (Apr-Jun), this could lead to a rapid and substantial worsening of the humanitarian situation. 

Rural populations are at a high risk of further deteriorating food security, given the direct and indirect impacts of these threats on rural livelihoods, related assets, food production and income. FAO’s proposal responds both to the lifesaving and life-sustaining needs of rural populations in IPC Phases 3 and above, against a Population in Need (PiN) of 3.1 million people prioritized for Food Security Cluster (FSC) assistance under the 2021 HRP. FAO’s planned activities will directly support 103,850 households in IPC 3-4 under both FSC Strategic Objectives (SOs), while further delivering support to protect food security in Somalia at a wider scale through countrywide animal health campaigns, among other activities. 

Under SO1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 76,300 rural households, including IDPs, in the form of Cash+, UCT and CFW activities delivered through FAO’s e-Platform for Mobile Money and Livelihood Assistance. All cash-based programmes include trainings on good nutrition practices, covering infancy to old age.

Under SO2, to protect livelihoods, FAO will provide in-kind and technical support to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security threats across Somalia’s rural livelihood zones, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to 53,500 households targeted for Cash+ interventions under SO1 (while supporting an additional 7,550 households with agricultural inputs only). FAO’s planned Cash+ activities combine cash transfers with tailored livelihood support packages to assist rural families out of hunger sooner. Alongside cash transfers, the assistance packages will protect and restore the livelihoods of households in IPC Phases 3-4 by providing: (i) farmers with quality inputs to produce a nutritious variety of food crop (cereal, pulse and vegetable seeds, storage bags, fertilizer and irrigation/tractor services, where appropriate; (ii) pastoralists with nutrient-rich feed blocks and deworming to improve livestock productivity especially milk supply; and (iii) coastal communities with a variety of basic fishing gear and processing equipment to improve catch and consumption.  

Also under SO2, in anticipation of drought conditions in early 2021, FAO will also strategically position water bladder tanks and provide nutritive animal feed blocks to protect the small milking animals of up to 20,000 pastoral households impacted by scarce pasture from dry conditions and/or locust damage. Countrywide livestock vaccination and supportive treatment campaigns will further protect livestock assets belonging to at least 2.2 million men, women and children. Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

Under SO2, to protect livelihoods, FAO will provide in-kind and technical support to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security threats across Somalia’s rural livelihood zones, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to 53,500 households targeted for Cash+ interventions under SO1 (while supporting an additional 7,550 households with agricultural inputs only). Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

project_text:
Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

project_text:
Emergency Food Security and Livelihoods for flood affected Households in Upper Nile Heavy rain and flooding created historical overflow of the Nile and Sobat Rivers since July 2020, creating the worst flooding in 60 years. The flood destroyed homes and livelihoods of people - damaged settlements, agriculture (crops and cattle), horticulture, and market access which are crucial for peoples’ livelihoods. 40% of the crops and vegetable gardens in GOAL operational areas have been affected and no yield has been harvested during harvesting in 2020. People are also displaced and feared to turn to negative coping mechanisms such as informal borrowing, selling productive assets, and depletion of working capital which might be used to protect from the impact of the disaster. The  flooding crisis came at the back drop of very grim hunger situation in these areas, where already 163,000 were suffering from acute and severe hunger (about 70% of population in Baliet, and 85% in Ulang) (IPC Phases 3, and 4). And 59,462 in IPC4. This situation was further impacted by the current economic downturn and higher inflation rates, in addition to food price hikes exacerbated by the impact of COVID-19 pandemic. The floods severely affected the opportunities for income generating schemes leading to loss of household income and inability to afford food and meet basic needs. Negative coping mechanisms of poor and most affected households have been reported, such as taking fewer meals per day (mostly amongst women and girls), selling assets or borrowing money at high rates to purchase food items, causing unmanageable debt. The flooding also resulted in increased incidences of human diseases such as malaria and acute watery diarrhoea that will affect productivity and deplete savings in the form of increased medical expenses – this will further contribute to household vulnerability and reduce resources available for purchasing food.
GOAL is requesting access to the HRP to cover the immediate needs of 25,800 vulnerable individuals severely  affected by the current flooding of the Sobat river. The individuals targeted will be from existing GOAL beneficiaries who have been flood affected. The flooding affected 68,502 people in Baliet  and Ulang counties. Under the GOAL programme, GOAL has been providing support to build the resilience of 160,000 people in Melut, Baliet, Ulang, Rubkona, and Panyinjar counties since 2016. Prior to the current flooding GOAL program has been implementing various flood risk preparedness and mitigation activities including: dissemination of Early Warning Information, and  development of an early response strategy to mitigate the impact of flooding, stakeholders coordination, formation of flood response committees, identification of most vulnerable people and high-risk areas; distribution of empty sacks to aid dyke construction, dyke construction and monitoring implementation of flood response actions. This request for HRP is sought as the scale and magnitude of the current flooding and livelihood crisis it has compounded requires additional interventions to help vulnerable households meet their immediate needs, reducing the hunger gap and mitigating negative coping mechanisms. This intervention will also provide support to host communities that had to cope with people displaced. 
There is a significant gap in the response to these needs. WFP food distribution covers only 50% of the monthly  households’ food needs. This presents an urgent need for emergency livelihood interventions. The HRP will support households through Cash for Assets to address their immediate food needs, while building assets, such as constructing flood control dikes that will improve their livelihoods, reduce risks and impact of shocks, increase food productivity, and strengthen resilience to natural disasters. The cash for assets will be conditional cash transfer with two components of conditionality – engagement on Cash for Asset, to rebuild community assets, for able bodied households; and mandatory attendance on trainings.

project_text:
Mejora de los servicios esenciales de Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene de las personas en situación de desplazamiento afectadas directa o indirectamente por la situación humanitaria  NRC Venezuela tiene como objetivo reducir riesgos de salud pública y la prevención de enfermedades relacionadas con el agua y el saneamiento inadecuados, garantizando el acceso al derecho al agua y al saneamiento, reduciendo los riesgos de protección ligados a la situación humanitaria en Venezuela. El programa ASH propone modalidades de (a) respuesta de emergencia, (b) respuesta con soluciones duraderas basada en un enfoque comunitario, y (c) una respuesta Integrada con otros programas de NRC tales como: Educación e ICLA. 

 

La respuesta ASH de NRC continuará incluyendo la provisión de un mínimo de servicios ASH durante la Respuesta de Emergencia (COVID-19 y crisis humanitaria venezolana). Por otro lado, durante la Respuesta con Soluciones Duraderas se pretende mejorar la resiliencia en comunidades meta, fomentando la participación de comunidades en el diseño e implementación del programa, desarrollando sus capacidades locales, y asegurando la sostenibilidad del programa. 

 

La componente de AGUA incluirá: (a) Provisión de agua segura (a nivel del hogar) a través de kits de tratamiento de agua para el hogar y/o kits de manejo de agua) y rehabilitación y sistema de tratamiento de agua a nivel comunitario; (b) Provisión de capacitación y sensibilización (tratamiento, calidad del agua y uso seguro). 

 

La componente de SANEAMIENTO incluirá: (a) Provisión de baterías de baños y duchas culturalmente apropiadas, desagregados por género y estaciones de lavado de manos. Las instalaciones se ubicarán en áreas públicas o institucionales en zonas clave de flujo migratorio; (b) Provisión de kits NFIs de saneamiento (mantenimiento / limpieza); (c)Provisión de contenedores de basura para gestión de residuos sólidos. 

 

La componente de HIGIENE incluirá: (a) Provisión de kits de dignidad e higiene, junto con sensibilizaciones sobre su uso apropiados; (b)Provisión de campañas de sensibilización sobre higiene personal, prevención de enfermedades, higiene menstrual y protección; (c) Creación, capacitación y sensibilización de comités ASH en colegios y comunidades que servirán como apoyo a la promoción de higiene. La respuesta ASH de NRC pretenden ser Integradas a otros programas como el de Educación que apunta a una mejora de la calidad de la educación, inclusivas e integradas con el programa ASH centrándose en la mejora de la infraestructura ASH, para garantizar las instalaciones satisfagan las necesidades de todos los grupos de NNAs, profesores y personas con discapacidad.

project_text:
Improving the protective environment and supporting access to HLP rights for the most vulnerable conflict affected populations in South Sudan In response to identified priority protection needs, including HLP needs, DRC will deliver General Protection services for conflict and displacement affected communities. DRC will implement protection activities in a variety of locations including hard to reach locations through both static, outreach and mobile modalities. In doing so DRC aims to contribute to the overarching intersectoral strategic objectives for the 2021 HRP through contributing to the four protection cluster strategic objectives of:
- Ensure the provision of critical protection related assistance and specialized services through an integrated approach to address the priority needs of targeted people among vulnerable women, men, girls and boys in hard-to-reach and priority geographical areas
- Prevent and mitigate protection risks through enhanced preparedness and resilience
- Enable durable solutions for IDPs and other population
- Enhance protection assessment and monitoring to inform protection and overall humanitarian response
DRC general protection activities will ensure protection services are available to women and girls, boys and men. DRC will facilitate access to life-saving protection assistance by working with community networks to identify and strengthen positive coping mechanisms and develop mitigation strategies for identified protection risks. DRC will strengthen referral mechanisms for specialised services; conduct awareness raising and information campaigns focused on rights including HLP rights, assistance opportunities and threats; establish or support Community Based Protection Networks (CBPN) for primary prevention and monitoring; provide capacity building support to duty bearers, including on HLP and provide IPA based on needs, including for resolution of HLP related concerns. Evidence-based programming and advocacy across the response will be be supported through regular protection monitoring and protection assessments, including HLP monitoring and HLP assessments, based on pre-identified triggers, with mechanisms to ensure inclusion of persons with specific needs such as persons living with disabilities, elderly people, adolescent girls at risk, and female headed households.
DRC currently has strong static presence in Unity and Upper Nile State. DRC will continue to provide static and outreach services in these locations. DRC also currently has 2 Mobile Protection Teams that respond to emergencies in hard to reach locations where there are limited services and high needs. These mobile teams will also provide General Protection services outlined below. As such the locations listed as targeted areas for intervention include those locations where DRC has static presence as well as locations where DRC may respond as part of the country wide mobile protection response team capacity.
DRC activities in the sectors of SNFI, FSL, CCCM and other sub sectors of protection including GBV will complement protection services and allow for multi-sectoral service delivery in response to multi-faceted protection needs. DRCs multi sectoral capacity will allow for opportunities for strong integration between SNFI and HLP in particular which is crucial to ensure a do no harm approach to service delivery.

project_text:
Comprehensive, safe and dignified SGBV prevention and response services for conflict and displacement affected individuals and communities in South Sudan In response to identified priority needs of protection risk mitigation and protection service provision, DRC will deliver Sexual and Gender Based Violence (SGBV) prevention and response services for conflict and displacement affected communities. DRC will implement SGBV prevention and response activities in a variety of locations including hard to reach locations through both static and mobile modalities. In doing so DRC aims to contribute to the overarching intersectoral strategic objectives for the 2021 HRP through contributing to the four-protection cluster strategic objectives:
-	Ensure the provision of critical protection related assistance and specialized services through an integrated approach to address the priority needs of targeted people among vulnerable women, men, girls and boys in hard-to-reach and priority geographical areas 
-	Prevent and mitigate protection risks through enhanced preparedness and resilience 
-	Enable durable solutions for IDPs and other population 
-	Enhance protection assessment and monitoring to inform protection and overall humanitarian response 

DRC GBV program activities will ensure GBV prevention and response services are available to women and girls, boys and men, those who are survivors or at risk of GBV. DRC prevention activities will include risk mitigation through protection awareness raising and information dissemination, distribution of dignity kits, capacity building for duty bearers and strengthening of community-based protection capacities. Gender-responsive action will include mobilising communities in the prevention of violence against women and girls through the SASA! community mobilization program, working with both men and women to challenge the negative consequences of gender inequality and harmful power dynamics. SGBV response activities will include case management for survivors of SGBV and focused non-specialized individual and group-based counselling for women and girls. DRC will also support where appropriate the establishment of community based safe shelters and/or safe homes. DRC will strengthen or support the establishment of safe referral pathways in areas of both static and mobile operation.  DRC currently has eight Women and Girls Friendly Spaces (WGFS) and/or Multi-Purpose Protection Centres (MPCs) located in Unity State and Upper Nile state. DRC will continue to provide services in these DRC established, women and girls owned, spaces. SGBV response services will be mainly provided in these static locations given the crucial need for confidentiality, privacy and ability to follow up when delivering such activities in order to avoid doing harm. DRC mobile SGBV services will focus mainly on prevention activities where response services are available. DRC currently has 2 Mobile Protection Teams that operate in hard to reach locations that have limited access to services. These mobile response teams will provide GBV prevention services where there are already response services available. As such the locations listed as targeted areas for intervention include those locations where DRC has static presence as well as locations where DRC may respond as part of the country wide mobile protection response team capacity.
 DRC activities in the sectors of SNFI, FSL and other sub sectors of protection including HLP and General Protection will complement SGBV prevention and response services and allow for multi-sectoral service delivery in response to multi-faceted protection needs.  
Overall, DRC aims to reach approximately 14,290 vulnerable individuals affected by displacement and conflict, including approximately  2,010 men, 7,290 women, 1,420 boys, and 3,570 girls.

project_text:
Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

project_text: Emergency Food Assistance for underserved communities in Aweil South , Aweil East and Panijiar Counties of South Sudan   The purpose of the project is to enhance emergency food production, diversify food consumption and strengthen the resilience of targeted communities. The project aims to achieve this purpose by distributing crop and vegetable seed kits, agricultural tool kits, fishing kits, provide agronomic training for 8,400 households, approximately 50,400 individuals. Food production trainings will be through provision of farmer extension services, establishment of farmer field schools and vegetable gardens in schools and nutrition centers. Diet diversity will be achieved by increased consumption of vegetables, increased availability of fish at household level and local markets as well as through targeted sensitization on food preparation (cooking demonstrations), IYCF and basic household hygiene. Further, the resilience of the target communities will be strengthened by encouraging them to participate in construction or rehabilitation of community assets through cash for asset approach. This approach is supplementary expected to provide an alternative source of income to targeted individuals. Additional measures of addressing underlying causes of food insecurity shall include capacity building in disaster risk reduction, natural resources management and establishment of referral pathways to other services including nutrition health care, education, protection, and WASH.

reportDetails_organization: Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
project_text:
Renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et de plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali. 
La situation humanitaire demeure complexe et instable, principalement en raison des conflits armés et intercommunautaires dans les régions du Centre et du Nord. Le retard dans la mise en œuvre de l’Accord pour la paix et la réconciliation au Mali paraphé en juin 2015 et dans le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration (DDR) contribuent à la persistance de l’instabilité sécuritaire dans les régions de Kidal, Gao, Ménaka, Tombouctou, Ségou et Mopti ainsi qu’à l’aggravation des tensions sociales. A cause des activités des acteurs armés, l’accès humanitaire demeure difficile mais fluide dans certaines zones. 

La présence limitée de l’État et l’insécurité dans ces régions demeurent l’un des facteurs clés obligeant les civils à fuir leurs communautés. La grogne sociale qui a conduit au changement de régime en août 2021 prouve l’inaccessibilité des populations maliennes aux services sociaux de base et l’aggravation de leur vulnérabilité à laquelle s’ajoute le poids de la pandémie de COVID-19. 

Le nombre de Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) a atteint la barre des 311,191 en octobre 2020 en comparaison aux 199 385 enregistrés à la même période en 2019 et 80 302 en 2018.  Les risques et les besoins de protection des populations fuyant leurs communautés sous la pression de la violence armée ou des tensions intercommunautaires, sont élevés. De graves abus et attaques contre les personnes, les biens et les services (écoles, centres de santé) sont régulièrement signalées alors que l’accès aux services appropriés est compromis. Comme les déplacements internes sont de longue durée, les risques de protection et les violations des droits fondamentaux augmentent, en particulier pour les plus vulnérables (femmes, enfants, personnes âgées, personnes handicapées ou malades). De graves conséquences humanitaires ont donc été notées, telles que des taux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire et de malnutrition ainsi que le faible accès aux services sociaux de base.

Avec près de 4,7 millions de personnes affectées par l’insécurité alimentaire, dont 2,3 millions personnes avec des besoins d’assistance d’urgence, l’année 2020 a été, selon les résultats des exercices du Cadre Harmonisé (CH), l’année la plus fortement marquée par l’insécurité alimentaire depuis 2014. Les conséquences de cette détérioration resteront perceptibles sur le niveau de vie de populations en 2021. Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent environ 200 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou et Gao ainsi que son antenne de Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud.

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CMCoord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer avec un accent accru dans le domaine de Civilo-Militaire et d’accès humanitaire afin de garantir la conservation et la consolidation de l’espace humanitaire. OCHA jouera un rôle essentiel dans la mobilisation adéquate des fonds en faveur des personnes dans le besoin, en plus de contribuer à dynamiser les efforts déployés par le Gouvernement et les acteurs du développement pour s’attaquer aux causes structurelles de la vulnérabilité.

OCHA continuera à jouer son rôle central dans la mobilisation des partenaires, l’utilisation des instrum

project_text:
Internally Displaced Population in South Sudan supported through provision of protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience, protection advocacy and achievement of solutions. The project aims to strengthen community and rights-based protection response for IDPs, IDP returnees and vulnerable persons within their host communities. The project will focus on providing physical and legal protection through advocacy, timely protection monitoring, life-saving protection response based on identified needs and solutions. The project will address Housing, Land and Property (HLP) rights issues through the provision of legal assistance, facilitate issuance of property and identity documents, and work with mediation mechanisms to support HLP related dispute resolution. Community-based networks will be utilized as part of the protection response to foster community buy in and ownership of protection. The project will use evidence-based planning to expand outreach and develop the capacity of displaced communities to cope, recover, contribute to and ultimately achieve solutions. Out of 1.6 million IDPs, 475,000 IDPs and IDP returnees will be supported with protection interventions and assistance in seven (7) states and an administrative areas. Recognising the protection concerns linked to food insecurity, the Agency activities also include a scaling-up of activities in South Sudan’s highly food insecure and prioritised locations, i.e. Pibor County, Akobo, Aweil South, Tonj East, Tonj North, Tonj South. There will be continuous advocacy and support in the area of law and policy with relevant government bodies such as the   Ministries of Justice Home Affairs, Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, and the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC) to ensure the centrality of protection, enact the “Protection and Assistance to Internally Displaced Persons Act 2018” (IDP) Bill, National Framework on Returns, and various HLP initiatives. The relevant line ministries will also receive capacity building and technical assistance. Building on UNHCR’s existing operational presence in Bentiu Bor, Juba, Malakal, Wau, Yambio, Yei, the Agency will continue to advance on the 2020 geographic expansion of IDP activities by leveraging both static and mobile presence through 15 partners to Central Equatoria, Unity, Upper Nile, Joinglei, Western Bahr El Ghazal, Northern Bahr El Ghazal, Lakes, Western Equatoira, Eastern Equatoris and Warrap. Response and monitoring will cover 19 identified priority counties and Pibor Administrative Area, including remote or hard to-reach areas, in full support to the Protection Cluster Strategy for mobile assessments and response. Partners comprise of both national and international organizations, with selection undertaken on the basis of their pre-existing presence, access to populations of concern and capacity to carry out static and remote protection monitoring and response. While not all proposed activity locations fall under the severity 3, 4 or 5 in terms of food insecurity, recognizing the fluidly and unpredictable nature of sub-national violence in South Sudan, UNHCR’s protection by presence approach requires presence in areas affected by conflict as well as areas of potential return in light of increased momentum in terms of solutions 
Resources and advocacy will focus primarily on protection response and solutions, either durable or transitional (where the former is not yet possible), including assessments on needs, risks, and intentions and feasibility of durable solutions, while also strengthening community-based structures, supporting HLP initiatives, promotion of livelihoods and peaceful coexistence. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will be a key component. A mobile tool was introduced in late 2019 that has enhanced data collection and triangulation of information through timely collection and analysis capabilities, which will further improve information products, leading to a more fitting risk-mitigation approach, reduced response time; while underpinning protection mainstreaming across other operational interventions, including of other Clusters.

project_text: Assistance agricole d'urgence et protection des moyens d'existences des ménages en vue de renforcer leur résilience face aux chocs Ce projet vise a apporte une assistance d'urgence aux ménages agricoles  identifiées à l'issue des résultats   campagne agro-pastorale de 2020   et à renforcer les capacités de résilience en protégeant les moyens d'existence . En lien avec la stratégie du cluster ce projet contriburera aux trois objectifs sectoriel . Ainsi, sur la base  chiffres du cadre harmonisé et des  jounées techniques du dispositif prévention et de gestion des crises alimentaires et  du plan de soutien, pour la répartition géographique.  la FAO se propose de couvrir 30 % des besoins  dans zones agricoles. Les zones prioritaires sont les communes extréments vulnérables dans toutes les régions à l'exception d'agadez pour le volet pluvial. En plus des ménages victimes des déficits de productions, le projet touchera aussi  aussi les ménages victicmes des  inondations ecxeptionnelle 2020, de   des crues de la komadou et du fleuve. Des intrants de qualité  pour les cultures pluviales, de décrues et irriguées  seront mise à la disposition d'environ 52 000 ménages. Dans le ciblage, les ménages vulnérables dirigés par des femmes seront prioritaires. En plus des intrants des appuis conseils et formations seront apportés avec  des partenaires de proximites ONG nationales et internationales sous la supervision des services techniques de l'état. En outre 18000 ménages recevront pour rébiliter les sites et ouvrages agricoles impactés par les inondations, la réabilitation des unités de transformations et de conservation des produits et des appui en AGR ou Kits de résilience afin de renforcer leur capacité à résister aux chocs. Les ménages dirigés par les femmes et les jeunes seront prioritaires .Dans le cadre de la coordination et la redevabilité, le  dispsoitif prevention et de gestion des crises  et les groupes de travail au niveau des régions seront renforcés dans l'analyse de la situation alimentaire et nutritionnelle et les mécanismes de veille. Des rapports trimestrielles soront  produits pour renseigner le cadre des résultats du RPM par région . La coordination apportera un appui aux régions et organisera des rencontres transfrontalières sur les problèmatiques majeures.

project_text:
Stabilizing the food access and livelihoods of conflict and disasters affected returnees, internally displaced persons and the host communities in South Sudan through integrated emergency and static Food Security and Livelihood response. This project aims to meet the immediate, medium and long-term food security needs of the target communities of IPC level 3,4 and 5, also having the focus on restoring livelihood, enhancing food production, building resilience and strengthening capacity of the targeted population.
This will be achieved by various means. One of them is access to cereal and/or vegetable seeds’ kits and tools, accompanied by agricultural extension activities, focusing on good agronomic practices. This intervention will be delivered using lead farmers and farmer field school approaches with demonstration plots. Lead farmers and extension workers will be trained as trainers for community farmers. This methodology ensures ownership and long-lasting effects, as the capacity of trainers stays within the community. PAH will introduce different irrigation methods including drip irrigation systems together with community training on their adequate and sustainable use to enhance the copying mechanism during the dry season. 
Additionally, to traditional plots, PAH will encourage setting up small-scale vegetable gardens, which can be established next to the houses. This facilitates planting and irrigation, allows higher diet diversity and minimize the protection risks in case of women walking long distances to access the plots. 
Access to fishing kits and learning of fishery practices is another means to improve food security and livelihood. Fishing has the potential to immediately address food security needs. It enables people to immediately harvest fish from the rivers and swamps in the areas. 
Conditional general food distribution may be considered within the project in case the targeted population is strongly affected by food insecurity. Food distribution will target the most vulnerable food insecure population with limited access to markets and having a poor road network. Contrary, in the communities with access to market and availability cash programming, will be considered. The decision will be based on initial market and community assessments, considering cash vouchers or cash for work. Food/cash for asset will be conducted in the areas where there are needs and local markets can support the project targeting the establishment of community structures and facilities like schools and infrastructures like community road projects and communal farms establishment.
Food for education and school feeding programme will be considered in the project areas where PAH carries food security and livelihood activities with seeds distribution and vegetable and cereal crops production. 
For a more  holistic approach, building resilience and long-lasting effects, PAH will integrate interventions with sectors of WASH, nutrition, education, protection and S/NFI through combined hygiene and nutrition promotion in addition to screening and referral to nutrition partners. Education and health will be integrated through training of school hygiene clubs and school gardening and awareness at the schools, nutrition and health centres. PAH will work with nutrition and health partners on the local level. Protection will be mainstreamed across all sectors and additional protection team will be supporting the communities.
Concerning the beneficiaries breakdown, while planning the responses PAH will follow OCHA population aggregation.

project_text:
Saving Lives and Livelihoods in Rural Somalia Somalia faced a growing number of threats to its food security in 2020, starting with the ongoing Desert Locust crisis, followed by COVID-19 first reported in March, severe flooding between April and September and poor rains forecast for the Deyr 2020 season. Based on latest projections, 2.1 million Somalis are in IPC Phases 3 and above through December 2020. Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of the La Nina developing, which tends to trigger dry conditions in Somalia. If the forecast below-average Deyr rains (Oct-Dec 2020) is followed by below-average or delayed 2021 Gu rains (Apr-Jun), this could lead to a rapid and substantial worsening of the humanitarian situation. 

Rural populations are at a high risk of further deteriorating food security, given the direct and indirect impacts of these threats on rural livelihoods, related assets, food production and income. FAO’s proposal responds both to the lifesaving and life-sustaining needs of rural populations in IPC Phases 3 and above, against a Population in Need (PiN) of 3.1 million people prioritized for Food Security Cluster (FSC) assistance under the 2021 HRP. FAO’s planned activities will directly support 103,850 households in IPC 3-4 under both FSC Strategic Objectives (SOs), while further delivering support to protect food security in Somalia at a wider scale through countrywide animal health campaigns, among other activities. 

Under SO1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 76,300 rural households, including IDPs, in the form of Cash+, UCT and CFW activities delivered through FAO’s e-Platform for Mobile Money and Livelihood Assistance. All cash-based programmes include trainings on good nutrition practices, covering infancy to old age.

Under SO2, to protect livelihoods, FAO will provide in-kind and technical support to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security threats across Somalia’s rural livelihood zones, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to 53,500 households targeted for Cash+ interventions under SO1 (while supporting an additional 7,550 households with agricultural inputs only). FAO’s planned Cash+ activities combine cash transfers with tailored livelihood support packages to assist rural families out of hunger sooner. Alongside cash transfers, the assistance packages will protect and restore the livelihoods of households in IPC Phases 3-4 by providing: (i) farmers with quality inputs to produce a nutritious variety of food crop (cereal, pulse and vegetable seeds, storage bags, fertilizer and irrigation/tractor services, where appropriate; (ii) pastoralists with nutrient-rich feed blocks and deworming to improve livestock productivity especially milk supply; and (iii) coastal communities with a variety of basic fishing gear and processing equipment to improve catch and consumption.  

Also under SO2, in anticipation of drought conditions in early 2021, FAO will also strategically position water bladder tanks and provide nutritive animal feed blocks to protect the small milking animals of up to 20,000 pastoral households impacted by scarce pasture from dry conditions and/or locust damage. Countrywide livestock vaccination and supportive treatment campaigns will further protect livestock assets belonging to at least 2.2 million men, women and children. Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of the La Nina developing, which tends to trigger dry conditions in Somalia. If the forecast below-average Deyr rains (Oct-Dec 2020) is followed by below-average or delayed 2021 Gu rains (Apr-Jun), this could lead to a rapid and substantial worsening of the humanitarian situation. 

Rural populations are at a high risk of further deteriorating food security, given the direct and indirect impacts of these threats on rural livelihoods, related assets, food production and income. FAO’s proposal responds both to the lifesaving and life-sustaining needs of rural populations in IPC Phases 3 and above, against a Population in Need (PiN) of 3.1 million people prioritized for Food Security Cluster (FSC) assistance under the 2021 HRP. FAO’s planned activities will directly support 103,850 households in IPC 3-4 under both FSC Strategic Objectives (SOs), while further delivering support to protect food security in Somalia at a wider scale through countrywide animal health campaigns, among other activities. 

Under SO1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 76,300 rural households, including IDPs, in the form of Cash+, UCT and CFW activities delivered through FAO’s e-Platform for Mobile Money and Livelihood Assistance. All cash-based programmes include trainings on good nutrition practices, covering infancy to old age.

Under SO2, to protect livelihoods, FAO will provide in-kind and technical support to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security threats across Somalia’s rural livelihood zones, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to 53,500 households targeted for Cash+ interventions under SO1 (while supporting an additional 7,550 households with agricultural inputs only). FAO’s planned Cash+ activities combine cash transfers with tailored livelihood support packages to assist rural families out of hunger sooner. Alongside cash transfers, the assistance packages will protect and restore the livelihoods of households in IPC Phases 3-4 by providing: (i) farmers with quality inputs to produce a nutritious variety of food crop (cereal, pulse and vegetable seeds, storage bags, fertilizer and irrigation/tractor services, where appropriate; (ii) pastoralists with nutrient-rich feed blocks and deworming to improve livestock productivity especially milk supply; and (iii) coastal communities with a variety of basic fishing gear and processing equipment to improve catch and consumption.  

Also under SO2, in anticipation of drought conditions in early 2021, FAO will also strategically position water bladder tanks and provide nutritive animal feed blocks to protect the small milking animals of up to 20,000 pastoral households impacted by scarce pasture from dry conditions and/or locust damage. Countrywide livestock vaccination and supportive treatment campaigns will further protect livestock assets belonging to at least 2.2 million men, women and children. Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

project_text:
Protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience and solutions for IDPs and non-IDP communities and refugee returnees. The project aims to strengthen a rights-based protection response for IDPs and non-IDP communities, as well as refugee returnees, in particular those most vulnerable through stronger advocacy, life-saving protection and assistance activities, evidence-based programming with the focus on developing and building the capacity of affected communities to cope and recover and better position them for the attainment of durable solutions. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will also be key components of the project. The project also foresees benefiting the entire displaced population through continuous advocacy and support in the area of Law and Policy, fostering the successful engagement with relevant authorities and partners with a focus on the approval and implementation of the new IDP Law. This activity will be built upon efforts by UNHCR that in 2020 culminated in the Somalia accession to Kampala Convention and development of draft IDP Law that is aimed to domesticate it.   
UNHCR will continue to make the best of its key membership of the protection cluster and ensure regular reporting to the clusters’ 5Ws and strong participation and contribution in the different clusters’ working groups to ensure coordination and complementarity of interventions, avoiding duplication with other members and ensuring regular sharing of protection reports with the cluster. 
Many IDPs in protracted displacement remain in situations with no progress towards durable solutions and suffer from systemic marginalization. Access to life-saving assistance and basic services, such as education and health, exclusion from services provided by government are other factors that contribute to heightened protection risks faced by displaced and other conflict-affected populations. Sexual and gender-based violence also remains a critical protection concern for IDPs. A significant proportion of IDPs are members of minority groups lacking the protection of major clans. COVID-19 pandemic has further exacerbated pre-existing risks and vulnerabilities. In Somalia internally displaced persons (IDPs) have been facing despicable acts of man-made violence including forced evictions and natural hazards which have led to multiple displacement and limited access to durable solution opportunities. Many newly displaced IDPs still remain in need of assistance. Many of the IDPs reside in overcrowded areas with poor living conditions and limited security provision. The basic needs of IDPs are often not met due to inconsistent service provision, exclusion from accessing services, or from the sheer absence of services due to poor targeting of settlements. Forced evictions remain one of the most severe and prevalent protection threats, particularly for IDPs and poor households, due to an underdeveloped regulatory framework, hampered access to justice, low awareness of and respect for HLP rights, and a weak protective environment. It is anticipated that opening of the borders and lifting some of the COVID-19 travel restrictions can lead to an increase of number of returns as compared to 2020 that will bring overall number of returnees in the Somalia that will be in need of variety of protection services to 109,989. Many returnees choose not to return to their areas of origin, preferring to settle in urban areas. Many of these contribute to and suffer the results of pressure on basic services, further compounded by recurrent influxes of IDPs. Any intervention will be vulnerability and needs based.  While there is increased effort to promote sustainable return and re-integration, a substantial number of returnees have limited access to basic services, precarious or no physical security and are constantly exposed to myriad protection risks that proposed project will seek to address. The project includes a sustainability/handover component where feasible, particularly in the areas of Law and Policy, as well as community mobilization and NNGOs engagement.

reportDetails_organization: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees; United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
project_text:
Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2021, there are more than 314,000 refugees from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, including from Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic.

At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for long-term stability, some 357,500 South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since November 2017, 122,000 of those in 2020 alone. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan at this stage, the increase in numbers warrants a scaling-up of support following an area-based approach, including strengthening linkages with development actors, to help returnees and the communities they settle in live in safety and dignity, with greater security and services.

Refugees largely reside in conﬂict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction of basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.

Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will beneﬁt from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Speciﬁc protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identiﬁed at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with speciﬁc protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as veriﬁcation exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the eﬃciency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to beneﬁt from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

project_text:
Protection and assistance to Nigerian refugees in the Diffa region  (Situation Lake Chad) L’intervention en faveur des réfugiés présents à Diffa va se décliner autour de 3 objectifs suivants : 1- Maintenir et renforcer un environnement de protection favorable (protection monitoring et réponse de protection, dont child protection, SGBV, PBS, apatridie, enregistrement/documentation), améliorer les capacités d’intervention des autorités nationales pour délivrer des services de protection conformes aux standards internationaux et maintenir ouvert l’accès au territoire nigérien et aux procédures d’asile.2 – Assurer une assistance d’urgence et une capacité adéquate au niveau du camp de Sayam Forage et améliorer l’accès aux services sociaux de base. 3 - Renforcer la recherche des solutions durables et l’intégration socio-économique des réfugiés installés au Niger notamment via le programme urbanisation et la construction de logements pour les plus vulnérables. .
La stratégie de réponse est conforme avec les orientations du Gouvernement du Niger en termes d’alternatives aux camps et avec le Pacte Mondial pour les Réfugiés. Le nexus humanitaire – développement est au cœur des réflexions qui accompagnent la mise en œuvre de la réponse. Cela suppose le renforcement de la capacité d’absorption des services de base pour alléger les pressions, et l’accompagnement de la coexistence pacifique, en parallèle d’une réponse multisectorielle urgente. Alors qu’une assistance de type communautaire est développée pour l’accès aux services de base tels que l’eau ou la santé, c’est le niveau de vulnérabilité et non le statut qui régit l’assistance individuelle.

reportDetails_organization: Agency for Technical Cooperation and Development; Agency for Technical Cooperation and Development
project_text:
Improving short-term and long-term food security and livelihoods access in Central and Eastern Equatoria and WBeG through investment in food production assets and utilization and strengthening of local capacities. In line with the FSL cluster strategy for 2022, ACTED will contribute towards improving food security of over 22,754 beneficiaries (excluding beneficiaries reached through WFP funding) to enhance emergency food production and reduce dependency on food and agricultural inputs through resilience building activities such as training and market support functionality. Millions of South Sudanese remain displaced across the country following years of violent conflict that resulted in one of the most devastating humanitarian crises in recent history. Based on the latest IPC analysis and projections, in October 2022, 53.6% of the population living in South Sudan facing high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above). Specifically, 4.36 million people are facing crisis (IPC Phase 3), 2.22 million people are facing emergency (IPC Phase 4) and 61,000 people are facing catastrophic (IPC Phase 5) food insecurity.  As such, the needs across South Sudan have severely increased, driven by flooding, insecurity, population displacements, declined crop production, diseases and pests, the economic crisis, the effects of COVID-19, limited access to basic services, and the cumulative effects of prolonged years of asset depletion and loss of livelihoods.  The project activity will be in line with the cluster Objectives : 
CO1 : Provide food assistance to prevent famine and improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies for vulnerable populations (in IPC 5, 4 & some 3)
“CO2: Enhance emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop seeds and fishing and livestock support (in IPC 3, 4 & 5)”

project_text:
Appui à la protection des moyens de subsistance des pasteurs et agropasteurs des régions de Tillabéry, Tahoua, Diffa, Agadez, Maradi et Zinder  		 Le projet vise à apportera assistance aux ménages pastoraux vulnérables par les interventions suivantes:   
   -  Un appui conseil à travers le renforcement de capacité en matière de traitement de fourrage grossier pour améliorer la valeur nutritive de ces fourrages ;
    - Un appui en aliment  bétail de 8 775 tonnes à mettre à la disposition de 22 600 ménages pasteurs et agropasteurs vulnérables pour 158 200 personnes. Un minimum de 13% de ces bénéficiaires doivent être des femmes.  223 200 têtes bénéficieront de cette assistance qui sera mise en place en nature et via coupon. Les bénéficiaires recevront 8325 tonnes pour assurer une complémentation alimentaire à 222 000 têtes petits ruminants  à raison de  250g/jour/tête par tête sur une période de 5 mois et 450 autres tonnes à 400 ménages  propriétaires de 3 gros ruminants pour assurer une complémentation alimentaire  pour 1200 bovins à raison de 2,5 kg par jour/gros ruminant d'animaux pendant une période de 5 mois. La mise en place de cet important stock se fera à travers deux approches: (1) vente à prix modéré par les partenaires; (2) distribution d'une partie du stock à travers des vouchers. Cette distribution interessera principalement les femmes  parmi lesquels la  priorité sera donnée aux veuves et aux femmes allaitantes pour soutenir l'alimentation de l'enfant de moins de 5 ans. Dans les deux cas l'assistance privilégiera les petits ruminants qui sont principalement élevés par les femmes carassez faciles d'entretien alimentaire. l'enquête ECVMA de 2011 de l'INS a rapporté que près de 40% des ovins et de 55% des caprins appartiennent aux femmes.
- distribution de 1 900 kits de petits ruminants de 3 chèvres et un bouc aux ménages ayant connu une forte décapitalisation de leurs animaux reproducteurs. les bénéficiaires serony vhoisis parmi la catégorie des très pauvres des régions de Maradi (Bermo) et de Tahoua (Tchintabaradene et Abalak). .
- Distribution de 2 000 ânes aux femmes pour leur réduire la pénabilité de l'exhaure et le transport de l'eau. beucoup d'an""""""""s assurant la corvée d'eau ont été décimés par la sous alimentation et les fortes précipitations enregistrées du début de l""""""""hivernage. Les zones touchées sont les communes de Tchintabaradene, Kao, Abalak et Bermo. Il sera mis une unité d'ane à la disposition de chaque femme . Il n'est pas en effet rare de voir 4  à 5 femmes puiser de l'eau des puits dont la profondeur moyenne est de 80 mètres ou plus à l'aide des puisettes de 35 à 40 litres de contenance.   
  - vaccination et déparasitage de 385 000  têtes de bétail dont 376 000 petits ruminants et 9000 gros ruminants appartenant à 40100 ménages contre les pathologies dominantes par zone d'intervention. Parmi ces maladies la peste des petits ruminants, les charbons, la Clavelée et la pasteurellose ou tout autre maladie jugée prioritaire par la DGSV.

project_text:
Assistance en abris et Biens non-alimentaires (BNA) aux personnes déplacées vulnérables dans les régions de Diffa et Maradi Le projet proposé par l'OIM vise la poursuite d'une réponse coordonnée pour couvrir de façon adéquate aux besoins en abris et en Biens non-alimentaires (BNA) aux populations affectées par la crise du basin du lac Tchad qui affecte les régions de Diffa et Maradi. L'objectif est de contribuer à l'amélioration des conditions de vies des populations déplacées à travers: i) la fourniture d'abris aux ménages vunérables, la distribution de kits BNA, dont  3 000 kits d'abris d'urgence et 3 000 kits de BNA à Diffa puis 1 000 kits d'abris d'urgence et 1 000 kits de BNA à Maradi, dans le cadre du HRP 2021. ii) Mettant à disposition 3 000 kits de BNA  et 2 000 kits d'abris  à titre de renouvellement des abris endomagés et Kits NFI n'existant plus, respectivement à Diffa et Maradi à travers l'option transferts monétaires conditionnel. 5 000 kits de Biens non-alimentaires seront distribués aux ménages à travers cette même modalité. iii)  La mise à disposition de 3 000  abris transitionnels qui seront  fournis  à Diffa pour améliorer les conditions de vie des ménages dont le retour dans les villages d'origine est incertaine du fait de l'insécurité dans cette région. En tant que Co-Lead du Secteur abris et BNA  l'OIM va continuer d'assurer la coordination du Groupe de travail abris et Biens non-alimentaires en étroite collaboration avec le Ministère de l'Action Humanitaire, en  renforçant la collecte des informations de façon régulière dans le souci d'informer les intervenants sur la localisation, la nature et l'ampleur des besoins exprimés et des activités de réponse, de continuer à appuyer les partenaires et membres du secteur pour mener les activités dans le respect de la strategie du Groupe de Travail et des principes humanitaires et d'appuyer les services étatiques dans leurs rôles de coordination et suivi des activités du secteur.
Les activiés de la réponse d'urgence se conformeront aux Principes de Protection tranversales et au Cadre institutionnel de l'OIM de lutte contre les violences basées sur le genre en situation de crise (VBV) , intégrera des mesures visant à assurer la sécurité, la dignité et le bien-être de la population touchée, et intégrera le respect strict de principe de tolérance zero pour toute exploitation et abus sexuels. Ce projet s'inscrira dans le respect des principes humanitaires et portera une attention particulière au principe ne pas nuire, de sécurité et non-discrimination. Les activités du projet seront mises en oeuvre dans le respect soutenu des règles de lutte contre la COVID 19 par l'observation de mesures barrières telles que le port du masque, le lavage des mains, le respect de la distanciation sociale afin d'endiguer tout risque de contamination et de propagation de la maladie aupres des bénéficiaires. Un système de gestion de mécanisme de plaintes sera mis en place afin que les plaintes sensibles soient traitées conséquement dans le but d'apporter une assistance respetant l'égalité et la dignité des communautés bénéficiares.  Dans le cadre de la redevabilité de sessions d'information sur le projet seront organisées avec les beneficiaires,la phase d'évaluation de besoins sera réalisée de commun accord avec les populations dans les communes ciblées, la communication avec les communautés et les autorités locales sur les criteres de ciblage seront organisées et apres intervention, les feedbacks de la communauté cible seront collectés à travers des évaluations post-distribution et des séances de discussion de groupe séparées par genre et âge avant et après l'assistance. Aussi, en tant qu’acteur humanitaire, l'OIM et ses partenaires de mise en œuvre s’assureront que les actions n’induisent aucune tension ou problème dans la zone et n’exposent pas les bénéficiaires en affichant les compositions de kits BNA et Abris. A cet effet. Une collaboration étroite sera faite avec les acteurs de protection aura lieu. Le cout total du projet sera de 9.563.333 USD.

project_text:
Protection services and interventions for Palestine Refugees in Syria In 2021, UNRWA will continue to provide critical protection assistance to Palestine refugees. It is anticipated that the vulnerabilities of Palestine refugee will further increase due to COVID-19 and the current economic situation.  
The Agency will seek to improve the protection of Palestine refugees in Syria through various interventions:
-	Mainstreaming protection within UNRWA services will remain a priority. Corresponding to needs, protection training, including on disability inclusion, GBV, PSEA, addressing violence against children, will be delivered to a wide range of staff and volunteers. 
-	Dedicated programmatic responses will be implemented through regular service-delivery and stand-alone initiatives to support the needs of vulnerable populations including those related to psychosocial distress. Areas most affected by conflict-related violence as well as displaced and returning populations will be prioritized.
-	Legal support services will be offered while prioritising women and children experiencing GBV by assisting them in obtaining civil documentation and referrals to external partners. 
-	Mine risk awareness campaigns will continue throughout the country targeting students and other community members, with a specific focus on areas of spontaneous returns. 
-	Protection monitoring, reporting and advocacy will continue to be prioritised through the participation of UNRWA in global protection mechanisms and the international human rights system (IHRS). This will be done through the interaction with relevant stakeholders, including the protection sector of the Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) in Syria. In parallel, UNRWA will focus specifically on monitoring the return of Palestine refugees displaced within and outside Syria.
In a cross-cutting approach, UNRWA will continue to strengthen Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) by systematically increasing the participation of Palestine refugees in programme identification, design, delivery and lesson learning. Feedback will be sought on programme quality and to assess Palestine refugees’ satisfaction with the services provided. This will help UNRWA to implement programmes that are of higher quality, with greater and more sustainable impact.

project_text: Health-related vulnerabilities of Rohingya and Host Communities are reduced through increased quality access to comprehensive health services The aims of IOMs’ health interventions aim to respond to the lifesaving needs and improve the resilience of affected populations, with special attention to gender and age considerations, and vulnerable groups. In the camps,34% Rohingya refugee populations, have reported going into debt to pay for health expenses, and 27% seeking lower-quality care or medication, due to a lack of money (Joint Multi-Sector Needs Assessment J-MSNA 2020). This demonstrates some challenges in the already strained health service system in Cox’s Bazar. To address this, this intervention aims to contribute  to  i) increased safe, dignified and meaningful access and utilization of quality comprehensive healthcare services, focusing on sexual, reproductive, maternal, neonatal, child and adolescent health; mental health and psychosocial support; and non-communicable diseases (NCD); ii) improved health seeking behavior, encouragement of  healthy living and promotion of the  utilization of essential service package and community engagement, with special attention to vulnerable groups iii) measures to prepare and (timely) respond  to health emergencies, during disaster (including monsoon and cyclone) and outbreaks of communicable disease (e.g.  COVID-19 and AWD). IOM also aims to contribute to the improvement of quality of services through performance monitoring, evaluation, coordination and capacity building.

project_text:
Provision of timely, equitable and integrated food security and livelihoods services to the conflict, epidemic and natural disaster affected populations in South Sudan South Sudan protracted crises have left 7.5 million people in dire need of humanitarian assistance in 2020 despite the signature of the Revitalized peace agreement, and continues to face conflict, natural disasters and climate instability, food insecurity, and lack of basic services. According to the latest IPC analysis for South Sudan published in December 2020, an estimated 7.7 million people are expected to experience acute food insecurity and worse (IPC 3, 4 and 5) in 2021. 
SI has started to implement its humanitarian response in South Sudan in 2006. Its long lasting presence has contributed to building a wealth of experience in Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) and Food, Security and Livelihoods (FSL). This allowed SI to pilot large-scale unconditional cash transfers, seeds distribution amongst IDPs and host communities in Western Bahr El Ghazal, Upper Nile, Jonglei and Central Equatoria states. SI aims at supporting the most vulnerable households, who are struggling to restore their livelihoods, in order to help them to improve their food security situation. Currently, SI is running five operational bases: Raja town and Wau town (Western Bahr el-Ghazal), Aburoc/Malakal (Upper Nile), Lankien (Jonglei) and Juba (Central Equatoria). For 2021, SI will focus on linking its first line response, through its EPR and static teams, with activities having longer-term impact in WASH and FSL sectors. In FSL specifically, this will mean emergency livelihood response to quickly replenish the destroyed assets. In second step SI will complement the response, wherever possible, with capacity building to allow for income generation and longer-term food preservation. SI will therefore aim at providing timely, equitable and integrated food security and livelihoods services to the conflict, epidemic and natural disaster affected populations of South Sudan.

destinationObjects_Project.name: Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan
project_text:
Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

destinationObjects_Emergency.name: Coronavirus disease Outbreak - COVID -19
project_text:
Lifesaving SRH-GBV integrated response with COVID-19 prevention and protection to ensure continuity of SRH services 4,7 million women are estimated as currently pregnant in Pakistan. 66% deliveries occur at health facilities, 22% of them are at government facilities.  3,5 million births expected by end of December, 2020. 
10%-20% decline in service coverage of essential maternal health care (ANC and post-natal care) may result in increasing of maternal deaths up to 2,056 -3,135 cases respectively.
There was not a tangible decline in institutional deliveries observed in the provinces where UNFPA mobile units are functional.  However, the number of ANC and Postnatal visits decreased by 30% due to lockdown and accessibility of the services. 
Distribution of COVID 19 positive cases among male and female population is unequal in different age groups. Most prevalent cases observed among male population in middle age group (65%). The impact of pandemic is frequently discussed by the government but more in economic terms and yet there is negligible mention of women or the gendered effects of the coronavirus. ‘The government’s approach towards women has always been paternalistic, and it is no different now; women are viewed as passive victims of a socio-economic and healthcare disaster’. 

Assessment conducted by OCHA in 2020 in collaboration with other UN organizations/agencies has unfold a gloomy picture of the health systems which also comes with some noticeable geographic disparities;  for instance; 
- Only 26.9% of the health facilities in Sajawal were having medicine available and on the other hand 88.9% of the health facilities in TM Khan were having medicine available in the health facility.
- Only 32.9% of deliveries take place in health facilities and 27.7% of post-natal care is provided by trained health staff. Recent estimates reveal that over 2.2 million people have limited or no access to essential health care services including women at reproductive age (15-49 years) 
- Access to health facilities by pregnant women is poor. For instance, only 52% in TM Khan and 28.2% in Sajawal have access to a health facility that assisting with birth 24/7, (Joint UN assessment 2020). 

Overall, 27% of the health facilities were reported as nonfunctional in the flood affected communities. Out of the functional health facilities only 27% providing 24/7 health care services. Overall, 52% of the respondents reported medicine available at the nearest health facilities, while 48% reported medicine were not available at the health facility.
The above situation is aggravated by:
- The ongoing outbreak of COVID-19 pandemic in Pakistan has increased burden on the already weak health system. Many of the existing resources (human, equipment, infrastructure, funds etc) have been diverted to support COVID-19 response. This and the additional financial resources allocated from routine health programmes have impacted negatively on the delivery of health services particularly those entrapped in protracted crises, such as, Afghan Refugees and Temporary displaced persons.   
- The non-pharmaceutical response to COVID-19 especially restriction to movements have adversely  affected  access to health services by the disaster affected population because repeated lockdowns with resultant supply chain breakdowns not only hampered services availability but also restricted population access to these services - Since, Health sector workforce including doctors from public and private sector, nurses, paramedics staff and pharmaceutical experts, lab technicians are at the forefront of Coronavirus. The workforce is facing disruptions and closure of the health care system for non-COVID related illnesses like routine immunization, maternal and childcare in many locations. Therefore, using national level PDHS 2017-18 Data, UN (2020) Socio-economic Impact assessment of COVID-19 on the Most Vulnerable Population has drawn two kinds of scenarios for the impact of COVID 19 on SRH services. According to the assessment report, if there is 10% reduction in the continuity of current services

project_text: Access to Humanitarian life-saving child protection and GBV response services in North Darfur, North / South Kordofan and White Nile states The project objective is to protect people from violence, neglect, and exploitation by providing access to life-saving child protection and GBV response services to targeted communities in White Nile, North Kordofan, and North Darfur. In order to accomplish this, Plan will provide high quality protection services and contribute to community stabilization and resilience. Protection services and capacity building activities will include: CP and GBV case management, distribution of dignity kits to vulnerable girls, multi-purpose cash transfer to vulnerable households and hosting UASC, and referrals mechanisms including to Family and Child Protection Units, training of social workers and partner staff on GBV, CP, and referral pathways, and psychosocial support to conflict affected children and youth. The provision of protection services must be paired with activities to increase knowledge of and access to those services. Therefore, Plan will also establish/strengthen and equip Community Based Child Protection Networks (CBCPNs), conduct community awareness session of CP, FGM, SEA and child marriage risks, and conduct sensitization on GBV prevention and response. Plan will foster communal stability and resilience by providing life skills training, parenting sessions, conducting community awareness sessions on peacebuilding and conflict transformation, and training duty bearers and community leaders on peacebuilding.  Additionally, Plan will establish child-friendly community feedback and response mechanisms so that all project beneficiaries are able to provide feedback and file complaints.
