destinationObjects_Project.name: Increase access to lifesaving sexual and reproductive health services to vulnerable population affected by Conflict and COVID19 pandemic in Libya.
project_text:
Increase access to lifesaving sexual and reproductive health services to vulnerable population affected by Conflict and COVID19 pandemic in Libya. In 2020, 3.5 million population lacks consistent access to primary and secondary health care services. This is due to the reason that more than half of the functional health facilities in 2019 are closed due to the intensification of conflict and the onset of COVID19 in 2020. Lifesaving health services such as reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent Health (RMNCAH) and mental health services have been severely disrupted, neglected and underfunded in the past many years. The situation amid COVID19 pandemic is further compounded by lack of personal protective equipment (PPEs), delays in payment of salaries to the health care providers, and closer of many health facilities or the suspension of operations especially in maternity hospitals in urban areas. The supply chain management for medical supplies, equipment and pharmaceuticals are globally and locally disrupted and it has closed many public health facilities. Due to this situation, majority of the patients are now referring to private health care facilities, which is making out of pocket expenditure more catastrophic for the people, especially for IDPs, migrants and people living in conflict zones or along the migration routes in Libya.

This project is designed to maintain and provide emergency reproductive and sexual health services amid covid19 pandemic to 53,800 women of child bearing age, among conflict affected, IDPs and migrant population and host communities. The services are planned to be provided in severely affected municipalities / geographical areas ranked above 3 on the severity scale with a focus on un(der)served population. The project intends to provide EmONC services to an estimated population of 9,157 pregnant women. Services will mainly target migrants, refugees, returnees and IDPs and host communities in Tripoli, Benghazi, Sebha, Misurata and Sirt and people in need among none-displaced and migrants are more specifically targeted in affected municipalities or hard to reach areas of Ghat, Sirt, Murzuq, Alkufra and Aljufra.
Considering the humanitarian situation in the country, scarcity of midwives and OBGYN specialists, low capacity level and limited availability of female healthcare providers (especially specialized nurses and midwifes) to provide quality SRH services and unavailability of SRH supplies in the health facilities, there is clearly the need for a humanitarian complementary service package. The services that will be provided through this project are in line with minimum initial services package (MISP) for life saving sexual and reproductive health services of UNFPA and Essential Health Service (EHS) package of WHO issued for the context of COVID19 pandemic. UNFPA will work with its partner agencies, stakeholders, communities and local authorities for the following:

1.	Provision of Lifesaving Essential Maternal, sexual and reproductive health services to prevent excess neonatal and maternal mortality and morbidity among affected population.
2.	Coordinate Sexual and Reproductive Health Services to ensure continuous provision of essential SRH services 
3.	Provision of Essential medicine, medical supplies and equipment to sustain health SRH services

destinationObjects_Project.name: Soutien à la réponse d'urgence en éducation  dans la région Diffa (SURE)
project_text:
Soutien à la réponse d'urgence en éducation  dans la région Diffa (SURE) Le projet contribuera au HRP 2024 par le ciblage de 25 320 bénéficiaires directs. Il répondra aux besoins éducatifs urgents dans 65 écoles suivant les objectifs sectoriels du Cluster Education à travers une approche basée sur trois axes : accès à l’éducation de qualité, la protection et la résilience des communautés scolaires.
1. Les filles et les garçons ont accès à des offres d’éducation inclusive continue et de qualité dans les écoles primaires formelles et non formelles.
Le projet sera en phase avec la campagne Back to school pour l’inscription/réinscription des filles/garçons en âge scolaire y compris ceux vulnérables. L’éducation à distance à travers les clubs d’écoute radio, des cours de rattrapade et la Stratégie de Scolarisation Accélérée pour Passerelle (SSA/P) seront développés pour répondre aux besoins d’accès et de continuité de l’éducation. L’approche d’éducation à distance de Concern développée dans la région de Tillabéri sera étendue à la région de Diffa. Pour améliorer la qualité des apprentissages, les élèves seront dotés en kits scolaires d’urgence selon les standards du Cluster Education. Les enseignants recevront du matériel pédagogique d’urgence ; ils seront formés et suivis sur la pédagogie inclusive au handicap et au genre. Ils seront également formés puis encadrés sur les didactiques de français et mathématiques. Les filles les plus vulnérables et les enfants handicapés bénéficieront de suivis pour leur maintien scolaire. Les filles vulnérables y compris celles handicapées recevront du cash transfert non conditionnel mensuel pour les besoins alimentaires et d’hygiène menstruelle.
2. Les filles et les garçons y compris ceux qui sont handicapés des communautés déplacées et hôtes touchés par les crises humanitaires bénéficient d’un environnement d’apprentissage sûr et protecteur.
L’accès à l’éducation sera soutenue par la réhabilitation d’urgence de salles de classes et de latrines, la mise en place d’espaces temporaire d’apprentissage (TLS) accessibles aux personnes handicapées, Ces infrastructures seront équipées et munies d’un dispositif de lavage de mains. Les enseignants seront formés sur les thématiques clés liées à la problématique des crises pour un environnement protecteur : soutien psychosocial, violences basées sur le genre en milieu scolaire (VBGMS), éducation en situation d’urgence. Ces enseignants formés seront encadrés pour la fourniture de soutien psychosocial et la mise en place des comités de protection scolaire. Les écoles bénéficieront de matériels ludiques pour le développement des activités créatives et récréatives. Un mécanisme de référencement pour la prise en charge psychosociale des enfants en détresse psychologique sera mis en place et piloté par un point focal au niveau des écoles. Concern participera au plaidoyer auprès des autorités nationales et locale en faveur la protection des écoles contre les attaques pour la mise en œuvre de la déclaration Safe school.
3. Les filles et les garçons y compris ceux qui sont handicapés des communautés déplacées et hôtes et le personnel scolaire ainsi que les membres de la communauté sont soutenus dans la préparation et la réponse aux urgences.
A la suite d’une formation des enseignants et des structures communautaires (APE/AME/CGDES), un plan de préparation et de réponse aux risques et aux urgences sera mis en place afin d’identifier les mesures de prévention et de protection pour la sécurité des enfants et des enseignants. Pour favoriser la gestion de l’école en mode décentralisé les APE, AME, CGDES seront redynamisées ou établies et leurs compétences renforcées/ Avec les enseignants, ils seront impliqués dans la lutte contre les violences basées sur le genre en milieu scolaire (VBGMS), la cohésion sociale et la protection de l’enfant. Dans chaque école, un mécanisme de gestion de plaintes sera mis en place aux côtés du comité de protection scolaire avec l’implication des Comités Villageois de Protection de l'Enfant.

destinationObjects_Project.name: Improving food security in Jonglei and Unity South Sudan
project_text:
Improving food security in Jonglei and Unity South Sudan In line with the South Sudan HRP and cluster objectives 1 and 2, the project will save lives by addressing the acute severe food insecurity of 57,000 conflict and natural disaster affected people in IPC3+ in Jonglei (Pigi/Canal, Bor) and Unity State (Rubkona and Guit) through distribution of food vouchers to 2,500 HH and enhanced and sustained food production through distribution of seeds, crop and fishing kits, training and cash for work to 9,500 HH. In support of nutrition centres, kitchen gardens will be established to improve the nutritional status of people. This will allow severe and acute food insecure people in IPC3+ to meet their immediate food needs whilst allowing them to rebuild their assets. In addition, by improving people's food security, acute malnutrition will be reduced. All the selected locations are affected by different natural and man-made disaster, showing high and multiple vulnerabilities and are priority areas as they are in IPC3 or worse, confirmed by Cordaid assessments. Assessments also showed that women (incl. PLW), children (incl. children under 5), PWD, elderly and chronically ill are impacted differently and are bearing the brunt of conflict, droughts/ floods and COVID-19. The project will therefore target these most vulnerable groups through inclusive assistance, and will ensure that protection, gender and COVID-19 is mainstreamed in the proposed activities. 
Protection will be mainstreamed throughout the project cycle to ensure beneficiary safety & dignity, avoiding doing harm as result of the intervention, providing meaningful access to all sets of beneficiaries and ensuring all groups are actively involved and participate in the project in an inclusive manner. Additionally, the project will ensure all necessary Covid-19 measures and protocols will be adhered to; for example, during distributions, beneficiaries will be encouraged to maintain safe social distance, always wash their hands and wear face masks.
Cordaid has been responding to the increasing humanitarian needs in all 4 areas providing WASH, FSL and ES&NFI assistance and is fully operational in the 4 areas with offices in Malakal, Bor and Bentiu.

destinationObjects_Project.name: Emergency WASH Response in South Sudan
project_text:
Emergency WASH Response in South Sudan UNICEF will provide women, men, girls, and boys affected by multiple shocks and hazards in South Sudan with critical water, sanitation, and hygiene services, items, and facilities.  The objective of this project is to provide lifesaving emergency water supply, sanitation and hygiene promotion services for conflict affected people, vulnerable host communities and people in disease prone (high GAM famine and outbreak related) areas including protection related actions to mitigate GBV, strengthening of communities’ resilience to cope with the impact of emergencies and recurrent shocks. This emergency WASH project will comprise of situation assessments, preparedness, transitional programs, frontline emergency WASH response, strengthening of partners’ capacity, and cluster coordination including sector information management. UNICEF will deliver emergency lifesaving support by providing access to WASH services as per Sphere and WASH Cluster standards.

The project will focus on addressing the following:
- Effective Cluster coordination mechanism in the country
- Provide timely equitable access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene for IDPs/host communities and returnees, including transitional programming
- WASH in Nutrition for famine prevention with a minimum package of interventions.
- WASH in Health for outbreak control at wider community level (i.e. Ebola, Cholera, etc.)
- While implementing projects a special attention will be given to mitigate WASH-related GBV.

The project will also support expansion of partnerships with local and international NGOs and CBOs in highly affected areas to ensure basic services are provided and long-term capacity built. The activities will be implemented in complementarity with other sectors such as Health, Nutrition, Protection and where possible Education projects including disaster risk reduction (DRR) focusing on strengthening community coping mechanisms.

project_text:
Ensuring access to quality, timely and confidential services for GBV survivors and strengthening coordination for GBV mitigation and prevention in Somalia  Needs:
GBV continues to be an issue of great concern in Federal members States Galmudug, South West State, Jubaland, Hirashebelle Puntland and Somaliland with the event of the COVID19.  Recent spikes in the increase of Intimate Partner Violence, rape, sexual exploitation, sexual harassment and abuse have multiplied GBV risks for women and girls with worsening impact on women and girls living with disabilities. In IDP camps and host communities – inadequate physical infrastructure, distance to water points, markets, health facilities and schools, poor lightening, lack of doors on toilets and lack of disaggregation of sanitary facilities are some of major factors that increase GBV exposure. In addition, distance to distribution centers and lack of specific measures to ensure women’s inclusion and participation in food distributions, continue to worsen levels of exposure of women and girls to GBV risks. In the July 2020 “GBV/FGM assessment during the COVID19”, 38 percent responders indicated that there has been an increase in GBV incidents; 35 percent indicated GBV incidents are the same.  The number of GBV survivors call in to hotlines for help also increased by 283% in FMS and 767% in Somaliland despite the inactivation of some of the hotlines in the states. 

In addition, GBVIMS 2020 data reports a trend indicating an increase of GBV noting that over half (61%) of reported GBV incidents were Physical Assault, 13% Rape, 12% Sexual Assault, 6% Psychological/Emotional Abuse, 5% experienced Denial of Resources, and the remaining 3% percent Forced/Early marriage.       Furthermore, Anecdotal media and programming report has indicated a spike in rape of women and girls including a specific targeting of recent on boys. Majority of Women and girls fleeing violence in Somalia do not have options for safety and protection. In 2020, there has been significant efforts to broaden women and girls’ safe spaces, however, this has been severely impacted by funding limitations and also due to COVID. 

GBV service provision remains low as compared to the need and geographical landscape. Recently, worsening relations between communities and service providers exacerbated by the heightened political atmosphere impacted provision of GBV services or coordination. GBV service provision in Somalia has historically been characterized by limited specialized services such as rape treatment for rape survivors, psycho-social support and higher levels of mental health care for traumatized women and girls are major hindrances to expanding provision of timely, confidential and quality GBV services. Also, lack of actors to provide specialized services undermines efforts invested to assure access to GBV services by survivors. At present, the GBV AoR in Somalia has 58 partners that reports on the 5Ws.

UNFPA interventions will target the displaced and non-displaced communities including all age groups and persons with disabilities, and with the following specific objectives: a) Facilitate access to comprehensive multi sectoral GBV services (medical, legal, psychosocial) for 6000 women and girls. B) Enhance the capacity/and mobilize 200 PSS counsellors; 150 health workers to provide timely, quality and confidential PSS and rape treatment. C) Promote mobilization of women and girls to access services through the establishment of 15 safe spaces for women and girls (WGSS) to reach 3000 women and girls. D) Support the operationalization of integrate referral pathways for dissemination and access to services reach 2000 women, girls, boys and men. E) Provide 2,000 dignity kits and 36 post rape kits dignity protection for women and girls and treatment of rape. F) Support 200 women and girls’ survivors of GBV with cash voucher assistance and grants for livelihood. G) Support the mainstreaming initiatives on IASC Guidelines for cluster programming on GBV for 300 cluster-coordinators at national and sub national levels.

project_text:
Protection and Legal Assistance for Displacement affected populations in South Sudan The NRC seeks to improve the overall protective environment in South Sudan by not only responding to people's most immediate material needs during a crisis, but also by promoting their safety and dignity, as well as preventing, reducing, or mitigating the protection risks they face. It is also to address the root causes of displacement and to contribute to the creation of conditions conducive to long-term solutions for displaced people. To achieve the project objective, NRC will focus on three key components i.e. 1) General Protection; Housing, Land and Property; 3) Gender Based Violence. 

NRC proposes a community-based approach to displaced and conflict-affected populations protection, including static, mobile, and emergency responses.  Protection context assessments will be done in all locations, as well as, where possible, community-based protection monitoring, in which community focal points will be trained to report on protection needs and risks. Protection incidents will be documented and analyzed in order to better understand trends and evolution in the protection context, and the findings will be disseminated to communities and relevant stakeholders. 

NRC will provide at-risk populations with both awareness-raising sessions and individualized assistance in obtaining national identity documentation. Foster improved ability to exercise HLP rights for individuals and groups affected by displacement with priority given to the most vulnerable, including female and child headed households, the elderly, individuals with physical and mental disabilities, and those who are extremely poor. NRC will target conflict-affected areas and areas of potential return.

NRC will also carry out GBV prevention and risk mitigation activities in 6 counties located in hard to reach areas. Activities will include awareness raising, referrals to response services, cash assistance to GBV survivors, distribution of dignity kits and training on GBV basic concepts among others.

To achieve the main objective, the will focus on the below key activities
1) Carrying out of information and awareness raising activities; awareness will focus on GBV (GBV risks, available response services, GBV referral pathways, timely reporting), HLP (social cohesion and collaborative dispute resolution mechanisms, land rights issues) and general protection (protection risks, available services)
2) Provision of cash assistance (individual protection assistance) to persons at GBV survivors and other persons at heightened risks including referral of GBV survivors for response services
3) Training frontline workers and community focal points on basic GBV concepts, GBV guiding principles and responses services.
4) Training of state-level authorities, community leaders and representative on HLP, alternative dispute resolution
5) Facilitating peaceful coexistence and inclusive resolutions of local conflict through training and mentoring the local community in collaborative dispute resolution (CDR) mechanisms
6) Distribute dignity kits to women and adolescent girls.
7) Provision of legal aid and counselling

project_text: Building Resilience of Conflict affected communities through a multi-sectoral approach for Women, men, Boys and Girls in Yobe and Borno states. The project will focus on the recovery of the crisis-affected populations through the provision of inputs for improved agricultural production as well as income generation activities for the development of sustainable livelihood opportunities. Action Against Hunger will contribute towards improvement in food security, nutrition status and improve household income for the most vulnerable people in the targeted locations through pro-poor economic empowerment initiatives and improved all year round agricultural production of diversified nutritious foods. The proposed project aims at improving the capacity of the vulnerable populations to be less dependent on aid and transit to a more sustainable livelihoods. The project will foster the resilience of Affected Communities by developing social cohesion through developing social networks and resilience of the displaced and integration with the host communities by developing social protection programs. The rebuilding and creation of community assets, as well as basic service infrastructure, which will build the capacity of communities to cope with crisis; infrastructure development includes, health facilities and WASH infrastructure as well as retraining and strengthening existing systems of government and capacity for relevant Ministries, local authorities and State actors to respond to the needs of conflict-affected populations. The project will prioritize the needs for different age-groups and sex will be prioritized and the protection of beneficiaries will be ensured during the implementation of activities.

project_text:
Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

project_text:
Comprehensive, safe and dignified SGBV prevention and response services for conflict and displacement affected individuals and communities in South Sudan In response to identified priority needs of protection risk mitigation and protection service provision, DRC will deliver Sexual and Gender Based Violence (SGBV) prevention and response services for conflict and displacement affected communities. DRC will implement SGBV prevention and response activities in a variety of locations including hard to reach locations through both static and mobile modalities. In doing so DRC aims to contribute to the overarching intersectoral strategic objectives for the 2021 HRP through contributing to the four-protection cluster strategic objectives:
-	Ensure the provision of critical protection related assistance and specialized services through an integrated approach to address the priority needs of targeted people among vulnerable women, men, girls and boys in hard-to-reach and priority geographical areas 
-	Prevent and mitigate protection risks through enhanced preparedness and resilience 
-	Enable durable solutions for IDPs and other population 
-	Enhance protection assessment and monitoring to inform protection and overall humanitarian response 

DRC GBV program activities will ensure GBV prevention and response services are available to women and girls, boys and men, those who are survivors or at risk of GBV. DRC prevention activities will include risk mitigation through protection awareness raising and information dissemination, distribution of dignity kits, capacity building for duty bearers and strengthening of community-based protection capacities. Gender-responsive action will include mobilising communities in the prevention of violence against women and girls through the SASA! community mobilization program, working with both men and women to challenge the negative consequences of gender inequality and harmful power dynamics. SGBV response activities will include case management for survivors of SGBV and focused non-specialized individual and group-based counselling for women and girls. DRC will also support where appropriate the establishment of community based safe shelters and/or safe homes. DRC will strengthen or support the establishment of safe referral pathways in areas of both static and mobile operation.  DRC currently has eight Women and Girls Friendly Spaces (WGFS) and/or Multi-Purpose Protection Centres (MPCs) located in Unity State and Upper Nile state. DRC will continue to provide services in these DRC established, women and girls owned, spaces. SGBV response services will be mainly provided in these static locations given the crucial need for confidentiality, privacy and ability to follow up when delivering such activities in order to avoid doing harm. DRC mobile SGBV services will focus mainly on prevention activities where response services are available. DRC currently has 2 Mobile Protection Teams that operate in hard to reach locations that have limited access to services. These mobile response teams will provide GBV prevention services where there are already response services available. As such the locations listed as targeted areas for intervention include those locations where DRC has static presence as well as locations where DRC may respond as part of the country wide mobile protection response team capacity.
 DRC activities in the sectors of SNFI, FSL and other sub sectors of protection including HLP and General Protection will complement SGBV prevention and response services and allow for multi-sectoral service delivery in response to multi-faceted protection needs.  
Overall, DRC aims to reach approximately 14,290 vulnerable individuals affected by displacement and conflict, including approximately  2,010 men, 7,290 women, 1,420 boys, and 3,570 girls.

project_text:
Integrating WASH in nutrition, health and protection response to ensure equitable and safe access to water, sanitation and hygiene among vulnerable IDPs, host communities and returnees in Upper Nile State, South Sudan. RI’s proposed 2021 Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) intervention is designed to contribute to improved health and nutrition outcomes, addressing key factors of wider
community disease outbreaks, vicious circle of malnutrition, timely and equitable access
to safe WASH and mitigation of related GBV, amongst 250, 000 IDPs, returnees and
vulnerable host communities in Upper Nile state in South Sudan.

The proposed WASH interventions will be implemented in close coordination with RI’s
health , nutrition , protection and FSL programming and teams, applying an integrated approach to improve people’s lives and well-being, thus contributing to South Sudan WASH Cluster objectives and the 2021 Humanitarian Response. Recognizing WASH services to be key drivers of health and malnutrition outcomes and women and girls to be the primary users of WASH
services, the project aims to reduce GBV risk by ensuring adequate and needs based
provision of WASH services that address key protection concerns. RI’s integrated approach will further address high levels of malnutrition by targeting SAM and MAM children and families and contribute to controlling disease outbreak.

Additionally, RI will ensure equitable, timely and sustainable access to improved safe and adequate water and sanitation facilities that address the vital WASH needs, public health and protection issues, respect sphere standards; engage communities in design and ownership, improve knowledge on appropriate hygiene practices to reduce and prevent WASH-related diseases including cholera, AWD, typhoid, skin diseases etc. RI will construct gender-sensitive water supply systems, mainly solar powered, boreholes through manual drilling, extensions to bring water points closer to vulnerable households,  schools, health and nutrition facilities, rehabilitate damaged / nonfunctional boreholes, increase access to safe water and mitigate the risk of GBV at WASH facilities. Comprehensive training will be provided to female and male members of Water User Committees (WUCs) and Health & Nutrition facility staff. RI will work with existing WUCs to reinforce technical skills for water point O&M (operations and maintenance), establishing new WUCs where relevant. Solid waste management training will be provided to solid waste/hygiene committees to implement community-driven solid waste collection and disposal campaigns. RI will also construct incinerators for medical waste disposal at health facilities.

At the household level, RI will construct 1,500 household/family shared latrines, with owner contribution, amongst displaced, returnee, and conflict-affected communities to ensure that immediate and long-term sanitation needs are adequately met and facilities are gender and culturally appropriate. Latrine construction will adhere to protection standards as elaborated in the guidelines for WASH Cluster partners in South Sudan. RI will also promote hygiene awareness aimed to support behavior change in hygiene practices through house-to-house hygiene education sessions, training of hygiene volunteers, and distribution of household package for famine prevention which will include: one 20-liter bucket with tap for proper water storage, one 20-liter bucket without tap or jerry can for water collection, filter cloth, water purifier (PuR), and soap for three months consumption.

project_text:
Prevention and response to S/GBV through Risk Reduction, Women Empowerment and Enhancement of Access to Services and Opportunities in Jonglei and Unity state.  In  Jonglei and Unity state, the risk of GBV is continuously exacerbated by a myriad of factors including  prevailing cultural norms, traditional gender roles, regional conflict, a highly militarized environment, and the frequent cattle raiding and revenge killings among the different clans.
 Protection concerns such as generalized violence and insecurity, limited access to food, water and firewood, expose women to a high risk of GBV, specially in county with high severity needs such as Pibor, Akobo, Nyriol, Canal/Pigi and Ayod. There is, therefore, an urgent need to enhance GBV prevention efforts with additional strategies to mitigate risks, such as fuel strategies and protective accompaniments. Furthermore, lack of recognition of GBV as violation of fundamental human rights continues a culture of impunity throughout the region. Therefore, notwithstanding the advancing of the peace process, it is important to continue to raise awareness, reduce prevalent stigmas in the communities and increase identification and documentation of GBV cases as well as providing survivors access to psychosocial support and other services for their recovery and healing. 

Through this project INTERSOS aims to strengthen the prevention and response to GBV risks in some of the counties with the GBV severity index of 5 (Akobo and Pibor), 4 (Ayod, Canal/Pigi, Nyirol) and 3 (Mayendit). The intervention will seek to  adress the immediate needs of GBV survivors  through the provision of safe spaces, Case management services, PSS  and the enhancement of access to services and opportunities, empowering women across locations through skill acquisition trainings. To promote durable solutions a strong component of GBV prevention has also been foreseen in the form of mass awareness through a community approach and the engagement of men on accountable practice training.

destinationObjects_Project.name: Protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience and solutions for IDPs and non-IDP communities and refugee returnees.
project_text:
Protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience and solutions for IDPs and non-IDP communities and refugee returnees. The project aims to strengthen a rights-based protection response for IDPs and non-IDP communities, as well as refugee returnees, in particular those most vulnerable through stronger advocacy, life-saving protection and assistance activities, evidence-based programming with the focus on developing and building the capacity of affected communities to cope and recover and better position them for the attainment of durable solutions. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will also be key components of the project. The project also foresees benefiting the entire displaced population through continuous advocacy and support in the area of Law and Policy, fostering the successful engagement with relevant authorities and partners with a focus on the approval and implementation of the new IDP Law. This activity will be built upon efforts by UNHCR that in 2020 culminated in the Somalia accession to Kampala Convention and development of draft IDP Law that is aimed to domesticate it.   
UNHCR will continue to make the best of its key membership of the protection cluster and ensure regular reporting to the clusters’ 5Ws and strong participation and contribution in the different clusters’ working groups to ensure coordination and complementarity of interventions, avoiding duplication with other members and ensuring regular sharing of protection reports with the cluster. 
Many IDPs in protracted displacement remain in situations with no progress towards durable solutions and suffer from systemic marginalization. Access to life-saving assistance and basic services, such as education and health, exclusion from services provided by government are other factors that contribute to heightened protection risks faced by displaced and other conflict-affected populations. Sexual and gender-based violence also remains a critical protection concern for IDPs. A significant proportion of IDPs are members of minority groups lacking the protection of major clans. COVID-19 pandemic has further exacerbated pre-existing risks and vulnerabilities. In Somalia internally displaced persons (IDPs) have been facing despicable acts of man-made violence including forced evictions and natural hazards which have led to multiple displacement and limited access to durable solution opportunities. Many newly displaced IDPs still remain in need of assistance. Many of the IDPs reside in overcrowded areas with poor living conditions and limited security provision. The basic needs of IDPs are often not met due to inconsistent service provision, exclusion from accessing services, or from the sheer absence of services due to poor targeting of settlements. Forced evictions remain one of the most severe and prevalent protection threats, particularly for IDPs and poor households, due to an underdeveloped regulatory framework, hampered access to justice, low awareness of and respect for HLP rights, and a weak protective environment. It is anticipated that opening of the borders and lifting some of the COVID-19 travel restrictions can lead to an increase of number of returns as compared to 2020 that will bring overall number of returnees in the Somalia that will be in need of variety of protection services to 109,989. Many returnees choose not to return to their areas of origin, preferring to settle in urban areas. Many of these contribute to and suffer the results of pressure on basic services, further compounded by recurrent influxes of IDPs. Any intervention will be vulnerability and needs based.  While there is increased effort to promote sustainable return and re-integration, a substantial number of returnees have limited access to basic services, precarious or no physical security and are constantly exposed to myriad protection risks that proposed project will seek to address. The project includes a sustainability/handover component where feasible, particularly in the areas of Law and Policy, as well as community mobilization and NNGOs engagement.

project_text: Improving Child Protection for vulnerable populations in Somaliland, particuarly IDPs in Hargeisa and Togdheer  In 2021 humanitarian response, Plan International will improve protection environment and promote child rights in Somaliland for IDP and vulnerable populations, particularly at-risk children. The country has one of the lowest child and gender indicators in the world with only one-quarter of girls – 24% aged 15-24 considered as literate, 45% married before 18 years and 98% subjected to female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C). The COVID19 quarantine measures to prevent and control the spread of COVID-19 exposed children and women to increased protection risks, particularly within the home, owing to increased stress caused by the outbreak, exacerbating existing gender inequalities and violence. Child Protection Areas of Responsibility in collaboration with UNICEF conducted a child protection survey in April 2020 showed more than half of the CP agencies (57%) reported an increase in physical violence particular on girls. There has also been increased exposure to violence especially to girls through FGM/C. According to the United Nations Population Fund, COVID-19 could have far reaching impacts on the effort to end FGM/C, with a potential 2 million FGM/C cases occurring over the next decade that could have otherwise been averted.  Plan will work with CSOs and other partners to effectively promote and support improving community-based child protection mechanisms. Key interventions will target young girls and boys, their parents and other decision-makers to raise awareness on child protection and GBV, establish and strengthen referral mechanisms for case management and other services including MHPSS and financial support, and capacity building and advocacy with local authorities and for national agenda on centrality of protection  (e.g. importance of child protection and campaigns on GBV, adoption of the positive discipline techniques, inclusion of children with disability) and distribution dignity kits. Plan and partners will also promote PSS for children and adolescents affected by crisis, support youth-led DRR initiatives, and establish girls groups to prioritize creating safe spaces for dialogue and peer friendships. Plan and partners will provide age-appropriate, gender-sensitive, and disability inclusive services that address the different impacts of emergencies on adolescents and young children, boys and girls and promote the potential for positive transformation of gender norms. Plan and partners will maintain child-friendly feedback and complaint mechanism and promote transparency across all activities.

project_text:
Internally Displaced Population in South Sudan supported through provision of protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience, protection advocacy and achievement of solutions. The project aims to strengthen community and rights-based protection response for IDPs, IDP returnees and vulnerable persons within their host communities. The project will focus on providing physical and legal protection through advocacy, timely protection monitoring, life-saving protection response based on identified needs and solutions. The project will address Housing, Land and Property (HLP) rights issues through the provision of legal assistance, facilitate issuance of property and identity documents, and work with mediation mechanisms to support HLP related dispute resolution. Community-based networks will be utilized as part of the protection response to foster community buy in and ownership of protection. The project will use evidence-based planning to expand outreach and develop the capacity of displaced communities to cope, recover, contribute to and ultimately achieve solutions. Out of 1.6 million IDPs, 475,000 IDPs and IDP returnees will be supported with protection interventions and assistance in seven (7) states and an administrative areas. Recognising the protection concerns linked to food insecurity, the Agency activities also include a scaling-up of activities in South Sudan’s highly food insecure and prioritised locations, i.e. Pibor County, Akobo, Aweil South, Tonj East, Tonj North, Tonj South. There will be continuous advocacy and support in the area of law and policy with relevant government bodies such as the   Ministries of Justice Home Affairs, Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, and the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC) to ensure the centrality of protection, enact the “Protection and Assistance to Internally Displaced Persons Act 2018” (IDP) Bill, National Framework on Returns, and various HLP initiatives. The relevant line ministries will also receive capacity building and technical assistance. Building on UNHCR’s existing operational presence in Bentiu Bor, Juba, Malakal, Wau, Yambio, Yei, the Agency will continue to advance on the 2020 geographic expansion of IDP activities by leveraging both static and mobile presence through 15 partners to Central Equatoria, Unity, Upper Nile, Joinglei, Western Bahr El Ghazal, Northern Bahr El Ghazal, Lakes, Western Equatoira, Eastern Equatoris and Warrap. Response and monitoring will cover 19 identified priority counties and Pibor Administrative Area, including remote or hard to-reach areas, in full support to the Protection Cluster Strategy for mobile assessments and response. Partners comprise of both national and international organizations, with selection undertaken on the basis of their pre-existing presence, access to populations of concern and capacity to carry out static and remote protection monitoring and response. While not all proposed activity locations fall under the severity 3, 4 or 5 in terms of food insecurity, recognizing the fluidly and unpredictable nature of sub-national violence in South Sudan, UNHCR’s protection by presence approach requires presence in areas affected by conflict as well as areas of potential return in light of increased momentum in terms of solutions 
Resources and advocacy will focus primarily on protection response and solutions, either durable or transitional (where the former is not yet possible), including assessments on needs, risks, and intentions and feasibility of durable solutions, while also strengthening community-based structures, supporting HLP initiatives, promotion of livelihoods and peaceful coexistence. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will be a key component. A mobile tool was introduced in late 2019 that has enhanced data collection and triangulation of information through timely collection and analysis capabilities, which will further improve information products, leading to a more fitting risk-mitigation approach, reduced response time; while underpinning protection mainstreaming across other operational interventions, including of other Clusters.

project_text:
Emergency WASH Response in South Sudan UNICEF will provide women, men, girls, and boys affected by multiple shocks and hazards in South Sudan with critical water, sanitation, and hygiene services, items, and facilities.  The objective of this project is to provide lifesaving emergency water supply, sanitation and hygiene promotion services for conflict affected people, vulnerable host communities and people in disease prone (high GAM famine and outbreak related) areas including protection related actions to mitigate GBV, strengthening of communities’ resilience to cope with the impact of emergencies and recurrent shocks. This emergency WASH project will comprise of situation assessments, preparedness, transitional programs, frontline emergency WASH response, strengthening of partners’ capacity, and cluster coordination including sector information management. UNICEF will deliver emergency lifesaving support by providing access to WASH services as per Sphere and WASH Cluster standards.

The project will focus on addressing the following:
- Effective Cluster coordination mechanism in the country
- Provide timely equitable access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene for IDPs/host communities and returnees, including transitional programming
- WASH in Nutrition for famine prevention with a minimum package of interventions.
- WASH in Health for outbreak control at wider community level (i.e. Ebola, Cholera, etc.)
- While implementing projects a special attention will be given to mitigate WASH-related GBV.

The project will also support expansion of partnerships with local and international NGOs and CBOs in highly affected areas to ensure basic services are provided and long-term capacity built. The activities will be implemented in complementarity with other sectors such as Health, Nutrition, Protection and where possible Education projects including disaster risk reduction (DRR) focusing on strengthening community coping mechanisms.

destinationObjects_Project.name: Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan
project_text:
Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

project_text:
Accès inclusif et durable à une éducation de qualité pour les enfants et jeunes déplacés et de la communauté hôte affectés par la crise sécuritaire dans les régions de Maradi et de Tillaberi ette proposition de NRC s’aligne sur les principales priorités de la Stratégie nationale de réponse aux vulnérabilités du système éducatif 2020 en apportant une contribution spécifique aux populations les plus vulnérables dans le cadre des crises identifiées dans la Stratégie en termes d’Accès, de Qualité et d’amélioration de la Gouvernance dans le secteur de l’éducation dans les régions de Maradi et de Tillabéry. L’action vise à soutenir l'éducation de 25 000 enfants et jeunes âgés de 6 à 17 ans touchés par la crise et le déplacement, tout en atténuant la propagation de COVID-19. Le NRC privilégie l'utilisation des normes minimales de l'INEE pour assurer une programmation de qualité dans tous les résultats.
NRC facilitera la réouverture des écoles au sein des communautés d'accueil et à fournir l’accès à un environnement d’apprentissage de qualité à tous les enfants touchés, y compris les enfants des communautés d'accueil et les enfants déplacés/réfugiés. L'intervention du NRC pour soutenir l'éducation formelle comprend des actions relatives au renforcement de la résilience des parties prenantes, à la sécurisation de structures éducatives fonctionnelles et à la construction et l'adaptation des infrastructures éducatives existantes et de l'environnement scolaire afin de se préparer aux multiples risques qui peuvent affecter le système éducatif, y compris le risque de catastrophes naturelles et les risques sanitaires, par exemple par la construction/réhabilitation de systèmes WASH (eau, hygiène et assainissement). Afin de répondre aux besoins des enfants qui ont manqué l'école à cause du conflit et du déplacement, le NRC introduira des cours de rattrapage ou de soutien scolaire de courte durée ainsi que des PEA pour les élèves réfugiés, déplacés et vulnérables afin d'assurer leur réintégration, leur maintien et leur progression dans le système officiel, tout en étant en accord avec les directives du gouvernement d'accueil. L’intervention de NRC visera aussi à offrir des possibilités de formation professionnelle aux jeunes déplacés internes et aux jeunes vulnérables non scolarisés dans notre zone d'intervention ciblée au Burkina Faso. Cela se fera en soutenant l'accès, la qualité et l'offre d'éducation, et en soutenant la création d'entreprises pour les personnes qui terminent leurs études (mentorat).

Afin de garantir le respect et la dignité des personnes assistées et surtout de nous rassurer que nos interventions ne nuisent pas à leur bien-être (Do Not Harm), NRC veillera à consulter systématiquement les communautés bénéficiaires avant toute intervention et activités sur le terrain. Des mécanismes déjà mis en place dans certaines de nos communes d’interventions (Ligne téléphoniques, boites à suggestions…) seront d’avantage renforcée en 2021 au sein des écoles et des communautés afin que les communautés puissent signaler et reporter toutes formes de nuisances du fait de NRC ou de ses partenaires de mise en œuvre.

reportDetails_organization: Agency for Technical Cooperation and Development
project_text:
Réponse aux besoins en Eau Hygiène Assinissement des populations déplacées, retournées et des communautés hôte dans les zones affectées par les crises dans les régions de Tillabéri, Tahoua, Maradi et Diffa au Niger (MVT - MUL) En se basant sur son implantation durable sur le terrain et son positionnement auprès des communautés dans les régions ciblées, ACTED continuera de soutenir les populations les plus vulnérables au Niger en 2021 avec des activités Eau Hygiène Assainissement (EHA). ACTED envisage de délivrer les activités suivantes : 
1/ Réhabilitation de 40 points d'eau :
Chaque point d'eau réhabilité bénéficiera à environ 500 personnes, pour un total de 20 000 bénéficiaires directs, comprenant principalement des populations déplacées et des communautés hôtes. les activités prendront place dans les régions de Tillabéri, Diffa, Tahoua et Maradi
2/ Sensibilisation aux bonnes pratiques d'hygiène et distributions de kits d'hygiène
activités auprès des ménages dans les 40 communautés. Les kits d'hygiène cibleront les ménages les plus vulnérables sur les plans sociaux économiques. En fonction de la situation des zones d'intervention (capacité d'absorption des marchés, sécurité et accès, ACTED pourra considérer de donner de l'argent aux ménages bénéficiaires plutôt que des kits """"""""in kind"""""""". Cette analyse sera réalisée au début des interventions à travers des évaluations des marchés. D'autres évaluations des marchés seront conduites au cours du projet pour confirmer que la méthodologie est toujours la plus adaptée et que l'intervention (distribution d'argent en espèce) ne dérègle pas le marché local.
3/ Construction de latrines individuelles et communautaires 
activité dans les 40 communautés cibles susmentionnées.
4/ Mise en place de systèmes de gestion des déchets 
activitié dans les 40 communautés : construction de parcs de gestion des déchets et mise en place de comités de gestion des déchets

Il est attendu que ces activités ciblent les mêmes bénéficiaires que les activités de réhabilitation des points d'eau afin de fournir un soutien plus complet aux personnes affectées.  Sur le plan de l'accessibilité, les infrastructures, de par leur conception et leur localisation viseront à faciliter l'accès physique et à réduire les risques de protection pour les utilisateurs et utilisatrices. Des comités de gestion dont les membres sont issues de la communauté seront créés pour permettre aux bénéficiaires d'entretenir et de s'approprier les installations, les comités des gestion communautaires permettront aussi une meilleure redevabilité envers des populations affectées.
Plus largement, la réponse d'ACTED pour le secteur EHA fait partie d'une stratégie multisectorielle à destination des populations les plus vulnérables, qui couvre aussi e.g. la sécurité alimentaire, la formation professionnelle et les activités génératrices de revenus. 
En tant que co-facilitateur du Cluster EHA au Niger, ACTED sera en position idéale pour s'assurer de la bonne coordination des activités EHA avec les partenaires humanitaires afin d'éviter la duplication des efforts et pour developper une réponse en lien direct avec les objectifs et priorités du Cluster EHA.

destinationObjects_Project.name: ​PROVISION OF PROTECTION AND HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE SERVICES TO MIGRANTS IN VULNERABLE SITUATIONS
project_text: ​PROVISION OF PROTECTION AND HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE SERVICES TO MIGRANTS IN VULNERABLE SITUATIONS The project’s aim is to provide a range of protection services to migrants in need, strengthen links between targeted community groups and services available, and enhance knowledge on migrant population groups in Lebanon. Services will target both male and female migrants, with a higher caseload of the latter group due to their increased number in country. Beneficiaries will typically be working age, between 18 and 40 years old. The services that IOM will deliver, either directly or through partners, include legal assistance, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), safe and temporary shelters for vulnerable migrants, provision of non-food items, multipurpose cash assistance (MPCA), and voluntary humanitarian return. These services will be made accessible to migrants by scaling up IOM’s pre-existing case management services, supporting enhanced capacity of, and referral with partners, strengthening translation and interpretation efforts to diminish language barriers facing migrants, and expanding community-level networks to strengthen targeted communities’ awareness of and access to IOM and partner services, as well as wider issues of concern. Finally, enhancing knowledge of migrant populations will involve nationwide data-collection efforts via key informant interviews in order to inform humanitarian planning. The project will be implemented by the IOM in partnership with civil society organizations (CSO) and community-based initiatives, with some services such as shelter, legal assistance referred from IOM. IOM will work with local service providers to strengthen their capacity, to enhance the overall protection network available for migrants in Lebanon. Onward referral to multisector assistance such as food or health support will be mainstreamed across the project.

reportDetails_organization: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
project_text:
Saving Lives and Livelihoods in Rural Somalia Somalia faced a growing number of threats to its food security in 2020, starting with the ongoing Desert Locust crisis, followed by COVID-19 first reported in March, severe flooding between April and September and poor rains forecast for the Deyr 2020 season. Based on latest projections, 2.1 million Somalis are in IPC Phases 3 and above through December 2020. Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of the La Nina developing, which tends to trigger dry conditions in Somalia. If the forecast below-average Deyr rains (Oct-Dec 2020) is followed by below-average or delayed 2021 Gu rains (Apr-Jun), this could lead to a rapid and substantial worsening of the humanitarian situation. 

Rural populations are at a high risk of further deteriorating food security, given the direct and indirect impacts of these threats on rural livelihoods, related assets, food production and income. FAO’s proposal responds both to the lifesaving and life-sustaining needs of rural populations in IPC Phases 3 and above, against a Population in Need (PiN) of 3.1 million people prioritized for Food Security Cluster (FSC) assistance under the 2021 HRP. FAO’s planned activities will directly support 103,850 households in IPC 3-4 under both FSC Strategic Objectives (SOs), while further delivering support to protect food security in Somalia at a wider scale through countrywide animal health campaigns, among other activities. 

Under SO1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 76,300 rural households, including IDPs, in the form of Cash+, UCT and CFW activities delivered through FAO’s e-Platform for Mobile Money and Livelihood Assistance. All cash-based programmes include trainings on good nutrition practices, covering infancy to old age.

Under SO2, to protect livelihoods, FAO will provide in-kind and technical support to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security threats across Somalia’s rural livelihood zones, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to 53,500 households targeted for Cash+ interventions under SO1 (while supporting an additional 7,550 households with agricultural inputs only). FAO’s planned Cash+ activities combine cash transfers with tailored livelihood support packages to assist rural families out of hunger sooner. Alongside cash transfers, the assistance packages will protect and restore the livelihoods of households in IPC Phases 3-4 by providing: (i) farmers with quality inputs to produce a nutritious variety of food crop (cereal, pulse and vegetable seeds, storage bags, fertilizer and irrigation/tractor services, where appropriate; (ii) pastoralists with nutrient-rich feed blocks and deworming to improve livestock productivity especially milk supply; and (iii) coastal communities with a variety of basic fishing gear and processing equipment to improve catch and consumption.  

Also under SO2, in anticipation of drought conditions in early 2021, FAO will also strategically position water bladder tanks and provide nutritive animal feed blocks to protect the small milking animals of up to 20,000 pastoral households impacted by scarce pasture from dry conditions and/or locust damage. Countrywide livestock vaccination and supportive treatment campaigns will further protect livestock assets belonging to at least 2.2 million men, women and children. Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

project_text:
Emergency Lifesaving Cash and Livelihood Support to IDP and Non- IDP Communities in Somalia Somalia is facing a severe and deteriorating humanitarian crisis as we enter 2022 as a result of the compounding effects of conflict, recurrent climate shocks, diseases and pests outbreaks with increased levels of vulnerability and substantial increase in the humanitarian caseload (Somalia HNO, 2022). There is a serious risk that the impact of consecutive below average to poor rainfall in most parts of the country will develop into a severe drought by early to mid- 2022 with the number of people facing acute food insecurity on the rise. It is likely that minority groups, women, children, people with disabilities, will experience heightened protection risks as a result, unless they are intentionally targeted to receive tailored assistance.

project_text:
WFP SOMALIA 2022 HRP - FSC Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas. As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation. The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

project_text:
Niger Country Strategic Plan La vision de la réponse aux urgences dans le cadre du Plan Stratégique Pays (PSP) 2020-2024 du PAM Niger est la réduction de l’empreinte humanitaire dans la mise en œuvre de l’Activité 1, relative aux urgences du PSP à travers la promotion de l’approche NEXUS. Cette réponse s’inscrit dans la Stratégie de Prévention et de Gestion des Crises Alimentaires 2021 – 2025 du Dispositif National de Prévention et de Gestion de Crises Alimentaires (DNPGCA). Ce plan s’inscrit aussi dans le Plan d’Action 2021-2023 du Comité Technique Tripartite sur le Nexus Urgence-Développement (CTTNUD), en vue d’une mobilisation des ressources financières pour une planification et une mise en œuvre concertée des activités relatives à la promotion du NEXUS.  Dans le cas spécifique de l’assistance aux retournés dans leurs villages d’origine, qui est envisagée en 2022, la Loi 2018-74, relative à la protection et à l’assistance aux Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) cadrera le processus. Rappelons que l’Activité 1, relative aux urgences s’inscrit dans l’effet direct stratégique 1 du CSP (2020-2024) du PAM Niger « Les populations affectées, y compris les réfugiés, les personnes déplacées internes, les communautés hôtes et les retournés dans les zones ciblées sont en mesure de répondre aux besoins alimentaires minimums pendant et après la crise ».  La réponse aux urgences du PAM concernant la SECAL, basée sur une approche flexible, concernera toutes les trois (3) composantes de cette réponse en 2022 :
•	Le Mécanisme de Réponse Rapide (RRM)
•	La réponse aux crises prolongées.
•	La réponse à la soudure agricole et pastorale.
Par ailleurs la prévention de la malnutrition aux enfants 6-23 mois est combinée aux trois composantes ci-dessus.

project_text:
Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre de son mandat et son rôle auprès des partenaires humanitaires et gouvernementaux au niveau des fonctions coordination, gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Le bureau national d’OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois sous-bureaux régionaux à l’Est (Abéché) au Sud (Goré) et la province du Lac (Baga Sola) mettent l’accent sur l’opérationnalisation de ses fonctions y compris en assurant un lien entre les activités humanitaires et de développement (nexus) en vue de promouvoir une solution durable visant à ne pas perpétuer une situation de dépendance humanitaire. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle façon de travailler outre l’opérationnalisation du nexus, le lien avec les objectifs commun des programmes développement, paix et sécurité sera mis en avant. L’accent est aussi mis sur le renforcement de la coordination civilo-militaire afin de faciliter l’accès et la protection des civils.

Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide et efficace afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire rapide et correctement évaluée au niveau des besoins de la population affectée permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.

Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP), la PSEA et la préparation aux urgences en plus d'intégrer une attention au genre et de renforcer la centralité de la protection.
Un plaidoyer pour plus de visibilité des résultats tangibles au niveau de la réponse facilitant la mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires) est aussi défini comme une priorité dans ce projet

OCHA continuera de jouer également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet humanitaire mondial de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW) et le renforcement de l’utilisation de la modalité de transfert monétaire.

Renforcement des mécanismes de Coordination et de Plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali En 2021, la crise humanitaire au Mali s'est aggravée en raison de l'augmentation et de l'expansion des de la violence intercommunautaire et des attaques des groupes armés non étatiques (GANE) dans les régions du centre, du sud et de l'ouest. Cette crise a été aggravée par les bouleversements politiques marqués par deux coups d'état en août 2020 et mai 2021, et l'incertitude persistante de la transition politique laisse l'État dans l'incapacité de répondre aux services sociaux de base des populations. 
Les déplacements internes de personnes ont augmenté de 100 000 en 2021, atteignant plus de 401 000 personnes soit quatre fois plus qu'il y a deux ans. Au total, 156 000 réfugiés maliens résident dans les pays voisins tandis que le Mali accueille 48 000 réfugiés et leur fournit protection et assistance. Les gains économiques du Mali se sont érodés, avec 900 000 personnes (0,04% de la population) qui sont retombées dans la pauvreté en raison de la crise socioéconomique de la COVID-19. la capacité des ménages est fragilisée à cause de la perte de revenus, de la réduction des transferts de fonds et à l'augmentation du coût de la vie. 
La Banque mondiale prévoit une augmentation du taux de pauvreté à 4,8 % en 2022. La crise de protection est également aggravée avec une augmentation des incidents de sécurité.  Les acteurs de la violence basée sur le genre (VBG) ont signalé 5 486 incidents de VBG, soit une augmentation de 41 % comparativement à la même période en 2020. Plus de 1 640 écoles sont fermées en raison de l'insécurité, affectant plus de 2,9 millions d'enfants dont 40 % se trouvent dans la région centrale de Mopti. Quatre districts centraux ont signalé que 40 % des écoles étaient fermées. Dans les régions du sud, 10 pour cent des écoles sont fermées à Koulikoro, Koutiala et Sikasso, privant 30 000 enfants de leur éducation. A ce jour, le Mali a rapporté plus de 15 800 cas de COVID-19.
En 2021, 1,3 million de personnes ont connu un niveau élevé d'insécurité alimentaire aiguë. le niveau le plus élevé depuis 2015, et 3 055 253 personnes ont été touchées par les mauvaises pluies et une saison de soudure prolongée. La situation humanitaire reste entravée par l'augmentation des besoins et la faiblesse des financements, avec 32 % des fonds mobilisés au 31 octobre 2021. Malgré les contraintes opérationnelles, les partenaires humanitaires ont aidé plus de 2,45 millions des 4,7 millions de personnes ciblées au 30 septembre 2021. 
Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent plus de 160 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou, Gao et ouvrira une antenne à Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud Est et Ouest. 

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CM-Coord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer. 

OCHA continuera à jouer son rôle central dans la mobilisation des partenaires, l’utilisation des instruments et des mécanismes de financement tout en veillant à ce que les besoins humanitaires croissants soient prises en compte. OCHA assumera son rôle clé dans la coordination militaire au niveau national et régional de concert avec les forces militaires présentes dans le pays tout en renforçant les capacités des autorités nationales en matière de coordination

project_text:
Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre de son mandat et son rôle auprès des partenaires humanitaires et gouvernementaux au niveau des fonctions coordination, gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Le bureau national d’OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois sous-bureaux régionaux à l’Est (Abéché) au Sud (Goré) et la province du Lac (Baga Sola) mettent l’accent sur l’opérationnalisation de ses fonctions y compris en assurant un lien entre les activités humanitaires et de développement (nexus) en vue de promouvoir une solution durable visant à ne pas perpétuer une situation de dépendance humanitaire. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle façon de travailler outre l’opérationnalisation du nexus, le lien avec les objectifs commun des programmes développement, paix et sécurité sera mis en avant. L’accent est aussi mis sur le renforcement de la coordination civilo-militaire afin de faciliter l’accès et la protection des civils.

Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide et efficace afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire rapide et correctement évaluée au niveau des besoins de la population affectée permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.

Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP), la PSEA et la préparation aux urgences en plus d'intégrer une attention au genre et de renforcer la centralité de la protection.
Un plaidoyer pour plus de visibilité des résultats tangibles au niveau de la réponse facilitant la mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires) est aussi défini comme une priorité dans ce projet

OCHA continuera de jouer également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet humanitaire mondial de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW) et le renforcement de l’utilisation de la modalité de transfert monétaire.

project_text:
Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.
