project_text: ​PROVISION OF PROTECTION AND HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE SERVICES TO MIGRANTS IN VULNERABLE SITUATIONS The project’s aim is to provide a range of protection services to migrants in need, strengthen links between targeted community groups and services available, and enhance knowledge on migrant population groups in Lebanon. Services will target both male and female migrants, with a higher caseload of the latter group due to their increased number in country. Beneficiaries will typically be working age, between 18 and 40 years old. The services that IOM will deliver, either directly or through partners, include legal assistance, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), safe and temporary shelters for vulnerable migrants, provision of non-food items, multipurpose cash assistance (MPCA), and voluntary humanitarian return. These services will be made accessible to migrants by scaling up IOM’s pre-existing case management services, supporting enhanced capacity of, and referral with partners, strengthening translation and interpretation efforts to diminish language barriers facing migrants, and expanding community-level networks to strengthen targeted communities’ awareness of and access to IOM and partner services, as well as wider issues of concern. Finally, enhancing knowledge of migrant populations will involve nationwide data-collection efforts via key informant interviews in order to inform humanitarian planning. The project will be implemented by the IOM in partnership with civil society organizations (CSO) and community-based initiatives, with some services such as shelter, legal assistance referred from IOM. IOM will work with local service providers to strengthen their capacity, to enhance the overall protection network available for migrants in Lebanon. Onward referral to multisector assistance such as food or health support will be mainstreamed across the project.

project_text: Assistance rapide en AME aux populations nouvellement affectées par les conflits dans les régions du Centre Nord, Est, Nord, Sahel, Centre-est, Boucle du Mouhoun La situation sécuritaire continue de se dégrader en 2020. Depuis janvier au 12 novembre 2020; 442 incidents ont été enregistrés causant le décès de 651 personnes, dont 31 enfants . La crise sécuritaire, couplée à l’impact de la COVID-19, ont créé une situation humanitaire sans précédent particulièrement dans 6 régions prioritaires du HRP/HNO . Ces crises viennent exacerber les vulnérabilités déjà existantes dans ces régions, causant le déplacement de 1,049,767 personnes , dont plus de 60% d’enfants. Les ménages affectés ont en majorité perdus leurs AME (Articles Ménagers Essentiels), leurs réserves alimentaires et autres moyens de subsistance affectant la survie des enfants et des familles. De nombreux ménages sont actuellement sans abris et ont intégré des familles d’accueil en attendant la remise en état de leurs abris. La majorité (80%) vivent dans des conditions de logement très précaires, avec l’incapacité financière et matérielle pour faire face aux multiples besoins notamment logement, nourriture les frais de scolarité et l’accès aux soins. La fragilité du contexte actuel exacerbe une vulnérabilité aigüe qu'une partie importante de la population locale vit déjà, et contribue à générer une pression accrue sur l'accès aux ressources d’une manière générale. Il apparait donc urgent d’apporter une réponse à cette situation. La présente action s’inscrit dans cette perspective et vise à « fournir une assistance humanitaire d'urgence en articles ménagers essentiels et en apport monétaire aux populations déplacées affectées par les conflits dans les régions du Centre Nord, Est, Nord, Sahel, Centre-est, Boucle du Mouhoun». Il s’agira de : (i) cibler environ 70,000 personnes dans le besoin en leur fournissant assistance rapide en kits AME de première nécessité alignes sur les standards du cluster et en apport monétaire multisectorielle inconditionnel. Le ciblage géographique selon le nombre des enfants déplacés sera combiné avec des enquêtes ménages de base. On utilisera les infrastructures communautaires pour allouer l'aide à des ménages ayant des enfants avec vulnérabilités aigues. (ii) de veiller à ce que cette assistance soit fournie dans un environnement de protection tout en respectant le principe de « Do no harm ». Les femmes seront les principaux récipiendaires des AME.

project_text: Assistance rapide en AME aux populations nouvellement affectées par les conflits dans les régions du Centre Nord, Est, Nord, Sahel, Centre-est, Boucle du Mouhoun La situation sécuritaire continue de se dégrader en 2020. Depuis janvier au 12 novembre 2020; 442 incidents ont été enregistrés causant le décès de 651 personnes, dont 31 enfants . La crise sécuritaire, couplée à l’impact de la COVID-19, ont créé une situation humanitaire sans précédent particulièrement dans 6 régions prioritaires du HRP/HNO . Ces crises viennent exacerber les vulnérabilités déjà existantes dans ces régions, causant le déplacement de 1,049,767 personnes , dont plus de 60% d’enfants. Les ménages affectés ont en majorité perdus leurs AME (Articles Ménagers Essentiels), leurs réserves alimentaires et autres moyens de subsistance affectant la survie des enfants et des familles. De nombreux ménages sont actuellement sans abris et ont intégré des familles d’accueil en attendant la remise en état de leurs abris. La majorité (80%) vivent dans des conditions de logement très précaires, avec l’incapacité financière et matérielle pour faire face aux multiples besoins notamment logement, nourriture les frais de scolarité et l’accès aux soins. La fragilité du contexte actuel exacerbe une vulnérabilité aigüe qu'une partie importante de la population locale vit déjà, et contribue à générer une pression accrue sur l'accès aux ressources d’une manière générale. Il apparait donc urgent d’apporter une réponse à cette situation. La présente action s’inscrit dans cette perspective et vise à « fournir une assistance humanitaire d'urgence en articles ménagers essentiels et en apport monétaire aux populations déplacées affectées par les conflits dans les régions du Centre Nord, Est, Nord, Sahel, Centre-est, Boucle du Mouhoun». Il s’agira de : (i) cibler environ 70,000 personnes dans le besoin en leur fournissant assistance rapide en kits AME de première nécessité alignes sur les standards du cluster et en apport monétaire multisectorielle inconditionnel. Le ciblage géographique selon le nombre des enfants déplacés sera combiné avec des enquêtes ménages de base. On utilisera les infrastructures communautaires pour allouer l'aide à des ménages ayant des enfants avec vulnérabilités aigues. (ii) de veiller à ce que cette assistance soit fournie dans un environnement de protection tout en respectant le principe de « Do no harm ». Les femmes seront les principaux récipiendaires des AME.

On utilisera les infrastructures communautaires pour allouer l'aide à des ménages ayant des enfants avec vulnérabilités aigues. project_text:
Provision of lifesaving assistance and sustainable solutions through safe Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services, for people in crises and their host communities in multiple regions in Somalia. IOM WASH is proposing to contribute to the continuation and restoration of access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to overall 380,000 beneficiaries from vulnerable IDP and host-communities in multiple regions in Somalia. 

Specifically, the project will target 228,000 Nondisplaced people (children 107,160; men 41,040; women 36,480; elderly 9,120 and disabled 34,200) and 152,000 displaced populations (children 71,440; men 27,360; women 24,320; elderly 6,080 and disabled 22,800). 

IOM will rehabilitate 50 strategic water sources for multi-use that will provide continued, equitable, safe, sufficient and sustainable water to regions, targeted by the cluster, prone to natural disasters. 

IOM further proposes to construct 3,000 new emergency sanitation facilities (following cluster specifications) targeting populations without access to basic sanitation and hygiene.

The project will also strengthen the capacity of the Federal Government of Somalia and Federal Members States, community leaders and water committees/technicians for better coordination with government authorities and communities and sustainability of the constructed/ rehabilitated WASH infrastructures. In addition, the project will nurture community participation in good hygiene practices through training and community sensitization campaigns.  All trainings, awareness raising and capacity building activities will follow national guidelines on COVID-19 preventive measures, e.g. on physical distancing, to avoid mass gatherings and minimize risks of exposure.

The project is aligned with protection mainstreaming to ensure safety and dignity of affected populations without causing harm. Affected populations and all relevant stakeholders including men, women, boys, girls, elderly and people with disability will be involved in decision making throughout the project activities/cycle. 

Furthermore, the project will be a part of an IOM integrated emergency response program and resilience building, where possible, efforts will be made to integrate IOM health, nutrition, shelter, CCCM and protection activities.

project_text:
Children (girls and boys) and their families affected by disaster are protected against violence, abuse, exploitation, discrimination and other violations of their rights. Child protection issues are exacerbated during disaster, requiring immediate protection services to bring normalcy back in the lives of girls, boys and women. Measures to prevent abuse and violence and respond to cases of survivors of violence and exploitation need to be strengthened by providing safe access to protective services. Likewise, psychosocial distress experienced by people at the onset of any emergency requires professional care and support. Hence, the project provides mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) and coordination as a core area of response. An increase of CP risks is being observed in the current COVID-19 pandemic as well. Some of these may include: Physical and emotional maltreatment, Gender-based violence (GBV), mental health and psychosocial distress, child labour, unaccompanied and separated children and social exclusion. Following are some of the interventions:

1.	Establishment of protective spaces to cater the needs of vulnerable girls, boys and women including disable. The protective spaces will be run by trained facilitators and provided with recreational and learning materials. It will offer opportunities for girls and boys to build resilience and recover from their experiences, provide a daily routine and a sense of normalcy.
2.	Provision of Psychosocial Support (PSS) is primarily aimed at those individuals or group of people who require care and support including those in isolation or quarantine in case of the current COVID-19 situation. Digital platforms will be used for delivering PSS while there are movement restrictions in place. The PSS will be provided at three levels tailored to the needs of target population:
•	Within facilities receiving suspected/infected people for care and support including isolation and quarantine facilities.
•	Community based support in areas identified with suspected/infected people or receiving people exiting isolation/quarantine facilities and going through the social reintegration phase. Families, relatives and caregivers of such people will also be able to avail such services and support.
•	Referral pathways in collaboration of case management for accessing social protection services/packages.
3.	People demonstrating exacerbated distress and signs of mental health concerns or adverse reactions, would be referred to specialized mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). Digital platforms will be used for delivery of MHPSS while movement restrictions are in place. 
4.	Provide CP monitoring and outreach social mobilization through dedicated and trained CP monitors and facilitators in coordination with community-based CP structures and CP Working Groups and Govt. counterparts;
5.	Establish and strengthen coordination amongst key stakeholders and community-based CP structures for the identification of vulnerable girls, boys and women, including missing, unaccompanied, separated and disabled children, and promote their access to protection, social and psychosocial services through an effective and efficient case management and referral system;
6.	Capacity building of relevant service providers, Govt. officials including DMAs, CSOs, rights-holders and duty-bearers in Child Protection in Emergency (CPiE), psychosocial support and strengthening advocacy and support for girls, boys and women affected by disaster to achieve enhanced protection for them;
7.	Dissemination of critical information for prevention of violence against children (VAC) using different communication channels. In the current context, service provision will prioritize prevention of stigma, labelling and discrimination of people who are perceived to be infected or affected by COVID-19. The promotion of correct information and addressing emerging myths and rumors including positive understanding and behaviours about ‘social distancing’ should therefore include actions that support people to adopt and maintain healthy and rationale lifestyles.

project_text: Health-related vulnerabilities of Rohingya and Host Communities are reduced through increased quality access to comprehensive health services The aims of IOMs’ health interventions aim to respond to the lifesaving needs and improve the resilience of affected populations, with special attention to gender and age considerations, and vulnerable groups. In the camps,34% Rohingya refugee populations, have reported going into debt to pay for health expenses, and 27% seeking lower-quality care or medication, due to a lack of money (Joint Multi-Sector Needs Assessment J-MSNA 2020). This demonstrates some challenges in the already strained health service system in Cox’s Bazar. To address this, this intervention aims to contribute  to  i) increased safe, dignified and meaningful access and utilization of quality comprehensive healthcare services, focusing on sexual, reproductive, maternal, neonatal, child and adolescent health; mental health and psychosocial support; and non-communicable diseases (NCD); ii) improved health seeking behavior, encouragement of  healthy living and promotion of the  utilization of essential service package and community engagement, with special attention to vulnerable groups iii) measures to prepare and (timely) respond  to health emergencies, during disaster (including monsoon and cyclone) and outbreaks of communicable disease (e.g.  COVID-19 and AWD). IOM also aims to contribute to the improvement of quality of services through performance monitoring, evaluation, coordination and capacity building.

reportDetails_organization: European Commission's Humanitarian Aid and Civil Protection Department
project_text:
Education in Emergencies Response for Crises Affected Children in Bay region of Somalia 
Conflict and environmental shocks have been the primary drivers of humanitarian needs in Somalia, leaving girls and boys out of school. According to the Protection Return Monitoring Network (PRMN), 593,000 people were displaced in Somalia between January and September 2021, of which 420,000 were displaced due to conflict and 98,000 due to drought1. Of the people displaced this year, an estimated 237,200 (40%) are school-aged children. In total, there is about 2.9 million displaced people in Somalia and an estimated 1 million of these are school-aged children.

FCA rapid needs assessment (10/21) highlighted the challenges faced by the assessed schools in baidoa and Dinsoor  which include  lack of accessible and gender friendly structures such as chairs,  desks, classrooms, latrines and handwashing facilities, accompanied by shortage of learning and teaching materials such as books, pens and chalks. Lack of qualified and inadequate number of teachers, especially female teachers as well as teachers who are trained in special education needs to handle children with CWDs and negative cultural norms have contributed to the low enrolment, attendance and retention of girls and CwD in schools. The barriers faced by CwD are not limited to those faced by girls, but their enrolment, retention and movement to education are hindered by additional stigma, discrimination and misconceptions. Lack of adequate fencing of the school compound to promote protection and safety and long distances to school cause safety concerns particularly for girls. EiE actors require capacity to provide quality education to CwD. Caregivers also faced with challenges in covering school fees, uniforms and scholastic materials. Strengthening the involvement of community in school management activities and mainstreaming child protection and child safeguarding mechanisms into education will improve access to education for girls and CwD.
Aligning with the 2022 Somalia Humanitarian Response Plan, the proposed initiative aims to restore and maintain access to and retention of crisis-affected school children to safe, protective, inclusive and continuous learning opportunities in Bay region of South West State of Somalia. The project will put a strong emphasis on an integrated approach to education focusing on access, quality of education, protection, child safeguarding, gender equality, conflict sensitivity, and disaster risk reduction (DRR) in the design, approach and activities. 
The proposed project will benefit 7100, crisis-affected children (4,400 children in Baidoa and 2,700 children in Dinsor) with at least 45% of girls. The vulnerable poor host community children (40%) will also be targeted since they are also affected by the crisis and have limited access to quality education. Protection and psychosocial well-being of the affected boys and girls as well as teachers is central to the project. FCA will closely work with Somalia Institute for Special Education Needs and Disability (SISEND), the only disability NGO in Somalia that specializes in special education needs, to provide capacity building to teachers, MoE and other education personnel. 
FCA has excellent capacity to scale up, applying best practices and lessons learned from its EiE experiences in other districts of South West State (Baidoa, El-berde and Hudur) to Dinsoor.. Utilizing FCA integrated and innovative approach based on well-known Finnish education system, FCA will take into account the potential impact of Covid-19 pandemic and develop innovative solutions to ensure uninterrupted access to education by the target children.

The proposed project will be implemented in Baidoa and Dinsoor where there are high number of IDP and are in IPC 3. The implementation will be done in close partnership with GREDO; a local NGO that is currently partnering with FCA on the ECHO funded EiE Projects. The project will also be implemented in close collaboration with MoE of Southwest State.

project_text:
Back to school Campaign in Flood Affected Areas of Sindh The Back to School Campaign through provision of food aims to encourage return and resumption to education in areas affected by natural disasters, with the aim of reducing barriers in access to  primary school  for boys and girls while supporting their families to meet their basic food needs at home. Targeted beneficiaries  will receive fortified wheat flour of 25 kg (bimonthly) as take-home ration, conditional upon enrolment and regular attendance at schools or temporary learning centers notified by the Government. The project will be implemented in collaboration with Education and Literacy Department, Government of Sindh and target 71,480 children (35,740 boys & 35,740 girls) enrolled in primary boys’ and girls’ schools with 3,574 MT of Wheat Flour in affected areas of districts Badin and Sajawal, Sindh. The project is in alignment with the objectives of Sindh Education Sector Plan and CM’s forthcoming Bokh Mitao Programme and will implemented in areas where WFP’s other interventions (nutrition, food assistance, DRR and social protection) are ongoing. 
 
Justification:
 According to UNDP’s latest Report on Multi-dimensional Poverty in Pakistan the incidence and severity of multi-dimensional poverty is high in the southern part of the province. For instance, approximately 84% of peoples live in multi-dimensional poverty in Badin while it is 68% for Sajawal district. Similarly, according to RNA 2020, 72% of assessed population in Badin and 63% in Sajawal reported inability to buy food and in the case of any emergency the average food stock for their own consumption may last for 5 days only. These districts also host many out of schoolboys and girls of age 5-16 years, and school completion rates are drastically low. Displacement, school damages and discontinuity of educational activities resulting from floods and other disasters further deteriorates education situation in the affected areas.

Disasters’ negative impact on lives, livelihoods, livestock, agriculture, infrastructure, access to social and life-saving services and income generation opportunities is significantly high on the children, women, disabled and elderly peoples. Among others, the incidences of less availability of food for children and women at home, engagement in labor and income generation activities, children dropout from school and early marriages of girls are common in most of the cases. 

WFP’s experience of emergency response in Pakistan suggests that school feeding programmes can play an instrumental role in bringing children back to school while reducing their chances of drop out, engagement in child labor or early marriages. Provision of take-home rations- a means to transfer resources to vulnerable households and subsidize families’ food basket, motivate families to send and retain their children in schools and hence, contribute to increase enrolment, retention and attendance at schools. 

Effectiveness of school feeding is evident from flood response in 2011-12. WFP field monitoring reports of school feeding under indicated that almost 97 percent of students were retained in schools in Sindh. Similarly, analysis of education indicators in WFP assisted vs non-assisted schools in Erstwhile FATA showed that enrolment rates increased at 15% in WFP assisted schools as compared to 3% in non-assisted schools. Moreover, the retention rate in WFP-assisted primary schools in 2016-2017 was as high as 80.1 %, against WFP’s target of 70 % (compared to 24% in all primary schools in erstwhile FATA).

The PIN has been determined by undertaking a severity analysis of the population in each vulnerable districts experiencing multiple shocks recently such as (drought, monsoon rains/flooding, winterized emergency, locust infestation and  COVID) which has affected their food security security situation. project_text:
Food & Cash-based Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia for 2021 Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas.  As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation.  The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of a La Niña that is currently developing (75 percent chance through Feb 2021). Potential drought conditions will likely develop as a result of below average 2020 Deyr (Oct-Dec), a harsh 2021 dry Jilaal (Jan-Mar) season and a possible delay and/or poor performance of the 2021 Gu (Apr-Jun). 

Continued emergency relief alongside a further scale up of support to increase resilience is required in order to avert the hardship situation. WFP is therefore seeking resources in 2021 to sustain the on-going efforts and enable households meet immediate food needs and help build resilience against shocks. WFP is planning to implement unconditional and conditional transfers to improve access to food under integrated multi sectoral assistance to meet needs of vulnerable girls and women, pregnant and lactating women, boys and men and leverage resources with other partners to meet the level of humanitarian assistance required. WFP will continue to participate in cluster, joint planning, assessments and regular meetings with other humanitarian actors in Somalia. WFP employs gender sensitive beneficiary targeting in all its projects and prioritizes female and single headed households. Community consultations are carried out with men and women to ensure that their voices are heard. Accountability to affected populations ensured through information sharing, surveys and beneficiary feedback mechanisms. Beneficiaries are targeted and registered through biometric SCOPE system that provides real time data.

project_text:
Programa de seguridad alimentaria basado en la escuela Con el objetivo de contribuir a la seguridad alimentaria de la población con mayores necesidades, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de Naciones Unidas (WFP, por sus siglas en inglés) en Venezuela desarrolla un programa de asistencia humanitaria basado en la escuela para garantizar el acceso de los más vulnerables a una alimentación adecuada y nutritiva en el entorno escolar, familiar y comunitario. 
Este programa inició en 2021 con comidas escolares en emergencias priorizando escuelas iniciales y de educación especial.

WFP proporciona comidas escolares acompañado de un paquete integrado de intervenciones para mejorar el acceso a alimentos nutritivos y diversificados a través de las escuelas, contribuyendo al mismo tiempo a mejorar la salud y la nutrición de los niños en edad escolar, los estudiantes con discapacidad y el personal escolar, y apoyando a las comunidades a reducir la dependencia en estrategias de afrontamiento. De manera gradual, el WFP está realizando compras locales de alimentos, e incluyendo acciones para apoyar los mercados locales con compras a pequeños productores y apoyo técnico para acceso a mercados.

En este sentido, el programa de comidas escolares en emergencias tiene los siguientes componentes, para asegurar un enfoque integral que apoye al estudiante en el entorno escolar y familiar:

1. Entrega de comidas escolares nutritivas para estudiantes y personal escolar, promoviendo las compras locales y a pequeños productores.
2. Apoyo a la seguridad alimentaria del hogar a través de comida en especie o transferencias monetarias.
3. Rehabilitación de cocinas escolares para garantizar condiciones adecuadas de preparación de alimentos.
4. Comunicación para sensibilizar acerca de los principios humanitarios, la adecuada preparación de alimentos, nutrición, higiene y mantenimiento de cocinas escolares.
5. Fortalecimiento de capacidades de socios implementadores y personal escolar.
6. Acciones sensibles a la nutrición, que incluyen, tamizaje en las escuelas, educación nutricional, referencia a servicios especializados y entrega de alimento complementario fortificado (Supercereal Plus).

destinationObjects_Project.name: Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan
project_text:
Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace.

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

project_text: Enhancing access to  lifesaving WASH services for  vulnerable host and IDP communities in Somalia The proposed project aims to cover the WASH needs of the vulnerable host and IDPs community, the high humanitarian needs in Somalia are driven by seasonal floods, severe drought conditions, acute water diarrhea/ cholera outbreaks and protracted crises, exacerbated by COVID-19 outbreak. In May 2021, 50 of the 74 districts in Somalia faced severe water shortages and water prices increased and this is expected to crossover to 2022 with an already delayed Deyr(October-November) rains, Drought remains the main driver of WASH needs in Somalia leading to displacement and communal conflict over water points and the project intends to cover the needs & offer both emergency and long term sustainable solution to avert the potential risk of losing life’s   through the multiple shocks, The WASH response will contribute to increased access to water and sanitation facilities for the vulnerable communities  and prevention of a further increase in AWD/Cholera which is endemic in Somalia , as well as raise awareness to prevent the spread of COVID-19 through risk communication and community engagement, and support compliance to recommended measures through hygiene promotion, hygiene kits distribution and increased access to water and soap. To further improve the contribution of WASH to the achievement of health outcomes, the proposed WASH response will invest improvements of  behavioral change through advocacy of attainment of community  ownership of projects to prolong the lifespan & sustainability of projects for  access to WASH facilities in health care facilities and other public institutions, the project intends to complement with Action Against Hunger Health and Nutrition projects in hard to reach areas to reach the elderly, disable and vulnerable person are included and targeted in activities,  Overall, the project envisages to reach 70,000 individuals (19,809M, 19180 F,15,505 B and 15,506 G) including 7,111 people living with disabilities for a period of 12 months in Bakool, Bay, Lower Shabelle,  Nugaal,  Banadir, ACF WASH project will be gender  sensitive through inclusion of women in WASH committee and are represented in crucial roles, are consulted in the design of the project especially during the planning,design and distribution of MHM kits to understand  women and girls preference & functionality of the products in the local  markets, The project will adopt protection mainstreaming in WASH  and that latrines are gender segregated and with a barrier screen for privacy   and WASH facilities are disable friendly through construction of ramps during distribution of WASH Kits triage sort of mechanisms will be adopted to give priority to those who cannot stand in line for long periods, such as older persons, persons with disability, unaccompanied children, pregnant and lactating women, so that they wait for less time. Community hygiene volunteers and community health workers will be trained and work closely with the targeted communities and ensure that WASH minimum at health facilities are attained and the project linked with other interventions(FSL, Health & Nutrition)  supported by  Action Against Hunger for optimal impact of the project

project_text:
Niger Country Strategic Plan La vision de la réponse aux urgences dans le cadre du Plan Stratégique Pays (PSP) 2020-2024 du PAM Niger est la réduction de l’empreinte humanitaire dans la mise en œuvre de l’Activité 1, relative aux urgences du PSP à travers la promotion de l’approche NEXUS. Cette réponse s’inscrit dans la Stratégie de Prévention et de Gestion des Crises Alimentaires 2021 – 2025 du Dispositif National de Prévention et de Gestion de Crises Alimentaires (DNPGCA). Ce plan s’inscrit aussi dans le Plan d’Action 2021-2023 du Comité Technique Tripartite sur le Nexus Urgence-Développement (CTTNUD), en vue d’une mobilisation des ressources financières pour une planification et une mise en œuvre concertée des activités relatives à la promotion du NEXUS.  Dans le cas spécifique de l’assistance aux retournés dans leurs villages d’origine, qui est envisagée en 2022, la Loi 2018-74, relative à la protection et à l’assistance aux Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) cadrera le processus. Rappelons que l’Activité 1, relative aux urgences s’inscrit dans l’effet direct stratégique 1 du CSP (2020-2024) du PAM Niger « Les populations affectées, y compris les réfugiés, les personnes déplacées internes, les communautés hôtes et les retournés dans les zones ciblées sont en mesure de répondre aux besoins alimentaires minimums pendant et après la crise ».  La réponse aux urgences du PAM concernant la SECAL, basée sur une approche flexible, concernera toutes les trois (3) composantes de cette réponse en 2022 :
•	Le Mécanisme de Réponse Rapide (RRM)
•	La réponse aux crises prolongées.
•	La réponse à la soudure agricole et pastorale.
Par ailleurs la prévention de la malnutrition aux enfants 6-23 mois est combinée aux trois composantes ci-dessus.

project_text:
Amélioration de la qualité et de la coordination de la réponse aux situations d’urgence Le Mali comme la majeure partie des pays de la zone Sahélienne, est confronté à une crise humanitaire depuis plusieurs années qui tend à s’aggraver au lieu de diminuer. Parmi les principales causes, il peut être citer les conséquences des changements climatiques qui frappent durement les pays de la zone avec des phénomènes comme l’irrégularité des pluies, les inondations, les sécheresses localisées ou généralisées. A ces phénomènes, il faut ajouter les épidémies comme le cholera ou encore la COVID 19. En effet, Afin de lutter efficacement comme la pandémie de la COVID 19, les pays de la zone sahélienne dont restreint les mouvements des populations, fermer des marchés ou encore instaurer des couvres feu. Ces mesures ont négativement impacté les revenus des ménages les plus vulnérables. De même, du fait des mesures de restriction liées à la COVID 19, les transferts monétaires des Maliens de l’étranger vers leurs familles restées au pays ont diminué de manière significative augmentant par la même occasion la vulnérabilité des populations. Mais c’est la situation d’insécurité qui prévaut dans le nord et le centre du pays qui est à la base de la plus grande crise humanitaire actuelle. En effet, un grand nombre de ménages ne sont pas en mesure de se rendre dans leurs champs pour cultiver du fait de l’insécurité qui règne. De même, du fait de la fermeture de nombreux marchés itinérants de fait de l’insécurité, les ménages ne sont plus en mesure vendre leurs surplus de récoltes ou de se ravitailler. Mais la conséquence la plus visible de cette situation d’insécurité est le déplacement d’un grand nombre de ménages principalement issus du milieu rural. Selon le DTM de septembre 2022, ce sont 401.736 personnes déplacées internes soit (69.696 ménages) qui ont été enregistrés sur l’ensemble du territoire malien. Les zones d’installation de ces personnes déplacées internes sont les suivantes, Bamako, Gao, Kayes, Kidal, Koulikoro, Ménaka, Mopti, Ségou, Sikasso. 
Afin de répondre à ces différentes situations d’urgence, plusieurs organisations développent des projets qu’ils mettent en œuvre au profit des ménages affectés. Cependant, force est reconnaitre qu’il y a souvent un manque de préparation et un déficit de coordination sur le terrain. 
Le présent projet vise à répondre à cette faiblesse de la réponse aux situations d’urgence en renforçant les capacités des organisations sur la préparation et la réponse mais également en renforçant la coordination entre les acteurs de la réponse humanitaire.

project_text: Assistance aux populations victimes du déficit céréalier de 2021 des Régions de Tahoua, Tillabéri, Dosso, Diffa, Maradi et Agadez A l’issue de la campagne agricole 2021, il a été enregistré 6430 villages déficitaires à plus de 50% pour une population estimée à 8 762 358 personnes.Ce déficite résulte du changement climatique (dont l'impact a été des sécheresses prolongées, des inondations, un arrêt précoce de la saison pluvieuse), une détérioration de la situation sécuritaire qui continue d’impacter négativement l'éffort de production des populations et leurs moyens d’existence dans certaines zones localisées des régions de Diffa, Tillabéri, le  nord Tahoua et le sud-ouest de Maradi. La production céréalière brute 2021 est estimée à 3 562 549 tonnes (contre 5 576 371 tonnes en 2020) soit une baisse de 36% par rapport à l’année 2020. A l'heure, c'est environ 2 554 833 personnes (364,976 ménages) qui sont en insécurité alimentaire sévère et qui nécessitent une aide humanitaire d'urgence.Pour répondre à cette crise alimentaire, le gouvernement a élaboré un plan d'urgence estimé à plus de  280 Milliards de Dollars USD pour la période de novembre 2021 à Mars 2022 en attendant l'élaboration du plan de soutien . Selon les résultats de cadre harmonisé de novembre 3.6 millions de personnes seraient en insécurité alimentaire en période de soudure s'y les réponses adaquates ne sont pas apportées. L’objectif global du Plan d’urgence est de contribuer à la sécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle des populations vulnérables affectées par cette crise humanitaire à travers des actions harmonisées d’assistance alimentaire et de protection de leurs moyens d’existence. Le plan vise à améliorer l’accès aux aliments pour les ménages vulnérables, protéger et renforcer les moyens d’existence des ménages vulnérables, faciliter l’accès aux intrants agricoles, vétérinaires et zootechniques des ménages vulnérables.Ainsi en soutien au plan de d'urgence, de soutien et du plan de réponse humanitaire  en lien avec la stratégie du ccluster sécurité alimentaire la FAO apportera un appui au volet agricole par un soutien à la production agricole à 91144 ménages vulnérables et des appuis AGR.

project_text:
Provision of life-saving WASH assistance and restoration of access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to drought, conflict, floods and diseases outbreaks affected most vulnerable communities including displaced, non- displaced populations and Institutions from Lower juba, Benadir, and Sool  region of Somalia/Somaliland. In the context of the current multi-faceted emergencies (increased risks of flooding, protracted conflict, droughts, Covid 19, Cholera/AWD Outbreaks, Alight proposes this emergency WASH project to target IDPs and most vulnerable host communities to save lives, restoring access to basic wash services, and reducing morbidities associated with WASH-related diseases. The project will target worst – affected districts such as Kismayo, Benadir, Afmadow, lascanod, Telex, Badade , and Xudun.
Alight understands that droughts and protracted conflicts are the key drivers of internal displacements and also the humanitarian needs in Somalia. Many IDPs and Poor vulnerable Host communities are currently residing in Urban and pre-urban informal crowded areas with insufficient access to water and Sanitation. According to JMCNA assessment done in August by REACH, 53% of the IDPs face challenges in terms of access to WASH services in Somalia. The situation of IDPs and non- IDPs vulnerable host community members are complicated by frequently forced evictions meted on them leading to disruptions of access to critical WASH services and loss of gains made on access to these essential services.  According to JMCNA 2021, 39 per cent of vulnerable people in Somalia do not have access to sustained, improved and safe water sources for drinking and other domestic uses, while 84 per cent still walk for more than 15 minutes to the nearest water source. Due to these constraints, one in five Somalis does not have enough water per day to cover their basic needs for both drinking and domestic use.
Cognizant of these contexts, Alight will provide emergency water trucking to 12000 (2000HH) drought-affected IDPs and vulnerable pastoral communities living in drought-prone areas of Lascanod, Xudun, Telex and Afmadow districts for two months as the agency will find and rehabilitate alternative water sources for the affected people. 12 critical shallow wells will be rehabilitated and protected targeting IDPs and Non- IDPs vulnerable communities and settlements from Kismayo, Kaxda & wartanabada (Banadir), Lascanod, Telex. Alight will also conduct Disinfections and chlorination of floods affected wells. 
Alight will Provide 10 Strategic boreholes in drought-prone locations in Lascanood, Telex, and Xudun and Afmadow district with generators, submersible pumps, cable wires and control panels to ensure drought affected peoples have access to safe, adequate and reliable water.
ARC will establish 6 Pipeline water extensions to identified IDPs Camps and non- IDPs camps including the construction of elevated water storage tanks, installation of solar-powered systems and water kiosk with a minimum of 6 taps to ensure increased access to adequate water by the IDPs and Non-IDPs. Alight will construct/rehabilitate 600 gender-segregated, disability-friendly communal latrines for IDPs and vulnerable host community members who have no access to any sanitation facilities. Alight will construct sex-Disaggregated, Disability Inclusive 40 Institutional latrines with water and Handwashing facilities for 24 target schools and 15 health centres.
 Hygiene promotion will remain a key component of the intervention to prevent the spread of Covid-19 and other WASH-related diseases through risk communications and community engagement promoting behaviour changes.  2000 Hygiene kits and basic MHM kits will be provided to adolescent girls in schools and villages/camps. Alight will target approximately 48, 000 beneficiaries from North and south-central Somalia (7488 women, 5823 men, 12165 boys, 12165 girls, 9201 disabled, and 1158 elderly people). Alight will consult men, boys, girls, elderly, and people with disabilities on their needs and preference regarding the type, Design and location of the water and sanitation facilities to address barriers relating to access. Alight will involve women, boys, girls and disabled people in the project monitoring and their feedback will be sought.

According to JMCNA assessment done in August by REACH, 53% of the IDPs face challenges in terms of access to WASH services in Somalia. The situation of IDPs and non- IDPs vulnerable host community members are complicated by frequently forced evictions meted on them leading to disruptions of access to critical WASH services and loss of gains made on access to these essential services.  According to JMCNA 2021, 39 per cent of vulnerable people in Somalia do not have access to sustained, improved and safe water sources for drinking and other domestic uses, while 84 per cent still walk for more than 15 minutes to the nearest water source. Due to these constraints, one in five Somalis does not have enough water per day to cover their basic needs for both drinking and domestic use.
Cognizant of these contexts, Alight will provide emergency water trucking to 12000 (2000HH) drought-affected IDPs and vulnerable pastoral communities living in drought-prone areas of Lascanod, Xudun, Telex and Afmadow districts for two months as the agency will find and rehabilitate alternative water sources for the affected people. 12 critical shallow wells will be rehabilitated and protected targeting IDPs and Non- IDPs vulnerable communities and settlements from Kismayo, Kaxda & wartanabada (Banadir), Lascanod, Telex. Alight will also conduct Disinfections and chlorination of floods affected wells. 
Alight will Provide 10 Strategic boreholes in drought-prone locations in Lascanood, Telex, and Xudun and Afmadow district with generators, submersible pumps, cable wires and control panels to ensure drought affected peoples have access to safe, adequate and reliable water.
ARC will establish 6 Pipeline water extensions to identified IDPs Camps and non- IDPs camps including the construction of elevated water storage tanks, installation of solar-powered systems and water kiosk with a minimum of 6 taps to ensure increased access to adequate water by the IDPs and Non-IDPs. Alight will construct/rehabilitate 600 gender-segregated, disability-friendly communal latrines for IDPs and vulnerable host community members who have no access to any sanitation facilities. Alight will construct sex-Disaggregated, Disability Inclusive 40 Institutional latrines with water and Handwashing facilities for 24 target schools and 15 health centres.
 Hygiene promotion will remain a key component of the intervention to prevent the spread of Covid-19 and other WASH-related diseases through risk communications and community engagement promoting behaviour changes.  2000 Hygiene kits and basic MHM kits will be provided to adolescent girls in schools and villages/camps. Alight will target approximately 48, 000 beneficiaries from North and south-central Somalia (7488 women, 5823 men, 12165 boys, 12165 girls, 9201 disabled, and 1158 elderly people). Alight will consult men, boys, girls, elderly, and people with disabilities on their needs and preference regarding the type, Design and location of the water and sanitation facilities to address barriers relating to access. Alight will involve women, boys, girls and disabled people in the project monitoring and their feedback will be sought.

project_text:
Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

project_text:
Strengthening Child Protection interventions for girls and boys most at risk of violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation across whole of Syria In line with the CP Area of Responsibility (AOR) Strategy and the “No Lost Generation” framework, UNICEF will enhance equitable access to quality CP services with a resilience focus, including for Survivors of abuse, violence, neglect and exploitation as well as children with disabilities, targeting 117 high severity sub-districts (3 to 5) and 38 low severity ones.

UNICEF’s CP Strategy in 2022-2023 includes:
• Addressing behavioural, social, cultural and economic determinants of CP violations as a prevention approach.  
• Improving the reach and quality of specialized CP services
• Capacity development of CP responders
•  Monitoring, evidence generation and advocacy 

UNICEF will support the delivery of integrated programming that will encourage social transformation, prioritizing:
• Structured and sustained CP MHPSS and EORE programmes
• Specialized integrated CP services including case management for survivors of violence, exploitation, neglect and abuse (child labour, CAFAAG, child survivors of GBV, child marriages, justice for children, birth registration and unaccompanied or separated children amongst others) 
• Parenting programmes to promote positive child rearing skills and experience for caregivers
• Elimination of violence against children, including GBV prevention and empowerment for girls, boys and women, prevention of violence in schools, homes and communities.
• Awareness-raising on CP risks
• Capacity development of CP responders and social workers

UNICEF will generate evidence to inform the humanitarian response and advocacy including setting up an information management system for case management. UNICEF will embrace new delivery modalities and implement cash transfers aimed at child protection outcomes for vulnerable families. UNICEF will also continue to support the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism on grave violations against children.

CP services will be delivered by partners based on minimum standards and IASC guidelines. 7,200 CP and social workers will be trained on case management, MHPSS, EORE, advocacy, evidence generation and coordination across sectors for a comprehensive CP response.
 
UNICEF will support MHPSS for 364,000 children to benefit from improved mental health and social wellbeing. UNICEF will equip 61,500 parents and caregivers with skills to provide a stimulating and safe environment at home, including reduced violence.  

Violence prevention is a key priority. Family violence prevalence is high for girls 12-17 years (47%), boys 12-17 years (44%), boys below 12 (45%) and girls below 12 (44%) (UNICEF 2018). UNICEF will work to protect children from violence and abuse through prevention activities in schools, homes and communities and providing survivors of violence with child-friendly and gender sensitive services. Support will be provided for PSEA mechanisms to protect beneficiaries and build the capacity of humanitarian actors. PSEA programming will be implemented with the Protection Sector AORs.

Based on HNO 2021, one in three communities in Syria is reportedly contaminated by explosive ordnance. One in four victims is a child (Joint MA & CP Analysis, 2020). EORE messages will be provided to 1,460,000 children and adults through humanitarian actors and public service providers using static facilities and mobile teams. UNICEF will build the capacity of partners to provide quality EORE that is age, gender and disability appropriate and to provide child victims with assistance.
 
UNICEF will strengthen the justice system to ensure that children in contact with the law victims, offenders or witnesses are protected through child-friendly, gender-sensitive services, that are community-based and family focused.

As Lead Agency for the CP AOR, UNICEF will ensure coordination needs at Hub and WOS levels. Two UN-led and one INGO-led coordination hubs in Damascus, Gaziantep and NES, as well as a WOS overall coordination system, to ensure coherence across the CP response.

project_text:
Fostering Resilience through Early Recovery response for the most Crisis impacted Communities in Syria The Integrated Response for Resilience Programme aims at providing a comprehensive
response through Early Recovery support in 80 communities impacted by the crisis.
Communities, particularly those most dramatically affected – and under additional stress
because of IDPs returns and other displacements - need assistance in reinforcing their
resilience to address these shocks as well as the consequences of the protracted crisis,
and to address their needs on seriously depleted infrastructures and service capacities.
The essence of the Programme is about providing Syrian communities with – still limited -
support to regain control over their basic needs (livelihoods, access to essential services)
and reduce their dependency on humanitarian assistance. Prioritization of locations, is the
outcome of a context analysis and needs assessment conducted on more than 5,000
Syrian communities, based on the following three criteria:
1) Hard to Reach Areas
2) Areas of major IDPs presence and IDPs returns
3) Highest scoring in the Severity Scale
The integrated response consists of the following components: strengthening of social
services-related capacities (access and coverage), livelihoods creation and rural recovery,
PWDs support, social cohesion/community safety, reducing gender inequality and youth
marginality, women empowerment, tensions reduction and rehabilitation of basic
infrastructure and public services.
The program is built in a modular manner both in terms of geographical and
sectoral/thematic interventions and foresees the allotment of average 1 Million US$ per
community. Hence, donors willing to support this approach will be able to pre-select
certain location(s) and/or area(s) of intervention of their preference, within the 200
prioritized communities.
The programme relates directly to the sector objectives:
1. Living conditions
2. Livelihoods
3. Access to social services
4. Access to productive and market infrastructure
5. Social protection
6. Strengthening of local public services delivery capacity
7. Reinforcing opportunities and capacities for civic engagement

reportDetails_organization: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
project_text:
Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2021, there are more than 314,000 refugees from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, including from Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic.

At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for long-term stability, some 357,500 South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since November 2017, 122,000 of those in 2020 alone. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan at this stage, the increase in numbers warrants a scaling-up of support following an area-based approach, including strengthening linkages with development actors, to help returnees and the communities they settle in live in safety and dignity, with greater security and services.

Refugees largely reside in conﬂict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction of basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.

Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will beneﬁt from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Speciﬁc protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identiﬁed at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with speciﬁc protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as veriﬁcation exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the eﬃciency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to beneﬁt from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

reportDetails_organization: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
project_text:
Internally Displaced Population in South Sudan supported through provision of protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience, protection advocacy and achievement of solutions. The project aims to strengthen community and rights-based protection response for IDPs, IDP returnees and vulnerable persons within their host communities. The project will focus on providing physical and legal protection through advocacy, timely protection monitoring, life-saving protection response based on identified needs and solutions. The project will address Housing, Land and Property (HLP) rights issues through the provision of legal assistance, facilitate issuance of property and identity documents, and work with mediation mechanisms to support HLP related dispute resolution. Community-based networks will be utilized as part of the protection response to foster community buy in and ownership of protection. The project will use evidence-based planning to expand outreach and develop the capacity of displaced communities to cope, recover, contribute to and ultimately achieve solutions. Out of 1.6 million IDPs, 475,000 IDPs and IDP returnees will be supported with protection interventions and assistance in seven (7) states and an administrative areas. Recognising the protection concerns linked to food insecurity, the Agency activities also include a scaling-up of activities in South Sudan’s highly food insecure and prioritised locations, i.e. Pibor County, Akobo, Aweil South, Tonj East, Tonj North, Tonj South. There will be continuous advocacy and support in the area of law and policy with relevant government bodies such as the   Ministries of Justice Home Affairs, Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, and the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC) to ensure the centrality of protection, enact the “Protection and Assistance to Internally Displaced Persons Act 2018” (IDP) Bill, National Framework on Returns, and various HLP initiatives. The relevant line ministries will also receive capacity building and technical assistance. Building on UNHCR’s existing operational presence in Bentiu Bor, Juba, Malakal, Wau, Yambio, Yei, the Agency will continue to advance on the 2020 geographic expansion of IDP activities by leveraging both static and mobile presence through 15 partners to Central Equatoria, Unity, Upper Nile, Joinglei, Western Bahr El Ghazal, Northern Bahr El Ghazal, Lakes, Western Equatoira, Eastern Equatoris and Warrap. Response and monitoring will cover 19 identified priority counties and Pibor Administrative Area, including remote or hard to-reach areas, in full support to the Protection Cluster Strategy for mobile assessments and response. Partners comprise of both national and international organizations, with selection undertaken on the basis of their pre-existing presence, access to populations of concern and capacity to carry out static and remote protection monitoring and response. While not all proposed activity locations fall under the severity 3, 4 or 5 in terms of food insecurity, recognizing the fluidly and unpredictable nature of sub-national violence in South Sudan, UNHCR’s protection by presence approach requires presence in areas affected by conflict as well as areas of potential return in light of increased momentum in terms of solutions 
Resources and advocacy will focus primarily on protection response and solutions, either durable or transitional (where the former is not yet possible), including assessments on needs, risks, and intentions and feasibility of durable solutions, while also strengthening community-based structures, supporting HLP initiatives, promotion of livelihoods and peaceful coexistence. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will be a key component. A mobile tool was introduced in late 2019 that has enhanced data collection and triangulation of information through timely collection and analysis capabilities, which will further improve information products, leading to a more fitting risk-mitigation approach, reduced response time; while underpinning protection mainstreaming across other operational interventions, including of other Clusters.

reportDetails_organization: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
project_text:
Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2021, there are more than 314,000 refugees from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, including from Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic.

At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for long-term stability, some 357,500 South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since November 2017, 122,000 of those in 2020 alone. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan at this stage, the increase in numbers warrants a scaling-up of support following an area-based approach, including strengthening linkages with development actors, to help returnees and the communities they settle in live in safety and dignity, with greater security and services.

Refugees largely reside in conﬂict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction of basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.

Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will beneﬁt from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Speciﬁc protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identiﬁed at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with speciﬁc protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as veriﬁcation exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the eﬃciency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to beneﬁt from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

project_text: Respuesta integral en seguridad alimentaria y nutricional de emergencia para la población más vulnerable afectada por la crisis en Venezuela. Acción Contra el Hambre (ACH) en Venezuela atiende las necesidades humanitarias de los grupos más vulnerables en riesgo de desnutrición aguda: < de 5 años, 5 – 14 años, mujeres embarazadas y lactantes (MEL), personas con discapacidades o con problemas de salud, en particular adultos mayores. Son agravantes las situaciones de pobreza y necesidades básicas no satisfechas como la falta de acceso a: alimentos, condiciones higiénico-sanitarias adecuadas, servicios de salud, y medios de vida. La desnutrición y el deterioro de la salud repercuten en una mayor exposición a factores agravantes como la violencia de género, embarazos adolescentes y criminalidad. A través del HRP, ACH brindará una respuesta humanitaria para la reducción del sufrimiento y ayudar a salvar vidas, identificando casos de desnutrición aguda y severa en las familias más a riesgo. Se trabajará a nivel comunitario y se coordinará con instituciones locales, en particular con escuelas y centros de salud. ACH trabaja con un enfoque de programa país y dentro de una estrategia regional, con intervenciones complementarias e integrales en: 1) Nutrición: sensibilización y consejerías; detección, tratamiento de la desnutrición aguda, y derivación de los casos con complicaciones médicas; capacitación en el manejo preventivo de la desnutrición aguda; 2) Salud: atención primaria, equipos, insumos, medicamentos, métodos anticonceptivos; 3) Seguridad Alimentaria y medios de vida: distribución de alimentos y apoyo para la producción de alimentos; 4) ASH: acceso a servicios de agua, saneamiento, e higiene, en escuelas y centros comunitarios; distribución de kits de higiene, y rehabilitación/reparación de sistemas de abastecimiento de agua y de saneamiento en comunidades. El sector de Protección y género, de manera transversal, trabajará en prevención de VBG, nuevas masculinidades y DSSR; establecimiento y/o fortalecimiento de espacios seguros para mujeres y niñas; atención psico-social, distribución de kits de higiene menstrual y protección para mujeres en riesgo. La respuesta actual de ACH se concentra en Caracas DC, Guárico, Carabobo, Miranda, Zulia, Bolívar, y próximamente en Falcón, Amazonas y Sucre.

reportDetails_organization: United States of America, Government of; United States of America, Government of
project_text:
Agricultural Seed Activity Project (ASAP) II Over the past three years, intercommunal conflict and extreme climate variability and shocks have displaced tens of millions of people in Ethiopia. In the Oromia, Somali and Southern Nations, Nationalities and People’s (SNNP) Regions there are over 1.1 million people in need . As the conflict subsides, the government continues to force IDP’s to return to their former homes, but in the haste of this operation, most return to their communities with few belongings and no productive assets. The provision of seed vouchers alongside basic agricultural advice, for major staple crops (e.g., wheat, tef, OPV maize, sorghum), pulses (e.g., haricot beans) and cash for nutritious vegetable seeds and/or other needed agricultural inputs are essential for the IDP returnees to provide a rapid restart to food production, diversify production for improved consumption and strengthen livelihoods for income generation. 

To support both vulnerable farmers and IDP returnees  Catholic Relief Services (CRS) and our local partners built on the effective response of the first phase of this project funded by USAID/BHA, the Agricultural Seed Activity Project (ASAP) in Oromia Somali, and SNNP by scaling up the cash and voucher-based seed response to benefit farming households who are vulnerable to acute seed insecurity caused by conflict and acute environmental shocks. The purpose of the project is to improve agricultural production through the provision of agricultural inputs (seeds), training in good agricultural practices and links to input suppliers by reaching out to 97,392 beneficiary households.

project_text:
Life-saving food assistance in North-East Nigeria WFP will provide unconditional food assistance to the most food-insecure, crisis-affected populations. Life-saving general food assistance (in-kind food and cash-based transfers) will be delivered to IDPs, returnees, and host populations in North-East Nigeria (Borno, Yobe, and Adamawa States). Early recovery and resilience to shocks will be promoted through asset creation and preservation, increased livelihoods opportunities, and enhanced agricultural value chains. Joint multi-sectoral assessments and Emergency Food Security Analysis will be conducted regularly to monitor the food security, and markets situation in crisis-affected states. 
A gender-transformative approach that meets the needs of women, men, girls, and boys will be adopted. WFP will mainstream protection throughout its work, supported by a solid understanding of the operational context and protection analysis. Training and capacity building of staff and partners in the protection and humanitarian principles will include on-the-job coaching. WFP will ensure that affected populations (women and men) will be consulted throughout the programme cycle; beneficiary feedback mechanisms will be tailored to their preferred means of communication. Beneficiaries will continue to be empowered with knowledge on their food assistance entitlements and their rights, including WFP’s zero-tolerance policy on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). Protection against Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) will be embedded in M&E tools, complaint feedback mechanisms, and training of partners and staff.
WFP will continue the collection of key information on beneficiaries and assistance provided as part of its M&E activities. Monthly monitoring will include distribution and activity site management; beneficiary and entitlement verification; and ensuring adequate protection and gender measures. Lessons will be regularly drawn from monthly process and biannual outcome monitoring and reporting, and periodic reviews and evaluation to inform strategic and operational decisions.
WFP will further consolidate partnerships to enhance national and state-level emergency preparedness and response systems, including food security and nutrition assessment and monitoring, early warning, protection, gender analysis, targeting and registration processes, safety nets, cash-based transfer capacities, and supply chain.
Where security and access to land allow, increasing livelihood activities will complement food assistance to support access to productive assets, income-generating activities, and self-reliance in the long term. Assistance will be coordinated with government distributions, ensure food assistance is complimentary and no gaps. self-reliance in the long term.
