reportDetails_organization: Agency for Technical Cooperation and Development; Agency for Technical Cooperation and Development
project_text:
Humanitarian coordination and provision of CCCM-integrated responses to displacement-affected populations in Juba and Bor former PoC sites (semi-static) in hard-to-reach areas (mobile) According to the South Sudan CCCM Cluster HNO 2022, 1.64 million people are currently IDPs in need of CCCM assistance across South Sudan. After a sudden shock, IDPs often gather in informal displacement sites in extremely precarious conditions, most of the time without access to basic services and information, and with limited decision-making power on issues that affect their daily lives and their future. These gathering places are often characterized by an increased exposure to security risks and protection needs, particularly for the most vulnerable groups. Poor living conditions; lack of financial resources and limited access to basic services can lead to outbreaks of disease, increased prevalence of GBV or domestic violence, and tensions between population groups within the informal camps. Likewise, overcrowding could led to challenges in maintaining safe levels of hygiene and sanitation. Continued political uncertainty, coupled with the increased risks of climate change has also largely resulted in the inability of the international community to return these IDP’s to more suitable locations and an unwillingness from the camps inhabitants to leave. Regarding Bor and Juba former PoC camps, as of February 2022, 2,745 IDPs resided in Bor IDPs Camp, 7,299 in Juba IDPs Camp 1 and 24,255 in Juba IDPs Camp 3. Since the transition from former PoCs sites under UNMISS management to conventional IDPs site under the South Sudanese government responsibility in November 2020, the 2,745 residents of Bor IDPs camp have continued benefitting from essential services provision. The RRC offices of Jonglei at State and County levels have taken up the camp administration responsibility after the transition and are well involved, present and committed in the camp activities. However, the state and county authorities are facing limited resources to fully take over the camp administration responsibility. ACTED will aim at reinforcing the local authorities’ resources and abilities in Jonglei, while continuing to build capacity of camp leadership representatives, leading to the full handover of the Camp management responsibilities to the Community Members Committees and Camp administration role to RRC office in Jonglei by the last quarter of 2022. On the other hand, the 31,554 residents of Juba IDPs Camp 1 and 3 have faced a drastic decrease of essential service provision since the transition from former PoC sites under UNMISS management to conventional IDPs camps under the leadership of the South Sudan Government. Since the transition and re-designation of roles over to the government of South Sudan the RRC office has not yet taken over the responsibility of the camps.
ACTED is aiming to continue to work to design a road map for RRC’s take over and to work closely with Juba IDP camps service providers. ACTED would continue to engage in discussions with key actors and communities impacted to take active role in several fora including the Durable Solutions Working Group. During the semi-static phase, ACTED is planning to provide in-kind support to local authorities, including RRC, that are facing a lack of resources to take over the camp administration role, while enhancing the camp leadership skills. Therefore, ACTED will continue implementing CCCM interventions in line with the following cluster objectives: CO1: Improve living condition of IDPs by facilitating safe, equitable and dignified access to cross-sectoral humanitarian services, including CCCM CO2: Enhance the protective environment, respond to vulnerable population with priority on addressing protection gaps and strengthen the predictability and effectiveness of multi sectorial interventions at site level CO3: Support vulnerable IDPs to recover from the crisis by strengthening community self-management, build resilience to promote solutions for displaced people in sites.

project_text:
Humanitarian coordination and provision of CCCM-integrated responses to displacement-affected populations in Juba and Bor former PoC sites (semi-static) in hard-to-reach areas (mobile) In line with the CCCM cluster strategy, ACTED will continue to provide humanitarian coordination and CCCM integrated response to displacement affected population in Juba former PoC sites and will provide mobile support in hard-to-reach areas in response to displacement shocks.  Due to natural hazards, localized and state conflicts, displacement waves remain high in South Sudan with 1.64 million people currently being Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) in need of CCCM assistance according to the South Sudan HNO 2022. The trend has been increasing in 2022 following massive natural hazards such as floodings in Jonglei state, leading to the multiplication of displacement sites. 
As South Sudan has been subject to displacement waves since its creation, and particularly following the 2013 civil war, some IDP sites have existed for several years with residents not willing to return to their areas of origin and ongoing humanitarian aid. To address this issue, ACTED aims to provide a more sustainable solution and support these IDP communities to become more empowered and increase their integration into host communities settings. Following a strategy implemented since 2021 in agreement with CCCM cluster, ACTED handed over camp management responsibilities to the community representatives and local authorities, especially Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC) in Bor and Juba former PoC camps in 2022. In 2023, ACTED will strengthen social cohesion between IDPs and host communities in Juba to foster peaceful coexistence and will provide ad-hoc support to community representatives if needed to ensure a smooth transition. 
In parallel, ACTED provides emergency CCCM assistance in response to displacement shocks across the country. Through a well-established coordination system with REACH, the Inter Cluster Coordination Group, the Needs Analysis Working Group and the clusters, ACTED has access to timely information on displacements, allowing for a rapid multi-sectoral intervention whose core is CCCM services. Within its CCCM rapid response, ACTED aims to provide life saving coordination activities among humanitarian actors and build local communities’ capacities to self manage the sites. 
Therefore, ACTED will continue implementing CCCM interventions in line with the following cluster objectives: CO1: Improve living condition of IDPs by facilitating safe, equitable and dignified access to cross-sectoral humanitarian services, including CCCM CO2: Enhance the protective environment, respond to vulnerable population with priority on addressing protection gaps and strengthen the predictability and effectiveness of multi sectorial interventions at site level CO3: Support vulnerable IDPs to recover from the crisis by strengthening community self-management, build resilience to promote solutions for displaced people in sites.

project_text:
Improving short-term and long-term food security and livelihoods access in Central and Eastern Equatoria and WBeG through investment in food production assets and utilization and strengthening of local capacities. In line with the FSL cluster strategy for 2022, ACTED will contribute towards improving food security of over 22,754 beneficiaries (excluding beneficiaries reached through WFP funding) to enhance emergency food production and reduce dependency on food and agricultural inputs through resilience building activities such as training and market support functionality. Millions of South Sudanese remain displaced across the country following years of violent conflict that resulted in one of the most devastating humanitarian crises in recent history. Based on the latest IPC analysis and projections, in October 2022, 53.6% of the population living in South Sudan facing high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above). Specifically, 4.36 million people are facing crisis (IPC Phase 3), 2.22 million people are facing emergency (IPC Phase 4) and 61,000 people are facing catastrophic (IPC Phase 5) food insecurity. Emergency assistance to crisis-affected displaced and host communities in Ouallam department, Tillabéri Region, Niger
Food Security

destinationObjects_Project.name: Assistance d'urgence aux déplacés et communautés d'accueil touchés par la crise dans le département de Ouallam, région de Tillabéri, Niger
reportDetails_organization: European Commission's Humanitarian Aid and Civil Protection Department
project_text: Assistance d'urgence aux déplacés et communautés d'accueil touchés par la crise dans le département de Ouallam, région de Tillabéri, Niger									 Le Niger est confronté à des situations d’urgence multiples et simultanées, dans un contexte humanitaire et sécuritaire de plus en plus grave, ce qui exacerbe les vulnérabilités déjà prononcées des communautés d’accueil et de personnes déplacées dans la région de Tillabéri, où l’ampleur et la complexité des besoins restent élevées. GOAL propose de mettre en œuvre une réponse d’aide alimentaire d’urgence par le biais d’un soutien en espèces et en bons d’achat dans les zones cibles de Mangaize, Diney, Tondikiwindi et Ouallam (toutes situées dans le département d’Ouallam, région de Tillabéri) pour les personnes déplacées et les communautés d’accueil les plus vulnérables. Le programme de 12 mois vise à fournir une aide vitale et vitale à 14 000 personnes pour répondre à leurs besoins alimentaires essentiels de base. Trois tours de distribution en espèces et en bons d’achat d’une valeur monétaire de 60,60 euros seront effectués. Le premier cycle en juin au début de la période de soudure, le deuxième en juillet et le dernier en août pour atténuer les impacts des chocs sur les prix des denrées alimentaires et les revenus sur la sécurité alimentaire et le bien-être économique des ménages. La distribution en espèces ciblera 700 ménages et le bon papier sera distribué à 1 300 ménages sur une base mensuelle. L’action proposée est basée sur la théorie du changement selon laquelle les PDI extrêmement vulnérables et les membres de la communauté d’accueil dans la région de Tillaberi ont accès à l’AVC pour l’aide alimentaire pendant la période de soudure, ainsi qu’à une alimentation complémentaire générale (BSF) pour la prévention de la malnutrition dans les ménages qui comprennent des enfants âgés de 6 à 23 mois, avec une protection et une inclusion intégrées tout au long de l’action, ALORS les besoins alimentaires et nutritionnels essentiels des individus, qui sauvent et maintiennent la vie, seront satisfaits,  réduisant ainsi leur vulnérabilité, leur marginalisation et l’utilisation de stratégies d’adaptation négatives. Des liens entre l’action et le déploiement de la feuille de route du lien seront recherchés au cours de la mise en œuvre afin de contribuer à des solutions durables pour les personnes déplacées et les communautés d’accueil, dans la mesure du possible.

destinationObjects_Emergency.name: Sudan Complex Emergency 2023
reportDetails_organization: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
project_text:
Enhancing IDP Protection Services in South Sudan to facilitate and scale up protection monitoring, targeted Protection Assistance and Services (including GBV and CP), as well as HLP support to the most vulnerable IDPs and Returnees The projects seek to ensure that those most in need, most vulnerable or at risk, so-called Persons with Specific Needs (PSNs) in IDP, returnee and host communities are supported with tailored protection services and assistance, focused on lifesaving support, while also investing in people’s resilience to shocks. Restoration of housing, land and property rights, civil documentation, child protection and prevention and response services for GBV will be part of this general protection project. The activities will be implemented through UNHCR’s offices in Juba, Wau, Bentiu, Bor, Malakal, Yei, Yambio and prioritized respective counties in line with the Cluster’s prioritization.

The project will support the implementation of the Protection Monitoring System that was launched in October 2022 under the umbrella of the Protection Cluster aimed at informing the protection and wider humanitarian response with protection analysis and based on a harmonized methodology and tools. Protection concerns identified will be dealt with both on individual protection services/case management basis and through community-based protection responses tailored to the specific needs and considering the age, gender, diversity among the people served. Community based protection components of this project will involve community owned projects with social cohesion and peace benefits in areas with social tension as well as areas where durable solutions are pursued.  Particular attention is paid to segments of the community particular at risk or marginalized, including women and youth empowerment, tailored support to GBV survivors and children at risk as well as people with disabilities and older persons. 

Protection risks and social tensions will be prevented and mitigated through awareness and information campaigns, community sensitization using an AGD approach and community engagement, such as community action committees, peace dialogues, including by involving leaders of faith-based institutions. Quality procedures to identify those most in need, vulnerable and at risk will be implemented across all project locations, building on the protection monitoring reports and implemented through protection desks and protection outreach, including through static and mobile teams. Protection services and assistance will be multi-faceted and tailored to the specific assistance and protection needs identified, including to survivors of gender-based violence and children at risk amongst other at risk categories. Direct protection services and assistance includes identification of people at risk, counselling, social accompaniment, enabling access to safety, case management, psychosocial support, legal aid (including assistance and representation), as well as material support tailored to the individual, including in kind (e.g. mobility device, core relief) or cash, implemented through a cash plus approach. The project will also specifically address housing, land and property rights and implement individual assistance and community-based mechanisms, such as through community-based land committees, to restore access to housing, land and property as well as to related documentation, including HLP, identity and civil documentation. This is complemented by community services, including child friendly spaces, rehabilitation of community infrastructure or basic services through community-owned approaches. 

Overall, the project empowers communities affected by displacement, conflict and disasters, and invests in their own agency and resilience through the multi-faceted nature of the protection response provided under this project.

reportDetails_organization: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
project_text:
Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

reportDetails_organization: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
project_text:
Enhancement of protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community-based protection activities. The project aims to strengthen protection and resilience of Syrian IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities through advocacy, coordination, provision of community-based protection services and legal services. UNHCR Syria will continue to lead the Protection Sector to ensure coordinated protection interventions programming for IDPs and affected people as well as executing leadership roles in refugee return programmes in collaboration with the Government. UNHCR’s protection interventions will include provision of integrated protection services through a network of 120 centers in all 14 Governorates. The network of Community Centres, paired with some 120 mobile units and around 3,600 outreach volunteers of multifunctional thematic capacities, are fundamental to the implementation of UNHCR’s Protection and Solutions Strategy for Syria through outreach to affected populations, assessment of protection risks and vulnerabilities, consultation, identification and mobilization of community resources, strengthening of community self-help networks, and offering protection services and support to displaced persons, returnees and host communities in response to the priority needs expressed by the communities, while applying a highly participatory age, gender and diversity approach. The protection services extended at the UNHCR Community Centres include, but are not limited to, psycho-social support, GBV prevention, risk mitigation and response and child protection case management, legal awareness and legal aid, non-formal education programmes, services for persons with disabilities and older persons, provision of general and medical in-kind assistance, social and recreational activities, curriculum based awareness activities on various subjects targeting women, men, boys and girls, referrals and information sharing, social protection through livelihoods support to most vulnerable population.
As part of its commitment to Accountability to Affected Population (AAP), UNHCR will ensure meaningful participation of communities based on age, gender and diversity approach, structured focus group discussions and enhancement of the community-based feedback and complaint mechanisms. UNHCR will continue its capacity building efforts to ensure services are delivered according to the standards and that accountability to affected population and do no harm principles are respected.
UNHCR will continue co-leading the AAP Technical Working Group and the Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) In-Country Network and coordinate activities to strengthen AAP and SEA prevention, risk mitigation and response.
Monitoring and evaluation of the planned interventions is based on the reports and observations by the partners and on regular direct observation and ongoing assessment and consultations with the community by UNHCR and partners and the comparison of achievements and related financial expenditures with objectives. Evaluation is conducted through different channels, including post distribution monitoring to determine the effectiveness of/measure the satisfaction of people of concern with the service and the distribution process in addition to multiple satisfaction surveys and tracking tools related to different protection interventions. Monitoring and evaluation activities are carried out at various levels by partners and agencies implementing subprojects, UNHCR Country Office, Sub and Field Offices. Situation reports are submitted by all UNHCR Field Offices to their respective Supervising Office and Country Offices submit a corresponding report to Headquarters.

project_text:
Enhancement of protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community-based protection activities. The project aims to strengthen protection and resilience of Syrian IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities through advocacy, coordination, provision of community-based protection services and legal services. UNHCR Syria will continue to lead the Protection Sector to ensure coordinated protection interventions programming for IDPs and affected people as well as executing leadership roles in refugee return programmes in collaboration with the Government. UNHCR’s protection interventions will include provision of integrated protection services through a network of 120 centers in all 14 Governorates. The network of Community Centres, paired with some 120 mobile units and around 3,600 outreach volunteers of multifunctional thematic capacities, are fundamental to the implementation of UNHCR’s Protection and Solutions Strategy for Syria through outreach to affected populations, assessment of protection risks and vulnerabilities, consultation, identification and mobilization of community resources, strengthening of community self-help networks, and offering protection services and support to displaced persons, returnees and host communities in response to the priority needs expressed by the communities, while applying a highly participatory age, gender and diversity approach. The protection services extended at the UNHCR Community Centres include, but are not limited to, psycho-social support, GBV prevention, risk mitigation and response and child protection case management, legal awareness and legal aid, non-formal education programmes, services for persons with disabilities and older persons, provision of general and medical in-kind assistance, social and recreational activities, curriculum based awareness activities on various subjects targeting women, men, boys and girls, referrals and information sharing, social protection through livelihoods support to most vulnerable population.
As part of its commitment to Accountability to Affected Population (AAP), UNHCR will ensure meaningful participation of communities based on age, gender and diversity approach, structured focus group discussions and enhancement of the community-based feedback and complaint mechanisms. UNHCR will continue its capacity building efforts to ensure services are delivered according to the standards and that accountability to affected population and do no harm principles are respected.
UNHCR will continue co-leading the AAP Technical Working Group and the Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) In-Country Network and coordinate activities to strengthen AAP and SEA prevention, risk mitigation and response.
Monitoring and evaluation of the planned interventions is based on the reports and observations by the partners and on regular direct observation and ongoing assessment and consultations with the community by UNHCR and partners and the comparison of achievements and related financial expenditures with objectives. Evaluation is conducted through different channels, including post distribution monitoring to determine the effectiveness of/measure the satisfaction of people of concern with the service and the distribution process in addition to multiple satisfaction surveys and tracking tools related to different protection interventions. Monitoring and evaluation activities are carried out at various levels by partners and agencies implementing subprojects, UNHCR Country Office, Sub and Field Offices. Situation reports are submitted by all UNHCR Field Offices to their respective Supervising Office and Country Offices submit a corresponding report to Headquarters.

destinationObjects_Project.name: Improved food security and livelihoods of IDPs, Returnees and Vulnerable host communities in South Sudan
project_text:
Improved food security and livelihoods of IDPs, Returnees and Vulnerable host communities in South Sudan The purpose of the project is to improve food consumption, food security, dietary diversity and coping strategies and enhance emergency food production of vulnerable populations in the targeted counties. This will be achieved through provision of Cash-Based Transfers (CBT) to address food needs of vulnerable communities during the lean season and provision of timely and appropriate complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs and fishing kits coupled with training in improved agronomic and fishing practices.
In line with the South Sudan FSL cluster HRP objectives and priorities, NPA will support vulnerable populations in IPC 4 and 5 locations as well as some IPC 3 locations. Specifically, NPA will target Canal/Pigi, Fangak, Pochalla and Bor South Counties of Jonglei State, Rumbek East, Rumbek Centre, Cueibet, Yirol East, Yirol West and Awerial Counties of Lakes State, Terekeka County of Central Equatoria State and Kapoeta North County of Eastern Equatoria State.

NPA seeks to support 86,200 HHs (517,200 individuals) through provision of complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs and fishing kits across the target counties. Some of the kits will be provided by FAO (core pipeline) while the rest will be procured and distributed directly by NPA to enhance food production.  NPA will build the capacity of the HHs supported with the kits through training on improved agronomic and fishing practices, marketing and group dynamics. A Training of Trainers (ToT) approach will be utilized whereby lead farmers and fisher folk will be trained by NPA. They will then train/share the knowledge and skills with other farmers and fisher folk in their communities. The kits provided through this project and the knowledge gained from the trainings is expected to improve the agricultural and fishing practices of the target HHs thus enhancing and sustaining food production. CBT interventions will target 1,000 HHs (6,000 individuals ) in Rumbek East, Rumbek Centre and Cuiebet Counties in Lakes State to improve their access to food, diversify and improve their food consumption and dietary diversity scores and promote the adoption of positive coping strategies. The planned interventions are aligned to the FSL cluster objectives 1 and 2 and will provide emergency assistance and livelihoods support to save lives and avert total collapse of livelihoods in the target counties.

NPA will integrate development-oriented and conflict-sensitivity activities in this project to enhance the resilience of  vulnerable HHs in line with the Triple Nexus. Therefore, 1,200 vulnerable HHs will be supported with small-scale cash grants to establish IGAs. The target HHs will be mobilized and sensitized to transition to and establish VSLA’s to ease access to financial services and encourage the spirit of saving among the VSLA group members. The IGAs will contribute to increasing and diversifying income and building the resilience of the target HHs at the same time improving functionality of local markets and boosting the local value chains.

NPA will employ a community-based beneficiary selection approach which will entail establishing Project Management Committees (PMCs) to lead the selection of eligible beneficiaries based on the beneficiary selection criteria. Vulnerable HHs with severe food insecurity including female, child, disabled/chronically ill headed HHs; persons living with or at risk of HIV/AIDS and the elderly will be targeted in this project. 
NPA will ensure meaningful engagement of the target communities throughout the project life-cycle through holding regular meetings with the PMCs and community members and Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM) to get their feedback on the project. NPA will ensure that the feedback is incorporated in the implementation of this project and design of future projects. Further, NPA will use a community-based complaints and feedback mechanism to provide a platform for beneficiaries to voice any issues or concerns.

Réponse intégrée en santé et nutrition dans la région de la Boucle du Mouhoun Faisant suite à la dégradation de la situation dans la Boucle du Mouhoun, et suite aux évaluations menées au début du mois de novembre 2022, PUI souhaite développer un soutien aux DS de Boromo un des 2 DS le plus affecté par la problématique de déplacement des populations, avec une augmentation de 61% du nombres PDI enregistrés la province du Balé (données issues des rapports sur la situation des PDI au 31 décembre 2021 et d’octobre 2022 par le CONASUR) 
L’évaluation fait ressortir des besoins en terme de personnels qualifiés, de couverture des soins et d’accès aux services de santé de manière générale, avec une absence de partenaires dans le domaine de la Santé. Ce positionnement permettra également d’anticiper une dégradation de la situation dans cette zone tout en repositionnant des capacités de réponses rapide en cas de besoin.

Au cours de ce projet, PUI contribuera à améliorer l'accès effectif aux services essentiels et vitaux de santé, de nutrition et de protection dans les situations d'urgence pour les populations touchées par les crises sécuritaires et humanitaires dans le domaine de la santé dans les situations d'urgence pour les populations touchées par la crise sécuritaire et humanitaire dans la région de la Boucle du Mouhoun

Lors de la mise en place du projet, PUI se coordonnera avec les différents acteurs présents, afin de permettre un ciblage plus précis des zones, d'éviter les doublons et de rester le plus efficient possible. 
A noter que PUI met au cœur de ses projets la lutte contre les EAS, la prise en compte du genre, la protection transversale. 
PUI s’inscrit dans un processus d’amélioration continu de la qualité de ses actions via une meilleure prise en compte des parties prenantes dans le cycle de projet. A ce titre, le système de Suivi-Evaluation, Redevabilité et Apprentissage (SERA) existant sera renforcé dans le cadre de cette intervention. La prise en compte des questions de redevabilité s’appuiera sur trois principaux piliers dont l’information, la participation et la consolidation du mécanisme de gestion des plaintes et retours d’informations.

Il est à noter que le transfert monétaire n'est pas prévu sur ce projet de par la nature des activités en santé, nutrition, wash in nut / wash in health

project_text:
SIDA 2023 RESPUESTA HUMANITARIA DE EMERGENCIA FRENTE A DESASTRES DE ORIGEN NATURAL O HUMANO Respuesta humanitaria de emergencia frente a desastres de origen natural o humano. El outcome del proyecto es proteger vidas y se enfoca en varios sectores.  La población meta - 220,000. 
Actividades WASH:
1.3.1 Rehabilitación/construcción de sistemas seguros de agua y/o saneamiento, así como la entrega de kits de lavado (sistemas de tratamiento de agua y/o tanques).
1.3.2 Autoconstrucción de instalaciones sanitarias familiares a través de capacitación práctica con liderazgo comunitario.
1.3.3 Implementación de capacitación en promoción de la higiene, saneamiento y gestión de residuos, uso adecuado de recursos hídricos escasos para mitigar enfermedades transmitidas por el agua, de acuerdo con enfoques de cambio de comportamiento.
1.3.4 Establecimiento de un Comité de Gestión del Agua Comunitario con participación de mujeres en los procesos de toma de decisiones y acciones de gestión según la estrategia de seguridad hídrica.
1.3.5 Distribución de kits/vales de higiene apropiados para género.
1.3.6 Entrega de asistencia para refugios (en efectivo o en forma de kit).
Actividades Salud y Nutrición:
1.1.1 Prestación directa y móvil de servicios de salud reproductiva, materna, infantil y nutrición para niños menores de 11 años y mujeres embarazadas;
1.1.2 Tratamiento con micronutrientes para niños menores de 11 años y mujeres embarazadas.
1.1.3 Tratamiento de niños menores de 11 años y mujeres embarazadas con anemia y/o desnutrición aguda moderada y grave (sin complicaciones).
1.1.4 Sesiones de sensibilización y capacitación realizadas sobre salud básica según la estrategia global para la alimentación infantil y joven en situaciones de emergencia (IYCF), seguridad alimentaria y hábitos saludables para mujeres, hombres, niñas, niños y personal de instituciones de salud locales, incluyendo hábitos nutricionales saludables en situaciones de emergencia.
1.1.5 Asesoramiento sobre métodos anticonceptivos para hombres y mujeres (asesoría, entrega de métodos anticonceptivos y píldoras de emergencia) y derivación de casos que requieran métodos anticonceptivos de larga duración o Interrupción Voluntaria del Embarazo (IVE).
1.1.6 Capacitación de familias y líderes comunitarios en la medición del perímetro braquial medio (MUAC) para la detección de riesgos de mortalidad debido a la desnutrición.
1.1.7 Capacitación culturalmente apropiada sobre salud sexual y reproductiva para mujeres, hombres y adolescentes de la comunidad migrante y anfitriona.
1.1.8 Apoyo psicosocial y primeros auxilios psicológicos brindados a mujeres, hombres, niñas y niños de la comunidad migrante, la comunidad anfitriona y/o afectada por conflictos.
1.1.10 Sesiones de sensibilización y capacitación sobre seguridad alimentaria y hábitos saludables.
Actividades protección: 
1.4.1. Proporcionar capacitación sobre violencia de género (GBV) de manera apropiada para género y culturalmente a mujeres, hombres y adolescentes de la comunidad migrante y la comunidad anfitriona.
1.4.2. Creación de infografías con datos basados en el análisis de género por región.
1.4.3. Establecimiento de un camino de servicios de referencia para violencia de género (GBV) y protección.
1.4.4. Entrega de kits de dignidad de acuerdo con las necesidades específicas de protección de mujeres y niñas.
1.4.5. Información sobre derechos, acceso a servicios básicos y activación de rutas.
1.4.6. Asistencia técnica en género y protección a instituciones locales y gubernamentales.
1.4.7. Infraestructura WASH en espacios de protección para niños y niñas (internados o escuelas).

project_text:
Programa de seguridad alimentaria basado en la escuela Con el objetivo de contribuir a la seguridad alimentaria de la población con mayores necesidades, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de Naciones Unidas (WFP, por sus siglas en inglés) en Venezuela desarrolla un programa de asistencia humanitaria basado en la escuela para garantizar el acceso de los más vulnerables a una alimentación adecuada y nutritiva en el entorno escolar, familiar y comunitario. 
Este programa inició en 2021 con comidas escolares en emergencias priorizando escuelas iniciales y de educación especial.

WFP proporciona comidas escolares acompañado de un paquete integrado de intervenciones para mejorar el acceso a alimentos nutritivos y diversificados a través de las escuelas, contribuyendo al mismo tiempo a mejorar la salud y la nutrición de los niños en edad escolar, los estudiantes con discapacidad y el personal escolar, y apoyando a las comunidades a reducir la dependencia en estrategias de afrontamiento. De manera gradual, el WFP está realizando compras locales de alimentos, e incluyendo acciones para apoyar los mercados locales con compras a pequeños productores y apoyo técnico para acceso a mercados.

En este sentido, el programa de comidas escolares en emergencias tiene los siguientes componentes, para asegurar un enfoque integral que apoye al estudiante en el entorno escolar y familiar:

1. Entrega de comidas escolares nutritivas para estudiantes y personal escolar, promoviendo las compras locales y a pequeños productores.
2. Apoyo a la seguridad alimentaria del hogar.
3. Rehabilitación de cocinas escolares para garantizar condiciones adecuadas de preparación de alimentos.
4. Comunicación para sensibilizar acerca de los principios humanitarios, la adecuada preparación de alimentos, nutrición, higiene y mantenimiento de cocinas escolares.
5. Fortalecimiento de capacidades de socios implementadores y personal escolar.
6. Acciones sensibles a la nutrición, que incluyen, tamizaje en las escuelas, educación nutricional, referencia a servicios especializados y entrega de alimento complementario fortificado (Super Cereal Plus).

project_text: Provision of life-saving interventions to displaced communities in POC, Camps and Camp-like settings through CCCM interventions in South Sudan. The objective of the intended project is to contribute and improve the living conditions in the targeted IDP camps through strengthening the predictability and effectiveness of service provision and protection for displaced communities with the aim to reach durable solutions through strengthening community-self management and in addition to that the project will strengthen coordination and information sharing among all stakeholders. Through this proposed project activities, DRC will ensure that all the displaced communities are enabled to partake meaningfully in the governance structures and management of the sites. This project will also encourage camp residents to participate community led care and maintenance activities aimed at improving safety and hygiene in sites, reducing protection and health risks. DRC will work with the camp management committees to facilitate site maintenance through cash-for-work while utilising members of the IDP community by enabling them to earn temporary income. Through this project, DRC will establish or strengthen an inclusive community governance structures and thematic committees at each site level, the engagement of these structures in CCCM coordination mechanisms alongside active humanitarian partners in the respective sites and representatives of relevant local authorities, as well as through continued support for capacity building, mainly through the delivery of trainings adapted to each type of participation (thematic IDP committee members, site governance members, local authority representatives). The proposed project will enhance Complain, Response and feedback mechanisms.

project_text:
Provision of integrated, equitable, and timely WASH services to emergency affected populations in South Sudan Protracted crises in South Sudan, including climactic shocks and continued conflict, have resulted in 8.9 million people projected to be in need of humanitarian assistance in 2022. As a result of the shocks, such as flooding, inter-communal violence (ICV) and ongoing armed clashes, the majority of the population are facing increased food insecurity, lack of access to basic services, and protection risks. The increased integration of protection, inclusion, and conflict sensitivity analysis in all programming will ensure that WASH services and resources can be safely accessed by all in the community. Greater engagement of communities and local markets will support the design of long term and flood resistant WASH infrastructure and supply chains to ensure that interventions produce durable results for communities.

project_text:
Provision of emergency nutrition services and support optimum early childhood development to crisis affected pregnant and lactating women and children aged below 5 years among vulnerable Lebanese and migrants in Lebanon. With Growing triple burden of malnutrition (undernutrition, both stunting and wasting; deficiencies in vitamins and other micronutrients; and overweight and obesity) among women, children and adolescents which affects health, growth and development. 
70% of young children are not exclusively breastfed; 90% of children aged 6-23 months lack dietary diversity and meal frequency; over 40% of all women and children, including Lebanese, are affected by anaemia. In October 2021, 53% of children skipped a meal due to insufficient food in the house, up from 37% just 6 months before. 453,000 Lebanese women and children need urgent nutritional support.
Nutrition and child development should be prioritized as part of the emergency response plan, hence UNICEF will be working under the ERP appeal through a multi-system approach from food, health, social protection, education and water and sanitation systems to protect and promote adequate diets, practices and services to prevent all forms of malnutrition among children and women and support optimum early childhood development. In 2021, the percentage of childcare service providers encountering families with payment difficulties has doubled, reaching 41%.  Additionally, due to the local currency devaluation and the significant increase in fuel prices, the monthly fees per child are no longer sufficient to cover the operational expenses of childcare providers. Therefore, to remain affordable, childcare providers are often constrained to compromise on quality which can negatively affect the healthy development of children, while children in rural areas, camps or informal settlements have little access to ECD.
Building on this momentum of a strengthened enabling environment for nutrition and child development, UNICEF will work with the government and partners to reach the most vulnerable children and women with an essential service package for prevention, early detection, referral, and management of all forms of malnutrition and development delays. Maternal and child nutrition during the first 1,000 days coupled with a nurturing care framework – from conception to age 2 years – remains core to the response.
This will be done by strengthening national capacity across multiple sectors and systems through better evidence, policies, and facility and community-based solutions and programmes.

project_text:
Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

reportDetails_organization: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
project_text:
Enhancement of protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community-based protection activities. The project aims to strengthen protection and resilience of Syrian IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities through advocacy, coordination, provision of community-based protection services and legal services. UNHCR Syria will continue to lead the Protection Sector to ensure coordinated protection interventions programming for IDPs and affected people as well as executing leadership roles in refugee return programmes in collaboration with the Government. UNHCR’s protection interventions will include provision of integrated protection services through a network of 120 centers in all 14 Governorates. The network of Community Centres, paired with some 120 mobile units and around 3,600 outreach volunteers of multifunctional thematic capacities, are fundamental to the implementation of UNHCR’s Protection and Solutions Strategy for Syria through outreach to affected populations, assessment of protection risks and vulnerabilities, consultation, identification and mobilization of community resources, strengthening of community self-help networks, and offering protection services and support to displaced persons, returnees and host communities in response to the priority needs expressed by the communities, while applying a highly participatory age, gender and diversity approach. The protection services extended at the UNHCR Community Centres include, but are not limited to, psycho-social support, GBV prevention, risk mitigation and response and child protection case management, legal awareness and legal aid, non-formal education programmes, services for persons with disabilities and older persons, provision of general and medical in-kind assistance, social and recreational activities, curriculum based awareness activities on various subjects targeting women, men, boys and girls, referrals and information sharing, social protection through livelihoods support to most vulnerable population.
As part of its commitment to Accountability to Affected Population (AAP), UNHCR will ensure meaningful participation of communities based on age, gender and diversity approach, structured focus group discussions and enhancement of the community-based feedback and complaint mechanisms. UNHCR will continue its capacity building efforts to ensure services are delivered according to the standards and that accountability to affected population and do no harm principles are respected.
UNHCR will continue co-leading the AAP Technical Working Group and the Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) In-Country Network and coordinate activities to strengthen AAP and SEA prevention, risk mitigation and response.
Monitoring and evaluation of the planned interventions is based on the reports and observations by the partners and on regular direct observation and ongoing assessment and consultations with the community by UNHCR and partners and the comparison of achievements and related financial expenditures with objectives. Evaluation is conducted through different channels, including post distribution monitoring to determine the effectiveness of/measure the satisfaction of people of concern with the service and the distribution process in addition to multiple satisfaction surveys and tracking tools related to different protection interventions. Monitoring and evaluation activities are carried out at various levels by partners and agencies implementing subprojects, UNHCR Country Office, Sub and Field Offices. Situation reports are submitted by all UNHCR Field Offices to their respective Supervising Office and Country Offices submit a corresponding report to Headquarters.

project_text:
CCCM Assistance to conflict and disaster-induced displaced persons in South Sudan According to Round 12 of IOM DTM’s monitoring of displacement and return movement, 2,229,657 people remain displaced in South Sudan, 78% of which are sheltering with already crisis-affected host communities. In a number of displacement sites and collective centers, including current and former PoCs, more than 440,000 individuals continue to live in situations of protracted displacement. Displacement figures have continued to increase despite the signing of the R-ARCSS in 2018 due to an increase of displacement-inducing incidents such as sub-national conflict and unprecedented climate-related disasters.

IOM CCCM aims to target 612,000 people of the total 1.4 million people targeted under the CCCM Cluster Response Plan. IOM will continue to provide displaced communities with basic and emergency camp management services, ensuring that the provision of protection and cross-sectoral humanitarian assistance is equitable, coordinated, monitored and adhering to standards. Of critical relevance to the current displacement environment in the country, IOM CCCM’s interventions will also integrate a robust, community-led disaster-mitigation lens in all care & maintenance interventions and capacity building exercises to enhance protective environments to increase resilience of infrastructure and communities to climate shocks. Further, fully committed to ensuring that AAP is streamlined in any and all activities, IOM will continue to develop and improve AAP mechanisms to ensure that the organization is accountable to the people that it serves and that programmes are informed by the voices of the displaced communities.

IOM intends to contribute to the sectoral objectives through the following interventions:

1)	Continued and adapted provision of critical CCCM activities to IDPs living in Bentiu, Naivasha and Hai Masna IDP Sites as well as critical care & maintenance activities in Malakal PoC.
2)	Deployment of emergency CCCM teams to deliver sustainable mobile responses promoting self-governance, community ownership and resilience in hard-to-reach locations following triggers at the ICCG-level.
3)	Co-lead the CCCM Cluster at national level and continue acting as SFP in WBeG, Jonglei and Upper Nile States in order to support national and state-level partner agencies in accountable CCCM responses and systems.
4)	Continue chairing the CCEWG in order to provide technical CCE support to partner organizations and to operationalize outputs under the 2021 South Sudan AAP Framework.

project_text: Increasing safe, equitable and dignified access to essential basic protection services reducing exposure of affected vulnerable populations to protection risks, including GBV in Pibor (IPC 5), Nyirol (IPC 4) and Akobo (IPC 4) in Jonglei State The proposed HRP 2022 interventions will be implemented in Pibor, Nyirol and Akobo West which have been classified as IPC 4 and 5 facing deteriorating humanitarian conditions, worsened by endemic violence, conflict, access constraints and operational interference, public health challenges such as direct and indirect effects of COVID-19 and climatic shocks resulting in the dual phenomena of extraordinary flooding and localized drought, which have a severe impact on people’s livelihoods, hampers access to education and water, sanitation and hygiene and health services. Protection concerns remain high, with people impacted by violence having limited access to justice and the rule of law. The proposed intervention will contribute to the HRP 2022 Protection Cluster, General Protection Objectives: Prevent and mitigate protection risks through enhanced preparedness and resilience; Enhance protection assessment and monitoring to inform protection and overall humanitarian response; and Ensure the provision of critical protection related assistance and specialized services through an integrated approach to address the priority needs of targeted people among vulnerable women, men, girls and boys in hard-to-reach and priority geographical areas. The main objective of the proposed intervention is to increase safe, equitable and dignified access to essential basic protection services reducing exposure of affected vulnerable populations to protection risks, including GBV in Pibor, Nyirol and Akobo in Jonglei State. To achieve this, the proposed intervention has the following specific objectives: SO1 To undertake effective and timely protection assessments in targeted areas for timely and robust humanitarian and protection decisions, influence and actions; SO2 To strengthen community-based protection mechanisms for risk reduction and promotion of local peace and security for women and youths; SO3 To provide Individual Protection Assistance to address priority protection needs for vulnerable women, men, girls and boys in targeted areas; SO4 To support ‘safe programming’ (protection mainstreaming) including safeguarding in all interventions in all the targeted locations. Targeted population are Host Communities, Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) and Returnees consisting of women, girls, boys and men. The intervention will be contributing to the Protection Cluster target of 105,320 women, men, girls and boys provided with individual, group, specialized PSS and other related general protection services. This project will be implemented by Oxfam and its local partners. The expected number of people reached through Oxfam intervention is 6,600 (across all locations 60% women, 20% girls, 10% boys, 10% men): Pibor HC-1000, IDPs-800, Returnees-400; Akobo HC-1000, IDPs-800, Returnees-400 and Nyirol HC-1000, IDPs-800, Returnees-400.

destinationObjects_Emergency.name: Sudan Complex Emergency 2023
project_text:
Provision of Integrated Emergency WASH Services for IDPS,  returnees and Most Vulnerable Host community in Uror, Ayod counties of Jonglei, Panyijiar and Mayom counties of Unity and Juba Mangateen IDP Camp of Central Equatoria States. Panyijiar and Mayom Counties are two of the Nine Counties in Unity State currently grouped in WASH Severity Classification 3&4. while Uror and Ayod Counties of Jonglei state are classified under IPC4.The four counties have been beset by conflict and instability since the  2013 civil strife in South Sudan; characterized by localized violence, inadequate infrastructure development, and the situation even compounded by incessant floods for the last three years (HNO 2022). This has aggravated the WASH needs in the aforementioned Counties thus recording poor WASH indices; low access to clean water per person per day, the average distance to the nearest clean water source exceeding the standard 500m, and access to safe sanitation facilities are inadequate. In Uror, Ayod, Mayom and panyijiar Counties like the rest of South Sudan, 18 percent of households reported feeling unsafe while collecting water, of those, 12 percent of women and girls reported avoiding water points due to GBV concerns (FSNMS, 2021). Humane Aid for Community Organization (HACO), therefore, proposes to support most vulnerable communities in Uror, Ayod, Mayom and Panyijiar Counties; returnees, IDPs, and host with emergency WASH services;  Distribution of WASH kits to unit “caretaker/SAM child”, WASH in nutrition facilities; with focus on water supply and hygiene) in Communities with high GAM and WASH vulnerability, Provide access to basic WASH services in emergencies including COVID-19 and EBOLA messages adopted from WASH Cluster and WHO, conduct WASH specific activities for mitigating WASH GBV-During Waterpoint rehabilitation, Construction or rehabilitation of Sanitation facilities and distribution of WASH NFIs,  Construction of disaster-resistant structures and infrastructure, Build/rehabilitate water points with flood-resilient designs, Build/rehabilitate toilets with flood-resilient designs and carrying out safety audits before conducting WASH activities. HACO intends to reach 24,000 Individuals in Uror, Ayod, Panyijiar and Mayom. The response targets 51% IDPs, 35% Vulnerable host, and 13% Returnees in Mayom County. 

Lower WASH standards in WASH Parameters has been recorded in the most recent WASH Severity mapping gains in service provision over the years have been eroded by adverse weather effects resulting in prolonged flooding, leading to the destruction of WASH infrastructure, displacement of communities, deprivation of markets, and access to most parts of the states in focus. Flooding has further increased WASH-related mortality and morbidity affecting mainly under 5s, pregnant and lactating women, persons with special needs as well as persons living with HIV/TB. Lack of adequate WASH services directly affects the well-being of persons and communities, contributing to health, nutrition, food security, education, and protection indicators within the affected communities. 

Humane Aid for Community Organization in Jonglie and Unity states of South Sudan  plan a robust WASH response aimed at improving community well-being while integrating and working closely with other thematic areas.
The project will focus on fostering community-driven WASH responses to triggers. The project will further seek to enhance the reduction of WASH-related morbidities and mortality, through the provision of adequate, safe, and clean water for both domestic and livelihoods purposes, mitigating WASH-related GBV, and prevention of livelihood deprivation associated with inadequate WASH standards. HACO further will roll out an integrated response modality, seeking to implement jointly WASH, Health, Nutrition, FSL, Education, and Protection projects in the aforementioned counties 60% target will be female and 40% are children and 20% male.

project_text:
Emergency food security and livelihoods surpport to IDPs, returnees and most vulnerable Host Communities in Mayom, Koch and Panyijiar Counties South Sudan is likely to experience severe food insecurity at peak of the lean season 2023 (May-July), an estimated 8.2 Million people; comprising the refugees, and Abyei (HNO 2023) this is comparable with the situation in food security, and livelihood sectorial Analysis (December 2021), IPC Analysis (March 2022) where the food security needs continue to be large and severe. The food insecurity in Unity State (75%) of the population is likely to face severe acute food insecurity, with the highest levels of severe acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 and worse) at the peak of the lean season 2023. The main drivers to face unprecedented levels of food insecurity. covariate climatic, conflict, and economic shocks (such as floods and dry spells, inflation and rising food prices, and the continued disruption of livelihoods due to conflict and insecurity); and household-level idiosyncratic stressors (such as the death of a breadwinner, gender-based violence, morbidity and mortality due to poor hygiene, and lack of access to essential basic services) which are greatly amplified by the compounded effect of shocks. Food insecurity is greatest when these shocks and stressors are compounded by the persistently high levels of vulnerability and poverty associated with the protracted crisis that has existed since December 2021 and progressively worsened over time reaching peaks in 2022 and it is continuing now in 2023.

This situation will be further exacerbated by the progressive reductions in funding against increasing humanitarian needs in recent years which has forced humanitarian agencies to reduce entitlements and prioritize the most vulnerable households. Given the high levels of severe acute food insecurity in the state, there is a need for an immediate scale-up of multi-sectoral humanitarian assistance to save lives and prevent the total collapse of livelihoods in the affected counties (Mayom, Koch, and Panyijar).  Based on the IPC findings, at least three-quarters of the population in the Mayom, Koch, and Panyijar counties are classified in IPC Phase 3 and above. The severe food insecurity situation pressed for calls for livelihood and food security support through the provision and distribution of Agriculture inputs of (crops seed, vegetable seeds, fishing kits, and agriculture hand tools. The intervention has to be supplemented by support training to target households in agriculture good agronomic practices, good fishing practices, i.e. seedbed and nursery preparation, all best agricultural practices, fishing, and fish postharvest handling, preservation, nutrition, and preservation techniques.  

Furthermore, there should be vaccination of livestock, and training in climate change adaptation. Humane Aid for Community Organization intends to target to support 13,033 Households (78,200 individuals) in Mayom, Koch, and Panyijar Counties/Unity State.

destinationObjects_Project.name: Humanitarian coordination and provision of CCCM-integrated responses to displacement-affected populations in Juba and Bor former PoC sites (semi-static) in hard-to-reach areas (mobile)
reportDetails_organization: European Commission's Humanitarian Aid and Civil Protection Department
project_text:
Humanitarian coordination and provision of CCCM-integrated responses to displacement-affected populations in Juba and Bor former PoC sites (semi-static) in hard-to-reach areas (mobile) According to the South Sudan CCCM Cluster HNO 2022, 1.64 million people are currently IDPs in need of CCCM assistance across South Sudan. After a sudden shock, IDPs often gather in informal displacement sites in extremely precarious conditions, most of the time without access to basic services and information, and with limited decision-making power on issues that affect their daily lives and their future. These gathering places are often characterized by an increased exposure to security risks and protection needs, particularly for the most vulnerable groups. Poor living conditions; lack of financial resources and limited access to basic services can lead to outbreaks of disease, increased prevalence of GBV or domestic violence, and tensions between population groups within the informal camps. Likewise, overcrowding could led to challenges in maintaining safe levels of hygiene and sanitation. Continued political uncertainty, coupled with the increased risks of climate change has also largely resulted in the inability of the international community to return these IDP’s to more suitable locations and an unwillingness from the camps inhabitants to leave. Regarding Bor and Juba former PoC camps, as of February 2022, 2,745 IDPs resided in Bor IDPs Camp, 7,299 in Juba IDPs Camp 1 and 24,255 in Juba IDPs Camp 3. Since the transition from former PoCs sites under UNMISS management to conventional IDPs site under the South Sudanese government responsibility in November 2020, the 2,745 residents of Bor IDPs camp have continued benefitting from essential services provision. The RRC offices of Jonglei at State and County levels have taken up the camp administration responsibility after the transition and are well involved, present and committed in the camp activities. However, the state and county authorities are facing limited resources to fully take over the camp administration responsibility. ACTED will aim at reinforcing the local authorities’ resources and abilities in Jonglei, while continuing to build capacity of camp leadership representatives, leading to the full handover of the Camp management responsibilities to the Community Members Committees and Camp administration role to RRC office in Jonglei by the last quarter of 2022. On the other hand, the 31,554 residents of Juba IDPs Camp 1 and 3 have faced a drastic decrease of essential service provision since the transition from former PoC sites under UNMISS management to conventional IDPs camps under the leadership of the South Sudan Government. Since the transition and re-designation of roles over to the government of South Sudan the RRC office has not yet taken over the responsibility of the camps.
ACTED is aiming to continue to work to design a road map for RRC’s take over and to work closely with Juba IDP camps service providers. ACTED would continue to engage in discussions with key actors and communities impacted to take active role in several fora including the Durable Solutions Working Group. During the semi-static phase, ACTED is planning to provide in-kind support to local authorities, including RRC, that are facing a lack of resources to take over the camp administration role, while enhancing the camp leadership skills. Therefore, ACTED will continue implementing CCCM interventions in line with the following cluster objectives: CO1: Improve living condition of IDPs by facilitating safe, equitable and dignified access to cross-sectoral humanitarian services, including CCCM CO2: Enhance the protective environment, respond to vulnerable population with priority on addressing protection gaps and strengthen the predictability and effectiveness of multi sectorial interventions at site level CO3: Support vulnerable IDPs to recover from the crisis by strengthening community self-management, build resilience to promote solutions for displaced people in sites.

project_text:
Assurer l’offre des soins de santé d’urgence aux populations vulnérables dans les zones enclavées. Le résultat ultime sera d’améliorer la santé des populations, des femmes, des enfants, des jeunes, des hommes, à travers une augmentation de la couverture des services des soins de santé primaires incluant la santé sexuelle et reproductive dans les 6 régions les plus touchées par la crise humanitaire. Ce projet entre en ligne droite avec le plan du cluster santé de 2023 et propose se dérouler sur quatre axes stratégiques : 
•	• Le renforcement de l’offre des soins de santé primaires intégrés d’urgence et de qualité pour les populations déplacées et leurs communautés hôtes qui sera apporté à travers (i) un appui à la réouverture des formations sanitaires par le déploiement de la réserve sanitaire, des médicaments essentiels et matériels médicotechniques, (ii) l’appui en médicaments, matériels médicotechniques et autres intrants aux formations sanitaires fonctionnelles qui assurent l’offre des soins de santé, (iii) la mise en place des postes médicaux avancés dans les zones d’affluence des PDIs, (iv) la mise en place des cliniques mobiles dans les zones d’accès difficiles. Ces dispositifs permettront d’absorber le surplus des besoins en soins de santé primaires des populations dans les 6 régions les plus touchées incluant les personnes handicapées .
•	La facilitation de l’accès aux soins de santé pour les urgences médico-chirurgicales, les soins des survivant-es de violences basées sur le genre par un transfert monétaire dans les six régions d’interventions.
•	Le renforcement du dispositif minimum en situation d’urgence pour l’offre des soins de santé mentale, la santé sexuelle et reproduction et la prise en charge clinique des violences basées sur le genre dans les trois régions d’interventions .
•	Le renforcement des capacités dans la détection et l’alerte précoce, les investigations et la confirmation au laboratoire, l’approvisionnement en intrants et en matériels médicotechniques, l’appui en ressources humaines et le soutien au fonctionnement des équipes de riposte et de coordination des réponses aux épidémies.
•	Le renforcement de la protection du personnel de santé et des agents de santé à base communautaires contre les risques infectieux

destinationObjects_Project.name: Améliorer la sécurité alimentaire et restaurer les moyens de subsistance agro-pastoraux des populations vulnérables hôtes et déplacées dans les régions de Tahoua et Diffa touchées par les crises sécuritaire et climatique
reportDetails_organization: European Commission's Humanitarian Aid and Civil Protection Department
project_text:
Améliorer la sécurité alimentaire et restaurer les moyens de subsistance agro-pastoraux des populations vulnérables hôtes et déplacées dans les régions de Tahoua et Diffa touchées par les crises sécuritaire et climatique L’objectif général du projet est d’améliorer la sécurité alimentaire et de renforcer les moyens d’existence et la résilience des populations déplacées et hôtes, affectées par les crises sécuritaires dans les régions de Tahoua et de Diffa, en fournissant une assistance humanitaire et un support pour le renforcement des moyens d’existence aux communautés les plus touchées par les crises sécuritaires, les déficits pluviométriques et les faibles productions agricoles et pastorales en 2021. 
L’Action répondra aux besoins alimentaires immédiats des ménages vulnérables pendant les périodes critiques (pré soudure et soudure pastorale et agricole) et soutiendra les principaux moyens d’existence des ménages les plus vulnérables. Elle ciblera les localités agro-pastorales et pastorales des départements de Diffa, Nguigmi, dans la région de Diffa, et le département de Tilia, région de Tahoua, les plus affectées par les crises sécuritaires (nombre de déplacés, taux d’insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle) et climatiques (déficit agricoles et pastoraux). Les activités bénéficieront directement à 5 600 ménages (39 200 personnes) déplacés, hôtes, identifiés comme les plus vulnérables selon une approche de ciblage participative (Household Economy Approach) impliquant les communautés, les services techniques, les autorités locales, les partenaires locaux, et les organisations paysannes.

Dans le cadre de cette intervention, le premier axe d'intervention sera la réponse aux besoins urgents de sécurité alimentaire des ménages les plus vulnérables des départements de Diffa, Nguigmi (Diffa) et Tillia (Tahoua) par une assistance alimentaire sous forme de Cash for Work. Les transferts d'argent liquide permettront aux bénéficiaires d'avoir accès à une nourriture de qualité et ainsi de faire face à l'insécurité alimentaire aiguë. En effet, selon tous les acteurs rencontrés (services techniques, autorités locales, partenaires locaux et communautés) lors de l'évaluation interne des interventions FSLH de Diffa réalisée par ACF, le changement le plus significatif apporté par les activités CFW a été l'amélioration de la situation alimentaire des ménages grâce à l'augmentation du nombre de repas (jusqu'à 3 repas par jour), et l'augmentation de la durée des stocks alimentaires des ménages. Au niveau de Tillia, l'évaluation des besoins menée par ACF a montré que le besoin d'assistance alimentaire était l'un des besoins prioritaires cités par les communautés, en particulier parmi les personnes déplacées.
Le deuxième domaine d'intervention consistera à protéger et à renforcer les moyens de subsistance des populations les plus touchées dans les zones ciblées.  Les activités prévues sont basées sur les principaux moyens de subsistance des populations. L'agriculture (32,5% des ménages bénéficiaires), le petit commerce (31,7%) et l'élevage (19,9%) constituent les trois (3) principales activités des bénéficiaires (source : ACF, précédents projets).  Au niveau de Tillia, l'activité principale reste l'élevage et la zone a une vocation pastorale selon la classification du gouvernement du Niger. Ainsi, les activités s'articuleront autour de la restauration et du renforcement du patrimoine pastoral des communautés du département. Afin de renforcer les activités agricoles des bénéficiaires à Diffa, un soutien sera apporté à la culture maraîchère et à l'agriculture pluviale.

Les principales activités qui seront menées à travers ce projet sont: i) les ciblages géographique et celui des ménages; ii) l'assistance alimentaire inconditionnelle en Cash ou en Vivre selon le contexte; iii) la distribution de suppléments alimentaires aux enfants de 6 à 23 mois issus des ménages bénéficiaires; iv) la mise en œuvre d'actions de relèvement au profit des populations bénéficiaires de l'assistance depuis un certain nombre d'années et qui ont des besoins spécifiques pour le relèvement (Reconstitution Sociale du Cheptel, Distribution d'aliments bétails, Distribution de semences, Renforcement de capacités tous azimuts, AGR) etc,
